channel.title: The Annotated Shelf
channel.description: Audio essays on organizations, power, and systems — from the Gervais Principle to the Unaccountability Machine.

item.title: Richard Hamming, You and Your Research: a 1986 lecture's case that important work is a choice, tested against a laboratory that no longer exists
item.description: The Bell Labs talk that asks why so few capable scientists do lasting work, its traits tested one by one against a worked example, then against Hamming's own admission that his sample is entirely winners, and landed on the choice a fellowship director and a study section make together.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Question at the Chemistry Table

A mathematician walks into a chemistry lab at lunchtime and asks to sit down. He has worked with one of the men there before, and the man is courting the department secretary, so it would be awkward to say no. For a week the mathematician just eats and listens. Then he starts asking a question: what are the important problems of your field? He asks it again a few days later, phrased slightly differently: what important problems are you working on? After a week or two of this he asks the version that ends the friendship: if what you are doing is not important, and you don't think it will lead to anything important, why are you at this laboratory working on it? Nobody invites him back to that table.

Five months pass. It is autumn now, and one of the chemists, a man named Dave McCall, stops the mathematician in the hallway. That remark got under his skin, he says. He thought about it all summer. He hasn't changed his research, but the thinking had been worthwhile. The mathematician says thank you and walks on. Within a few years McCall is head of his department. Later he is elected to the National Academy of Engineering. The mathematician never again hears the names of the other men who sat at that table, the ones who found the question rude rather than useful.

The mathematician is Richard Hamming, and on the seventh of March, nineteen eighty-six, he stood in front of roughly two hundred people at Bell Communications Research in Morristown, New Jersey, and told that story as evidence for a claim he had spent forty years assembling: that the gap between a scientist whose work lasts and one whose work is forgotten by the time he retires is not, mostly, a gap in raw ability. Hamming had earned the right to make the claim from the inside. Born in Chicago in nineteen fifteen, he took a doctorate at the University of Illinois, worked the last desperate year of the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos, and then spent thirty years at Bell Labs, where he built the error-correcting codes that let computers catch and fix their own mistakes, work that later won him the Turing Award. His own epitaph, by his own choosing, was a line about method rather than result: the purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.

The talk was called "You and Your Research," and it was never written for publication. Someone in the audience taped it, a colleague transcribed it, and the transcript circulated inside Bell Labs and then well beyond it for decades before Hamming's own book, "The Art of Doing Science and Engineering," gathered it as the closing chapter, reissued by Stripe Press in a lecture-hall edition slim enough to read in one sitting. It is the second stop on this shelf, after last week's tour of Patrick Collison's own web pages, and it answers a narrower version of the question those pages kept circling. Collison asked why some institutions produce more than others. Hamming asked the version one level down: inside any institution, however good, why do so few of the individually capable people in it do work that lasts?

Chapter Two: The Stooge at Los Alamos

Hamming's answer began, by his own account, in envy. He had been brought there to run the computing machines so the physicists could get back to the actual science, and he watched them do it at close range: Richard Feynman, Hans Bethe, who was his boss, Enrico Fermi passing through, Robert Oppenheimer running the whole enterprise. He was, he said plainly, the stooge who kept the machines fed. Physically he was the same species as these men. Something else was different, and he wanted to know what.

That is not a scientist's question so much as a clinician's. Rather than build a theory of genius from first principles, Hamming did what a diagnostician does with a disease of unknown cause: he watched, he asked pointed questions of people who had already done great work, he read biographies and autobiographies hunting for the pattern that recurred across physics, mathematics, and the coding theory that was his own field. He was honest, from the first minute of the talk, about what kind of evidence this was. He was not testing a hypothesis against a control group. He was interviewing survivors and inferring the disease from what they had in common. That method carries its own weakness, and it stays relevant all the way to the end of this hour, because Hamming himself names it once, in passing, and the rest of the talk proceeds as if he hadn't.

Chapter Three: The Prepared Mind

The first objection Hamming anticipated was the easiest one to raise and, he thought, the easiest to answer badly: that great science is simply luck. He didn't deny that luck exists. He denied that it explains the pattern. Consider Einstein, he said: not one good idea but a whole career of them, publishing across radically different problems for decades. Consider Claude Shannon, who did not stop at information theory but had already done substantial work in cryptography before it, work still classified when Hamming gave the talk. A single stroke of luck does not repeat itself decade after decade in the same person. Hamming reached for Louis Pasteur's old formula and made it the spine of the whole lecture: luck favors the prepared mind. The particular discovery may be chance. That a person keeps discovering things is not.

He offered Einstein again as the clean case of preparation without luck. Around the age of twelve or fourteen, long before any physics training, Einstein asked himself what a beam of light would look like if he could travel alongside it at its own speed. Electromagnetic theory said a light wave cannot have a stationary crest. But ride alongside one at the speed of light and a crest would appear to sit still. A boy noticing that contradiction is not the same event as a man resolving it into special relativity thirteen years later, but the first event is a necessary seed for the second, and most people who could pass the same physics exam never noticed the contradiction at all. This is the gap Hamming's whole talk lives in: not who can solve a problem once handed it, but who goes looking for the problem before anyone hands it to them.

Chapter Four: Brains Is Not Enough

Raw intelligence, in Hamming's account, sits closer to a necessary condition than a sufficient one, and he had two colleagues at Bell Labs to prove it. Bill Pfann, who invented zone melting, a purification technique now standard in semiconductor manufacturing, came into Hamming's office with an idea he could barely articulate and equations he couldn't quite finish. Hamming did the mathematics for him and taught him to run the computers himself. Pfann went on, with almost no recognition inside his own department at first, to collect most of the major prizes in the field, and the shyness and inarticulateness fell away once the ideas started landing. A colleague named Clogston arrived with so little apparent promise that Hamming would have let him go; only the department head's patience kept him on. Clogston went on to develop the Clogston cable, after which, in Hamming's phrase, one success brought him confidence, and confidence brought a steady stream of good ideas afterward.

The trait underneath both stories, Hamming argued, was courage: the willingness to trust a half-formed idea long enough to finish it. His clearest example was Shannon's own founding theorem of information theory. Shannon wanted a method for coding messages so they could survive noise. He didn't know how to construct a good code directly, so he asked an almost absurd question instead: what would the average of every possible random code do? He then proved that the average random code was arbitrarily good, which meant at least one actual good code had to exist somewhere in that average. Hamming's verdict on the maneuver was blunt: only a man of complete courage could have dared think that far past what he could prove directly. Courage, on this account, is not a personality trait so much as a willingness to keep working on an idea after the part of your mind that wants a guaranteed answer has already voted no.

Chapter Five: What a Bad Office Can Teach You

Working conditions, Hamming insisted, do not behave the way anyone expects. He pointed to the Cambridge Physical Laboratory, some of whose best physics was done in what amounted to shacks, and then told a story on himself. When he arrived at Bell Labs it was clear he would never get the small army of programmers that the era's absolute-binary machines seemed to demand. He spent a long while resenting the shortfall before turning the question around: if the machines could do practically everything else, why couldn't they be made to write programs themselves? The limitation that looked like a defect pushed him early into what became automatic programming, years ahead of most of the field. A fault, looked at from a different angle, is often the asset in disguise; you are simply never in a position to see that while you're still angry about the fault.

Underneath conditions sat drive, and Hamming's clearest lesson on drive came secondhand, from his department head, Bode. Hamming had discovered that his colleague John Tukey, whose command of the field left him in awe, was in fact slightly younger than he was, and stormed into Bode's office to ask how anyone his own age could know that much. Bode leaned back and told him he would be surprised how much he'd know too, if he worked as many hours as Tukey did. Knowledge and productivity, Bode said, behave like compound interest: two people of near-identical ability, one working ten percent harder than the other, and over years the harder worker's output is not ten percent greater but something closer to double. Hamming took the remark home and, he admitted, neglected some evenings with his wife because of it. Edison had said something cruder about the same fact: genius is ninety-nine percent perspiration and one percent inspiration. Hamming's addition was that the perspiration had to be aimed; plenty of his hardest-working colleagues at Bell Labs had less to show for it than he did, because effort misapplied is still misapplied.

He added one more trait that looks, on the surface, like a contradiction of everything said so far: tolerance for ambiguity. The best scientists believe their own theory enough to keep building on it, and simultaneously distrust it enough to catch the small facts that don't quite fit. Darwin wrote in his own autobiography that he forced himself to record every piece of evidence that seemed to contradict his theory the moment he caught it, because otherwise his mind would let the inconvenient fact slide and remember only the comfortable one. Believe a theory completely and the cracks stop being visible. Doubt it past a certain point before you've built anything, and there is never enough standing yet to show a crack.

Chapter Six: The Attack You Actually Have

This brings the talk back to the chemistry table, and to the definition Hamming built the rest of his argument on. An important problem, in his usage, is not defined by the size of its consequences. Time travel, teleportation, and reversing gravity were, by his own account, never worked on at Bell Labs despite guaranteeing a Nobel Prize and unlimited funding to whoever solved them, because nobody had so much as a plausible first move against any of the three. What makes a problem important is that a person can see a route into it: a reasonable attack, in his phrase, not a reasonable payoff. Most working scientists, he argued, spend nearly all their time on problems they privately believe are neither important now nor likely to lead anywhere important later, because an attack on them is obvious and safe, never mind whether the outcome would matter to anyone.

To force himself off that path, Hamming adopted a private discipline he called Great Thoughts Time: an hour set aside, generally at the end of the week, reserved for nothing but the largest questions in his field, with the smaller safe problems banned from the conversation entirely. One product of those hours was a prediction he made out loud to Bell Labs vice presidents years before it looked plausible: that the ratio of experiments done on a computer to experiments done in the physical laboratory, then roughly one in ten, would flip to nine in ten. He was treated, in his own telling, as the crazy mathematician with no sense of reality. The laboratories the company built anyway, on the assumption he was wrong, stood mostly unused within his own working lifetime. Great Thoughts Time was not daydreaming. It was reserving deliberate hours to ask which of the safe, fundable, obviously attackable problems in front of him were actually pointed somewhere, and which were just comfortable.

Chapter Seven: The Door

The most quoted single observation from the talk is also the one Hamming himself hedges hardest. He noticed, watching colleagues at Bell Labs over years, that the people who kept their office doors closed got more done today and tomorrow than the people who left them open, and were more productive by any short measure you could name. Ten years on, the closed-door workers somehow didn't know which problems in the field were the right ones, and the open-door workers, interrupted constantly, kept picking up the one fragment of information that mattered later. He could not prove which way the causation ran. A closed door might simply be a symptom of a mind that was already closing, rather than the cause of one closing. He said so, in the same breath as the claim, and then moved on without resolving it.

His own best story for what an open door actually buys came from an ordinary morning years earlier at the labs' New York site, though he never told it in this particular talk. A relay computer had run his job unattended for a weekend and caught an error in its own checking circuit, which meant it simply stopped rather than delivering a wrong answer, and when the office reopened Hamming had nothing to show for the lost days. His first reaction was irritation at a machine smart enough to catch its own mistake but too dumb to fix it. His second reaction, the one that mattered, was the same move he made with the automatic-programming shortfall: if the machine can detect the error, why can't it correct it too? Three years of work later, in nineteen fifty, he published the error-correcting codes that made his professional name, the ones a generation of engineering students would come to know simply as Hamming codes. The frustration was private. The reframing of the frustration into a general, attackable problem happened in a building full of colleagues he talked to constantly, not behind a closed door working the specific weekend's specific failure alone.

The productivity writer Cal Newport, reading the talk decades later, offered the complication that anyone trying to apply it today has to sit with. Bell Labs in the nineteen sixties and seventies meant an open door produced, at most, one or two unplanned conversations in a day. The distraction available to anyone with a laptop and a notification badge now runs, in Newport's own words, at a level orders of magnitudes larger than what Hamming was ever weighing against a closed door. The advice to stay interruptible was built for an interruption rate that no longer exists anywhere a person might read this sentence.

Chapter Eight: Selling It, and the Cost of a Bolo Tie

Hamming was unusually direct, for a scientist of his generation, about the fact that doing the work is not the end of the job. Nobody is waiting to rush out and celebrate a result the moment it exists; everyone else is busy with their own work, and a scientist has to write and speak well enough that a reader stops turning pages and lands on his. He described watching colleagues who stayed silent through a hard meeting and then, weeks later, filed a report explaining what should have been done, arriving too late to matter, and he taught himself, at real personal cost, to say the unpopular thing out loud while the decision was still open.

Two stories about personality carried the sharper lesson. Early in his career, dressing in the western clothes he preferred, Hamming noticed he was getting worse service at a rented computing facility than colleagues who looked more conventional. Nobody had ordered it; the secretaries controlling the queue were simply reading him as someone who didn't belong, and adjusting accordingly. He chose to dress the way the room expected rather than the way he preferred, and the service improved immediately. His friend and colleague John Tukey made the opposite choice, dressing however he wanted into important meetings for his whole career, and paid for it every time with a room slower to take him seriously than his actual ability warranted. Hamming's judgment on his friend was not gentle: a genius anyway, who spent decades of needless friction defending a preference that cost him more than it was worth. He drew the line carefully. He was not against asserting yourself. He was against paying a permanent, compounding tax for an assertion nobody actually needed you to make.

The same discipline showed up in how he handled institutions rather than people. A colleague who wanted his office moved back near the library filed the request and got, in return, a demand for a map showing which paths he would take so the company could insure him, followed weeks later by a demand for exactly how his bicycle would be stored and locked. He eventually gave up the fight rather than the job, and went on to become president of Bell Laboratories. Another colleague wrote a testy letter of protest to a professional society about the physical height of a journal's spine relative to the lab's shelving, sent it up for his boss's signature, and never learned whether it was actually mailed. Hamming's own rule for himself was to treat that kind of institutional friction as something to twit occasionally, for the amusement of it, and then drop, because the researchers who let a small grievance escalate into an ongoing war with the system were, without exception, the ones who never produced the work the war was supposedly protecting.

He was equally blunt about the excuses people give themselves for not having done the work in the first place. Look at the history of any real discovery, he said, and you typically find a handful of people who were close enough to have made it and didn't; every one of them has a story ready for why. I had the idea already. I was building the equipment. I would have gotten there eventually. Hamming's advice was to let other people believe whatever excuse gets offered and to refuse the same excuse in private: credit in science goes to whoever actually finished, and the difference between the person who finished and the nine who had the same idea first is rarely talent. It is usually just the finishing.

Chapter Nine: Seven Years, and Whose Vision

A pattern he never mentioned in the prepared part of the talk came out only when the floor opened for questions, and it is harder to defend than anything that came before it. Hamming told the room he thought a researcher should force a real change of field roughly every seven years, on the theory that everyone eventually exhausts a vein of original ideas and starts coasting on technique, marching in a direction that used to be right long after the world has moved. He had done it to himself deliberately: from numerical analysis to hardware to software and on, refusing even to keep reading the literature in a field once he'd decided to leave it, so that nothing could pull him back. Then he turned the same yardstick on a friend. When Claude Shannon left Bell Labs, Hamming told the audience flatly that Shannon's scientific career was over, and when colleagues objected that Shannon was every bit as sharp as before, Hamming's answer was that sharpness was never the question; what mattered was that Shannon had stopped starting over as a beginner in something new, and a mind that stops doing that stops producing, however fast it can still think.

It is a hard verdict to check. Shannon's decades after Bell Labs were, by any conventional measure, quiet: no theorem to rival his nineteen forty-eight paper, though he kept a legendary workshop of gadgets and games that colleagues who visited him never forgot. Whether that counts as ruin, or simply as a man who had done one era-defining thing and preferred, afterward, to build a rocket-powered frisbee, is a judgment about the value of a life's second half that Hamming makes with a confidence the evidence doesn't obviously support. He is scoring Shannon against Hamming's own definition of a scientific career, and awarding a loss, in a single sentence, to a man not in the room to answer for himself.

The same question period supplied a gentler idea, about the choice between doing the work yourself and building the conditions for other people to do it. Hamming once asked his own department head, Bode, why he had left research to run the department instead of staying a working scientist. Bode's answer was that he had a picture of what mathematics at Bell Labs could become, and the picture was larger than anything he could build with his own two hands, so making it real meant becoming the person who decided who worked on what. Hamming's gloss on the exchange was the closest the whole lecture comes to a career map rather than a list of traits: a project one person can finish alone is one you should stay and finish yourself; a project too big for any single set of hands, his own included, only gets built by someone willing to become the person who decides who works on what. Neither choice beats the other in general. The mistake, in his telling, is drifting into either one without ever working out which size of project you're actually holding.

Chapter Ten: The Biased Sample

Near the very end of the talk, answering a question about whether any of this is actually worth the personal cost, Hamming said something that undercuts the entire lecture more than any outside critic has managed to since. He admitted that his survey, if you could call it that, was drawn entirely from people who had already succeeded. He had never gone and asked the scientists who worked with their doors open, believed in important problems, and showed real courage, and still produced nothing lasting, how any of it had felt from the inside. It's a biased sample, he said, and moved straight on to his answer anyway.

He offered that admission about one narrow question, whether greatness is worth the personal cost of pursuing it. It is true of the entire talk. Every story in "You and Your Research" is a story about someone who worked hard, took risks, and won. There is no comparable account of the Bell Labs scientist who kept meticulous Great Thoughts Time, left his door open for thirty years, defined an important problem the way Hamming recommends, and still produced nothing anyone remembers. That scientist almost certainly existed, in numbers, inside the same building, during the same decades. Hamming never interviewed him, because there was no reason to; he wasn't famous enough to be worth the question. A talk built entirely from the survivors cannot tell you which of the survivors' traits actually caused their survival and which merely traveled alongside it, any more than a hospital chart review of patients who recovered can tell you, without a control arm, which of the treatments they happened to receive actually did the work.

The online annotated edition of the transcript, maintained by the writer Gwern Branwen, catches two smaller instances of the same problem inside the talk's own evidence. Hamming's favorite line, attributed to Newton, that others would get his results too if they thought as hard as he did, turns up nowhere in Newton's actual writing and reads, on the annotator's own inspection, nothing like him; it is most likely a line Hamming half-remembered and made Newton's for the sake of the authority. And Hamming's harshest single verdict in the whole lecture, that the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton ruined more good scientists than any institution ever created, judged by what its fellows did before arriving against what they did after, runs into an obvious rival explanation the annotation names directly: the Institute recruited people at the exact moment they were already at the peak of a career, which means a falloff afterward looks less like an institution's failure and more like an ordinary statistical fact about peaks. In two thousand seven, the medical researchers Thomas Erren, Paul Cullen, Michael Erren, and Philip Bourne condensed the talk into ten rules for a journal audience of working scientists, rule nine telling a reader to commit single-mindedly to a problem and rule ten telling the same reader to leave the door open; their own gloss is that the open door serves the commitment, feeding a mind that is already immersed rather than competing with it, which restates Hamming's hedge in tidier language without actually settling which one governs on a given working day.

None of this makes the talk worthless. It makes it something narrower than it presents itself as: not a proof that these traits cause important work, but a rich, honestly-told description of what important work has looked like from the inside, gathered by someone who was there and cared enough to ask. That is still valuable. It is just not evidence in the sense the confident, declarative sentences keep implying it is.

Chapter Eleven: What an R01 Is For

Strip away the parts of the talk that only make sense inside a monopoly-funded industrial laboratory with lifetime employment and no grant cycle, which is most of the working-conditions material and a good deal of the door-open advice besides, and one working tool survives the trip into a modern research career essentially intact: the definition of an important problem as one you have an actual attack on, rather than one whose stakes are simply large.

That distinction does real, specific work for anyone who sits on the other side of a funding decision from where Hamming stood. A study section reading a grant application is not asking whether the disease under study matters; almost every disease that gets proposed against matters enormously to somebody, so stakes alone were never going to be the filter. The section is asking, whether it says so explicitly or not, whether this particular investigator has a plausible route from the money to an answer nobody currently has. The same test applies one level earlier, when a fellowship director decides which of a dozen plausible projects a trainee should spend the two or three protected years of a career-development award chasing. The question to put to a fellow is not which question is biggest. It's which question the fellow, specifically, right now, with the data and collaborators actually available, has a real move against. Hamming kept a working list of ten to twenty such problems for his own field at any given time, revised as attacks appeared or failed, so a list already existed the moment a genuine opening showed up rather than being invented under deadline pressure.

Run down a list of your own open problems and ask honestly of each one whether you actually have a move or are simply carrying it around out of loyalty, and the talk holds up as a diagnostic that has outlived the laboratory it was written in. Treat it instead as license, as permission to read every institutional safeguard as the moral equivalent of the man filing his bicycle-storage paperwork, and it produces the same ego-driven, system-fighting researcher Hamming spent an entire section of his own talk warning against. The lecture supplies both readings and does not, on its own evidence, tell you which one you are giving in to on any particular day.

Hamming's shelf touches the one this feed left last week at exactly this joint. Patrick Collison's own question, still open, was why an institution as large and consequential as the National Institutes of Health has almost no serious literature examining it as an institution making choices, only literature examining the science it funds. Hamming's talk supplies one small piece of the missing account: a description, from inside a very different kind of institution, of what it actually felt like to distinguish a real attack from a comfortable one, written by someone with thirty years and a body of durable work behind the claim. It is not a study of NIH. It is the closest thing available to a first-person account of the exact judgment a study section is trying, mostly without a shared vocabulary, to make on paper.

Go find the list you already keep, the ten or twenty problems in your own field that you privately believe matter and privately suspect you'll never quite get to. Pick the one nearest the top and ask, honestly, whether you have an attack on it or only the reasons everyone already agrees it should have one. If you don't, that's not a failure; it's information about where to spend the next year of reading rather than the next grant cycle of writing.

Next time, the man who built the funding world underneath all of this: Vannevar Bush's "Pieces of the Action," on the wartime office that moved radar, penicillin, and the proximity fuze from idea to battlefield in years rather than decades, and the administrative trick, contracts to universities rather than conscription of scientists, that made the speed possible without a single Bell Labs office door. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Patrick Collison, Fast, Questions and Advice: three web pages that map the mind of a reader before the books he chose to publish
item.description: The first of eight episodes on the Stripe Press shelf opens with its curator's own pages: a list of ambitious things finished quickly, a list of questions nobody has answered, and advice to a younger self, read for what they say fast institutions need, tested against the survivorship the list conceals, and tied back to the question this whole series on organisations has been circling: how anything that cannot die gets replaced.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Day Before Yesterday

On a Thursday evening in July of nineteen forty-one, a brigadier general in the United States Army named Brehon Somervell decided that the War Department needed a single building to house its forty thousand scattered clerks and officers. By that Sunday, initial drawings existed. Ground was broken two months later, on the eleventh of September, with the country still at peace. The building was finished on the fifteenth of January, nineteen forty-three, four hundred and ninety-one days after the first shovel, and it was, on completion, the largest office building in the world. It still is. Somervell, when asked when something was needed, had a standard answer: the day before yesterday.

Now hold the Pentagon beside a bus lane. In two thousand and one, the city of San Francisco proposed a dedicated lane for buses along Van Ness Avenue, a wide, straight, existing street about two miles long. The lane opened in twenty twenty-two, around seven thousand six hundred days later, at a cost of three hundred and forty-six million dollars, which works out to about a hundred and ten thousand dollars per metre of road. A spokesman for the transit agency, asked about the delays, cited an increase in wet weather since the project began. The Alaska Highway, seventeen hundred miles of military road pushed across remote tundra in two hundred and thirty-four days in nineteen forty-two, cost, in the same year's dollars, seven hundred and ninety-three dollars per metre.

Both of those entries sit on a single web page, one above the other, under a one-sentence heading: some examples of people quickly accomplishing ambitious things together. The page is maintained by Patrick Collison, and it closes with a request for more entries, preferably with sources, and then with a question he does not answer. The physical projects on the list, he observes, happened before nineteen seventy to a disproportionate degree. Why?

Chapter Two: The Reader of the Two

Patrick Collison was born in Ireland in nineteen eighty-eight, sold his first company with his younger brother John before he was twenty, and in twenty ten the two of them founded Stripe, which processes payments for a large share of the internet's commerce and is, as I record this, one of the most valuable private companies in the world. That would earn him a business profile. It would not earn him an episode of this show, and it is not why he is here.

He is here because he reads, and because he has done something with his reading that almost no one in his position does. In twenty eighteen Stripe started a publishing imprint, Stripe Press, with a stated purpose of publishing ideas about progress, and over the years since it has issued about twenty titles, each one an editorial bet that a particular book should have found a wider audience the first time around. Several were out of print when he chose them. This series will spend its next seven episodes inside that shelf, and the discipline I am holding myself to is that the shelf is the source: what he chose to publish, and what he has written in his own name, rather than the sprawling list of seven hundred and some books on his personal site that he notes he has not maintained in about a decade. A curated press is a considered statement. A bookshelf page is an attic.

He has also written a little himself, mostly essays with co-authors and mostly about one theme. With the physicist and writer Michael Nielsen he argued, in the Atlantic in twenty eighteen, that science is producing less per dollar and per scientist than it used to, and backed it with a survey asking scientists to rank the importance of Nobel-winning discoveries by decade, which showed the rankings falling. With the economist Tyler Cowen he called, in the same magazine the following year, for a new field they named progress studies, devoted to understanding why some places and periods produce so much more than others. In April of twenty twenty, with Cowen again, he launched Fast Grants, which gave out more than fifty million dollars for COVID research with funding decisions made within forty-eight hours of application, an experiment I will come back to. And he co-founded the Arc Institute, a research organisation that funds scientists rather than projects, on a model this series will meet properly when it reaches Donald Braben. Every one of those is a practical attempt to answer a question on the second of his three pages. That is the order the pages should be read in: what got done fast, what he does not understand, and what he would tell a younger version of himself. Together they are the map of the mind that chose the books.

Chapter Three: The List

The Fast page is best heard as a sequence, because the entries share a rhythm. Dee Hock was given ninety days to launch the BankAmericard, the card that became Visa, starting from nothing. He did it, and signed up more than a hundred thousand customers in the same window. Kelly Johnson and his team at Lockheed designed and delivered the P-eighty Shooting Star, the first jet fighter the Air Force used, in a hundred and forty-three days. On the ninth of August, nineteen sixty-eight, NASA decided that Apollo Eight should go to the moon rather than stay in earth orbit; it launched on the twenty-first of December, a hundred and thirty-four days later. Ken Thompson wrote the first version of Unix in three weeks. Brendan Eich built the first prototype of JavaScript in ten days in May of nineteen ninety-five. The Xerox Alto, the first computer with a graphical interface, got built because Chuck Thacker said a futuristic computer could be done in three months and an executive bet him a case of wine that it could not.

Two of the entries need to be told more slowly. Marinship, the shipyard at Sausalito, began with a telegram from the Maritime Commission received by the Bechtel company on the second of March, nineteen forty-two. The site was chosen the next day. A proposal was presented in Washington on the ninth, and ten minutes into the presentation the commission told Bechtel to build it. Physical construction started on the twenty-eighth of March, a fortnight later than it might have, because forty-two families lived on the point that was to be demolished and were given two weeks to move. The first ship was finished on the fifteenth of September. That is a hundred and ninety-seven days from telegram to launched hull, and the two-week delay for the families is the only human cost the entry records.

The other is the one entry from this decade, and it is the one a clinical trialist will not be able to hear neutrally. The genome of the new coronavirus was published on the tenth of January, twenty twenty. Three days later Moderna had finalised the sequence of its vaccine candidate. The first batch was manufactured on the seventh of February, and on the twenty-fourth, forty-five days after the sequence appeared, it shipped to the National Institutes of Health for a phase one trial. Then, in Collison's phrasing, two hundred and sixty-six days of clinical trials and regulatory coordination followed, until on the sixteenth of November the company announced an efficacy of ninety-four and a half percent. Read the proportions. Designing the thing took three days. Making the first doses took a month. Establishing that it worked and was safe took nine months, and nine months was, by every historical standard, absurdly fast: the previous record for a vaccine from sequence to licence was measured in years. The entry does not editorialise about which of those phases was the bottleneck. It does not need to.

Chapter Four: What Fast Needed

Set the list's entries side by side and a set of conditions falls into view, none of which Collison states and all of which the entries share. Almost every one had a single person who could say yes and did not have to ask anyone else: Somervell, Hock, Johnson, the Maritime Commission administrator who interrupted a presentation at the ten-minute mark. Nearly all of them ran against a deadline that was not negotiable, and the deadline was usually a war. The Pentagon, Marinship, the Alaska Highway, the P-eighty and the Berlin Airlift, in which the Western allies flew two hundred and seventy-seven thousand flights in four hundred and sixty-three days to feed two million people, and built an entire airport at Tegel from first spade to first landing in ninety-two days along the way, are all products of a state at war or on the edge of it. Apollo Eight was a Cold War move made in a year when the Soviets seemed likely to send a man around the moon first. Moderna had a pandemic. Collison makes the wartime point himself on the Questions page with a number that is easy to forget: American involvement in the Second World War lasted three years, eight months and twenty-three days. The whole of it, from Pearl Harbor to the Japanese surrender, fits inside the time it took to complete the Second Avenue subway's environmental review. He sets that against a contemporary comparison from his own city: a sixteen-mile extension of the Bay Area's rail system, costing about two point three billion dollars and taking around seven years, delayed for more than a year because the wrong networking equipment had been installed. A country that built Marinship in six months could not, seventy-five years on, get the right router into a train station in less than twelve.

The third condition is the one that matters for anyone who runs anything, and it is the absence of veto points. The forty-two families at Marinship were given two weeks. Nobody sued. No environmental review was filed, because none existed. No neighbouring agency could demand a design change and decline to pay for it. Collison's own hypotheses section gathers the writers who have tried to date the change: a foreword to Herbert Kaufman's book on red tape claiming the nature of bureaucratic constraint in America shifted in the nineteen sixties; the political scientist James Q. Wilson's textbook contrast between an old system and a new system of American government, with the same decade as the seam; Mancur Olson's argument that stable societies accumulate interest groups the way a hull accumulates barnacles, each with a small claim and a veto; and Francis Fukuyama's word for the endpoint, vetocracy, a government in which so many parties can block a decision that none can make one. The transit writer Alon Levy adds, from the page's own citations, that it is not only construction that slowed but operation: American agencies run their existing systems worse, too. Ed Glaeser, reviewing a history of the fifteen-year fight over rebuilding Ground Zero, supplies the closing number for this whole line of thought. In nineteen thirty-one the Port Authority of New York built the George Washington Bridge, then the longest suspension span on earth, in forty-nine months.

Chapter Five: The List's Missing Column

Now the case against, and the list makes it easy to state because the list is honest about what it is: examples of success. A list of ambitious things finished quickly is, by construction, a list with no failures on it, and the fast failures are what the vetocracy was built to prevent.

Robert Moses built faster than anyone on that page. He put expressways through the Bronx in years rather than decades, and the neighbourhoods he cut in half did not recover for a generation; Robert Caro's account of him is the founding document of the new system Collison's sources describe, and the environmental review, the community meeting and the lawsuit are the direct descendants of what he did to East Tremont. Pruitt-Igoe in St. Louis, thirty-three eleven-storey towers, went up fast in the mid nineteen fifties and came down, on television, in nineteen seventy-two. Thalidomide moved from a German laboratory to the pharmacies of forty-six countries in under four years at the end of that same decade, and the two hundred and sixty-six days of clinical trials that Collison's Moderna entry records exist in their modern form because of what that speed cost. The forty-two families on Pine Point got two weeks. The thing that stands between a modern agency and a two-week eviction is not wet weather.

So the vetocracy is an antibody, and the honest form of Collison's question is the one an immunologist would ask: not how to get rid of the antibody but why it now attacks the host. The process that stops a Moses and the one that adds seven thousand days to a bus lane are the same mechanism at two doses, and the list shows the disease without measuring the dose. The Van Ness lane needed no one evicted, no river crossed, no neighbourhood destroyed. It needed a decision, and the system had distributed the power to say no so widely that a decision was the one thing it could not produce. Dan Davies would recognise the shape from this feed's second episode: an accountability sink, where a bad outcome, twenty-one years for a bus lane, arrives with nobody's name on it because every party that delayed it was exercising a legitimate check. And Scott Alexander's trap from three episodes back is here too. Any single agency that waived its review would carry the blame alone if anything went wrong, so none does, and the sum of everyone's prudence is a city that cannot paint a lane.

Both sides of this exist in miniature in the maternal mental health counselling programme this show's listener runs at a distance in Sierra Leone, whose monitoring I have had a hand in building. When the team needs to change a data form, a new question, a fixed skip pattern, a safety screen, it can be written, tested and on every counsellor's phone across ten districts in a few days, because one small group owns the forms and nobody else has a veto. That is the Fast list in miniature, and it is the reason the programme can respond to what its own data show. The same programme's protocol changes, the ones that touch what is done to a participant rather than what is recorded about her, go through ethics committees in two countries and take months, and nobody involved would have it otherwise, because the antibody exists for a reason. The skill is knowing which of the two you are looking at, and most institutions have stopped being able to tell.

Chapter Six: The Question Underneath the Series

The second page, Questions, is a list of things Collison says he finds interesting and cannot answer, seventeen or so of them, with a note that he has left out the ones about Stripe. The range is the portrait. Why is American economic growth, plotted on a log scale across a hundred and fifty years, so eerily close to a straight line through wars and depressions, and what does that say about whether anything a government does matters in the long run? Is the finding that one-to-one tutoring moves a student two standard deviations up the distribution real, and if so why has nobody built a system around it? What is the successor to the scientific paper, a format designed for the printing press and still, he notes, typeset in software from the nineteen eighties? Why are so many ordinary things, trains, food, public toilets, so much nicer in Switzerland and Japan? Why does a city of under a million people, Stockholm, keep producing globally successful companies? Each is asked in a paragraph, with the best sources he knows linked, and with named responses from other writers appended when they arrive, so the page is less a list than a slow correspondence. Two of the questions are the reason this series is starting where it is. The first is one this feed spent its last two episodes on: why certain things keep getting more expensive. His framing is a set of numbers, health spending up ninefold in real terms since nineteen sixty, school spending per pupil up two to three times, college more than doubled since the mid eighties, and a pointer, for more, to Slate Star Codex. So the bridge from the Alexander episodes to this shelf is one he built himself. The interesting part is the sub-question he adds that Alexander did not: how would you predict, in advance, whether a given sector will get cheaper or dearer over the coming decades? Nobody has a good answer. If someone did, it would be the most useful single tool a health system planner could own.

The second question is the one I think ties this entire feed together, and it is phrased with unusual care. How do you ensure an adequate replacement rate in systems that have no natural way to die? He credits Schumpeter with the observation that capitalism's real problem is not how capital gets allocated among existing structures but how structures get created and destroyed, and notes that systems and institutions inevitably get stale while working very hard to survive. Bankruptcy, he says, takes care of senescent businesses. What does the same job for everything else?

The short book he points to for that question is Herbert Kaufman's "Are Government Organizations Immortal?", published by the Brookings Institution in nineteen seventy-six, and it is the empirical floor under the whole of this show's first thirty episodes. Kaufman took the federal organisations that existed in nineteen twenty-three, a hundred and seventy-five of them, and checked which still existed fifty years later. About eighty-five percent did. Twenty-seven had gone, and in the same half-century two hundred and forty-six new ones had been created, so the population had more than doubled while barely anything left it. He had expected to find immortality was a myth. He found instead that it was very nearly the rule, and that the organisations which did die were mostly small, young, and killed by a specific political enemy rather than by any general process of selection. That is the finding behind Parkinson's growing staff, Peter's incompetent plateau, Jackall's managers who survive by managing blame, and Davies's sinks: none of those pathologies would matter much if the organisations that harboured them were subject to anything resembling a death rate. They are not. So the pathologies compound, and the vetocracy of the Fast page is what a population of immortal organisations looks like from the outside: everyone still here, everyone with a claim, no one with the power to finish anything.

Chapter Seven: The Question He Could Fund

A third question gives the series its later episodes. How, he asks, can we understand the dynamics of progress in science, when the National Institutes of Health spends about thirty-seven billion dollars a year and there are, in his words, essentially no books about the NIH and little investigation of whether the allocation works? Anyone who has spent a career writing grants to that institution will feel the observation land, because it is true. There is a large literature on the science the NIH funds and almost none on the NIH as an institution making choices, and the choices are consequential: which questions get asked, by whom, at what age, for how long, with how much reporting.

The reason he thinks the question is urgent is the argument he and Nielsen made in the Atlantic, and the evidence behind it is stronger than a magazine essay usually carries. They surveyed working physicists, chemists and biologists, asking each to compare pairs of Nobel-winning discoveries from different decades and say which mattered more, and the later decades lost: the discoveries of the nineteen eighties and nineties were rated, by the scientists best placed to judge, as less important than those of the nineteen twenties and thirties, even as the number of scientists and the money spent had grown many times over. A team of economists led by Nicholas Bloom published a more formal version of the same finding in twenty twenty under the title "Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?", showing that across semiconductors, crop yields and medicine, the research effort required to sustain a constant rate of progress has been rising steeply for decades; in the case of the doubling of transistor density, by their estimate, it now takes something like eighteen times as many researchers as it did in the early nineteen seventies. There are serious objections to how both studies measure output, and this series will take them up properly when it reaches the science-as-an-institution run. What matters here is what the finding did to its author. A man who believes that the returns to science are falling, and that nobody is studying why, is a man who will end up publishing Bush and Braben and Waldrop, and funding an institute, and asking whether the paper and the journal are the right containers for knowledge at all. The shelf is downstream of the survey.

Fast Grants was his attempt to run an experiment on that question rather than write about it. In April of twenty twenty, with the usual funding bodies taking months to review pandemic proposals, he and Cowen and a small group of donors set up a fund that promised decisions within forty-eight hours and money within a week, with a one-page application reviewed by working scientists. It disbursed more than fifty million dollars. What interests me is less the grants than the survey the organisers published afterwards. They asked the recipients, established scientists with ordinary federal funding, two questions. Roughly four in five said that if their existing grants could be spent however they judged best, they would change their research programme substantially. Roughly two in three said their work would move faster with fewer constraints on how funds were used. Those are self-reports from people who had just received money from the people asking, so discount them as you would any satisfied customer's testimonial. Even discounted by half, they describe a funding system in which a large share of the funded scientists believe the grant's conditions, not the grant's size, are what slows them. That is Kaufman's immortal organisation seen from inside the grant: a set of constraints that nobody chose, that everyone follows, and that no one has the standing to remove. The Arc Institute, which he co-founded in twenty twenty-one with the biologists Silvana Konermann and Patrick Hsu, is the same experiment run for the long term rather than the emergency: investigators receive multi-year funding for themselves rather than for a specified project, renewable, with no grant applications in between, on the theory that the best people should be chosen once and then left alone. Whether that produces more science per dollar than the NIH's project-by-project review is, at the moment, unknown, and to his credit he says so. The episodes on Bush, Braben and Licklider that follow are all earlier attempts to answer the question of what a funder should do instead, and each was published by the man who asked it.

Chapter Eight: Advice to a Boy

The third page is the shortest and the most revealing about its author. Every so often, Collison writes, someone emails to ask how to change the world, and with the caveat that he has lived only a fraction of one life, here is what he would tell his past self. The advice is addressed to someone between ten and twenty, and much of it is about depth: go deep on things, on several things, and by twenty know the shape of what you enjoy, because that will not change much. Make things, because operating under uncertainty is a different experience from learning. Make friends over the internet with people who are great at what you care about. Find vivid examples of success in your domain and spend time near them. Nobody, he warns the boy, is going to teach you to think for yourself, and a large fraction of what the people around you believe is mistaken, so the correlation between your worldview and theirs should not be too high unless you think you were unusually lucky in your starting conditions. He offers a heuristic for checking: do your friends at school think your path is a bit strange? If not, it may be too normal. Then two observations that carry more than the rest. Status lags by a generation or more, so if you think something is important and older people do not, there is a reasonable chance you are right and they are wrong. And people who did great things very often did them young; they were grey-haired when they became famous, not when they did the work. So, he tells the boy, hurry up.

Then the section for ages twenty to thirty, which reads in full: I don't know yet. I plan to think about this when I'm thirty-five to forty.

Read that page with a clinician's habits and the diagnosis is easy. It is the advice of someone for whom the advice worked, written to someone with the same starting conditions, and it does not know which of its recommendations were causes and which were luck. The Schelling-point paragraph, urging the reader to find a way to San Francisco because that is where the high-openness, energetic, optimistic people gather, is true of a particular fifteen years and a particular industry, and would have been terrible advice to a young Ostrom or a young Perrow. The Fast list's survivorship problem reappears on the Advice page, one level down: a list of what worked, assembled by someone it worked for.

And yet I have come to think the honesty of that blank section redeems the rest. Almost every advice page on the internet is written by someone confident about decades they have not yet understood. This one stops where its author's knowledge stops, and the two observations that survive the survivorship discount, that status lags a generation and that the work gets done young, are ones a fellowship director should carry around. The first says the thing your trainees are excited about and your senior colleagues dismiss is more likely to be the future than the past. The second says that the years in which they could do their best work are the years they are currently spending on the requirements you set them, and that a training system optimised for the safety of the institution is spending the scarcest resource its trainees have.

Chapter Nine: The Dose

The three pages, taken together, prescribe an attitude rather than a method, and the dosage question is how much of the attitude to swallow. In diagnostic doses it is a set of comparisons that anyone running anything should keep in a drawer. The Pentagon and the bus lane. The three days to design a vaccine against the nine months to prove it. Kaufman's eighty-five percent. The four in five funded scientists who would do something different if allowed. Each is a number that tells you where in your own system the days are going, and Collison's habit of asking why, without pretending to know, is the habit this show most wants to import from him. It is also, I should say, a habit that costs him nothing. A man whose company has never needed a grant, a permit or an ethics committee can afford to find the slowness of institutions merely interesting; the people who work inside them find it exhausting, and the difference in temperature is not a flaw in his questions so much as a limit on who gets to ask them that calmly. In identity doses the same attitude becomes the Moses posture, in which every check is red tape and every objector is a veto point and the forty-two families should be grateful for their two weeks. The Fast page does not endorse that reading. Its own hypotheses section is full of people explaining why the checks exist. But a reader who takes the list and skips the question at the bottom will end up there, and a great many readers of that page have.

Chapter Ten: The Thing That Could Be Done by Friday

There is something in your working life that a single person with authority and a deadline could finish in a tenth of the time it currently takes. This week, name it, and then do the harder part: list every party that can currently say no to it, and for each one ask whether its veto is an antibody, protecting someone from a real harm, or a barnacle, a claim that accreted because nothing ever scraped it off. If the list is all barnacles, you have found the bus lane. If any of them is an antibody, you have also found why speed alone is not the whole story, and Collison's question, asked properly, is what you do with the barnacles while keeping the antibody.

Next time, the first book from the shelf: Richard Hamming's "The Art of Doing Science and Engineering," with his nineteen eighty-six Bell Labs lecture "You and Your Research" as its spine, on why most scientists never work on important problems, what the open door costs and buys, and the uncomfortable half of his own argument that the people with the door closed get more done this year. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Scott Alexander, Beware the Man of One Study and The Control Group Is Out of Control: what parapsychology proves about everyone else's evidence
item.description: Two 2014 essays read as one argument: how a literature gets weaponised one paper at a time, why a field studying a phenomenon that almost certainly does not exist still clears the standard bar for proof, and what a trialist owes the next person who reads her paper, tested against the replication crisis that arrived on schedule.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: Ninety Replications

In twenty eleven the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the most cited journal in its field, published a paper by Daryl Bem, a Cornell professor emeritus with four decades of respectable work behind him, reporting nine experiments on more than a thousand undergraduates. The experiments were ordinary social psychology procedures, priming, memory rehearsal, habituation, with one alteration: Bem ran them backwards in time. Students were shown a list of words, tested on their recall, and only afterwards given a subset of the list to practise. Recall was better for the items the students would later rehearse than for those they never saw again. The cause came after the effect. Across the nine experiments the average effect was small, about a fifth of a standard deviation, and eight of the nine were statistically significant at the conventional threshold.

The paper had passed peer review at a top journal. The methods were the field's own, and so were the statistics. And the finding was that undergraduates can feel the future.

Three years later, Bem and colleagues published a meta-analysis of ninety experiments attempting to replicate the effect, from thirty-three laboratories in fourteen countries, involving tens of thousands of participants. The pooled result was significant at a p-value below one in ten billion, with a Bayes factor of several billion to one in favour of precognition, and a funnel plot that showed no obvious sign of publication bias. By every quantitative standard that a medical journal, a nutrition journal or a psychology journal applies to decide whether a finding is real, precognition had been established. Scott Alexander's essay of April twenty fourteen, "The Control Group Is Out of Control," takes that result as its starting point, and the question it asks is not whether Bem is right. It is what it means for everyone else that he can look right.

Chapter Two: The Placebo Science

The essay opens by crediting the frame to a writer named Allan Crossman, who called parapsychology the control group for science. The analogy is exact enough to spell out. In a drug trial, the fact that patients on the drug got better tells you nothing until you know how many patients on a sugar pill also got better, because that second number is the rate of recovery that happens whether or not the drug works. Move up a level. The fact that a research field studying some phenomenon produces positive findings tells you nothing until you know how many positive findings a field would produce studying a phenomenon that does not exist, because that second number is the rate at which the machinery of science, applied by sincere and competent people, generates "evidence" regardless of whether there is anything there.

You could never set that control up on purpose. You would need a phenomenon that certainly does not exist, a community of trained scientists who sincerely believe it does, and several decades of funding to let them study it with the field's standard tools. Nature ran the experiment anyway. Parapsychology is a small but real research community, with journals, conferences, university affiliations and, by the essay's account and by the account of several sceptics who have gone to look, methodological standards that are in some respects better than mainstream psychology's, in part because the sceptics have been arguing with them for decades. Ray Hyman, one of the most persistent critics of the field, co-authored a set of methodological recommendations with the parapsychologist Charles Honorton in nineteen eighty-six, and the field adopted them. So the control condition has been running for a long time, with the safeguards turned up, and the result is that parapsychologists produce significant findings for psychic phenomena at roughly the rate mainstream researchers manage for ordinary ones. Alexander quotes Eliezer Yudkowsky's summary: the standard statistical methods are, on this evidence, "so weak and flawed as to permit a field of study to sustain itself" without a subject.

Chapter Three: The Staring Experiment

The essay's centrepiece is a paper Alexander says sends him into nervous laughter every time he reads it, and once you have heard it you will understand why. There is a classic parapsychology protocol in which a subject sits alone in a room, wired to a skin-conductance monitor, while at random intervals an experimenter in another room stares at them through a video link. The hypothesis is that being stared at raises a person's physiological arousal even with no ordinary channel by which they could know it is happening. Marilyn Schlitz, a believer in psychic phenomena, had run the experiment repeatedly and found the effect. Richard Wiseman, a psychologist and sceptic, had run it just as often and got nothing.

They did what almost nobody in a scientific dispute ever does. They designed a single joint experiment, agreeing on every detail of the apparatus and procedure, and ran it in the same laboratory with the same equipment, alternating who conducted each session. Because everything else was fixed, "conducting" a session meant greeting the participant, reading the instructions, and doing the staring. Schlitz's sessions found the effect. Wiseman's found nothing. Same room, same wires, same script, same randomisation, and the only variable that predicted the result was which of the two authors had shaken the participant's hand. In the discussion section, where authors are supposed to propose explanations for their findings, each of them raised the possibility that the other had tampered with the data.

Alexander's reading is that this is the experiment that ought to be replicated ninety times, because it exposes a category of problem that none of the standard safeguards is built to catch. Randomisation defends against confounding between groups. Blinding keeps the experimenter from knowing which group a subject is in. Preregistration stops the analyst choosing the test after seeing the data. None of them defends against whatever it is that lets one experimenter's presence in the room produce a finding and another's abolish it, and the parapsychologists, who have been living with this for decades, have a name for it, the experimenter effect, and a body of theory about believers emitting the right kind of aura. Other fields have no such excuse and the same problem. Alexander cites the psychotherapy outcome literature, where the most reliable finding across dozens of meta-analyses is that whichever therapy the investigator running the trial happens to favour is the one that works best, with an effect size around half a standard deviation. That is an allegiance effect of the same size as the effect of many treatments themselves, and it appears in a mainstream field that does not believe in auras.

Chapter Four: What Bem Actually Did

Having granted the meta-analysis its numbers, Alexander does the thing this show has come to value him for, which is to go and read the ninety studies. What he found is instructive for anyone who has ever cited a pooled estimate. Most of the ninety were not peer-reviewed. Many were conference presentations, unpublished manuscripts, or student projects that Bem had solicited directly. That is a legitimate way to combat publication bias, since it captures results that no journal would print, but it also means the meta-analysis is only as good as the worst laboratory in it, and nobody outside those laboratories had checked the work. Many were not exact replications either, despite being presented as such; small changes in procedure that a believer would consider immaterial and a sceptic would consider decisive.

So Alexander filtered the list down to the studies that were both exact replications and peer-reviewed. He found seven. Three found sizeable positive effects, two found effects near zero, and two found sizeable negative effects. In the subset a sceptic would trust, then, the distribution looks like what you would expect if the true effect were nothing and the noise were large. Among the seven were three experiments by a team including Wiseman, whose careful attempt to replicate Bem had initially been rejected by the same journal that published the original, on the grounds that it did not publish replications. The journal later reversed the policy under public pressure, which tells you something about the machinery Bem's result had passed through on its way to print.

Alexander's conclusion about Bem is unambiguous: he thinks Bem is wrong. But he refuses the comfortable version of that conclusion. The scrutiny he had to apply to demonstrate that Bem's meta-analysis was not trustworthy, reading every included study, checking review status, checking whether replications were exact, is a standard that, in his estimate, almost no study in any field would survive. A handful of very large medical trials might. The ordinary paper, in the ordinary journal, that the ordinary clinician cites when she changes what she prescribes, would not. Bem is the control condition returning a positive result, and the appropriate response when the placebo arm improves is to distrust the assay, not to congratulate yourself on catching the one false positive you happened to look at closely.

Chapter Five: The Man of One Study

Eight months after the control group essay, in December of the same year, Alexander published a shorter and more practical companion under a title adapted from a warning attributed to Thomas Aquinas, who is supposed to have said he feared the man of one book. Alexander's version swaps the book for a study, and the essay explains why a literature, even an honest one, is a weapon waiting to be picked up.

Suppose a drug is weakly effective against some condition. Over a few years a dozen or two research groups study it, with different designs, different populations, and different degrees of care. Even with no fraud and no incompetence anywhere, the results will scatter. Most studies will find the true small effect. A few, by chance and design variation, will report that the drug works dramatically well. A few will show nothing. One or two will suggest harm. The scatter is not a flaw in the science. It is what sampling variation and heterogeneity of design produce when many people study the same thing, and the more rigorous the field, the narrower the scatter, but it never collapses to a point. Now add the ordinary fact that the studies were not all asking the same question: some tested the drug for acute illness and some for maintenance, some in a mild form of the disease and some in a severe one. Alexander uses valproate in bipolar disorder as his example, a drug that works well for mania, poorly for depression, and differently again for prevention. Pool those into one literature titled "does this drug work" and the scatter widens further, all of it defensible study by study.

Into that literature walks anyone with a case to make. The alternative medicine site does not deny the science. It cites the one study from the harmful tail, by respectable authors at a respectable institution, and says doctors are ignoring it. The pharmaceutical representative at the sponsored lunch brings the one from the dramatic tail. When the doctor says one study proves nothing, the representative produces a second and a third from the same tail, plus a replication, and the doctor, who has not read the literature and has patients to see, nods. Both parties have evidence. Both have several studies. Neither is lying about any individual paper. The only thing missing from each account is the shape of the whole distribution, and the shape is the finding.

Alexander adds a detail about how the stripping happens that anyone who has written a paper will wince at. A trial of that bipolar drug for six-month maintenance in ninety-one patients will be titled something like that, and will trust that the professionals reading it know that maintenance is a different question from acute mania. It will not say, in the title or the abstract, that it makes no claim about acute treatment, because no paper says what it is not about. So the study enters the literature as "Smith and colleagues found the drug ineffective," the scope gone without anyone noticing, and every subsequent citation inherits the amputation. Nobody misquoted anything. The paper's authors simply assumed a reader who would supply the context, and the reader who actually arrived was a partisan looking for a citation.

Chapter Six: The Minimum Wage, and Why It Never Ends

Alexander's worked case is the one literature almost every educated person believes they know: whether raising the wage floor costs jobs. He walks through what an honest reader encounters. The famous Card and Krueger study from nineteen ninety-two, comparing fast food employment across the New Jersey and Pennsylvania border after New Jersey raised its minimum, finding no job loss. The counterclaims that it was statistical malpractice. The authors' rebuttal. Then a generation of larger and more sophisticated studies, some finding no effect, others finding substantial ones. Then the meta-analyses, which ought to settle it, except that there is a meta-analysis of fourteen studies concluding the negative effects are publication bias, another of sixty-four reaching the same verdict, one of fifty-five countries finding effects in most, and a systematic review of about a hundred studies finding strong and consistent job losses. Then the expert surveys: five hundred economists signed a letter saying a rise would be harmful, and six hundred signed one saying it would be beneficial. One survey of leading economists found them agreeing nearly four to one that the benefits outweigh the costs; another, of labour economists, found seventy-three percent expecting job losses.

Alexander then writes the two summaries a partisan would produce from this material, one for each side, and the exercise is uncomfortable to read because both are accurate in every particular and each would convince a smart reader who saw only it. Each cites real studies, real meta-analyses, real letters signed by hundreds of real economists. Each is a list of true things arranged to conceal the existence of the other list. His warning follows from the demonstration. A smart person learns early not to accept an argument from authority. What most have not learned is that a list of dozens of studies, several meta-analyses, hundreds of experts and a survey of the field can also be assembled to prove either side of a contested question, and that this is the form an argument takes when someone wants to convince an educated audience of something.

He does not leave it at radical scepticism, and the tool he reaches for is one a trialist will recognise. Only one side of the minimum wage argument, he observes, had produced a funnel plot, the diagram that puts every study's effect estimate against its precision. The plot is the whole bell curve made visible. It shows the studies clustering around zero, with a longer tail on the job-loss side than the job-gain side, an asymmetry that in any other literature would be read as publication bias, small negative results getting printed while small positive ones went in the drawer. So there is a signal in the noise, and it points somewhat toward the side that says the effect is small. He also concedes, in the next breath, that the eleven studies in the far tail may each be right about the specific industry, wage level and economic moment they studied, the valproate problem again, and that the real answer is almost certainly "it depends" in ways no single number captures.

Chapter Seven: The Crisis Arrived on Schedule

Read in twenty fourteen, both essays sounded like a blogger's provocation. Read now, they look like a forecast that came in early. The year after Bem's paper, three psychologists, Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn, published "False-Positive Psychology," a demonstration that a researcher using only the ordinary, accepted flexibilities of analysis, choosing when to stop collecting data, which of several outcome measures to report, which covariates to include, could produce a significant result for essentially any hypothesis, and they illustrated it by showing, with real data and standard methods, that listening to a particular Beatles song made undergraduates measurably younger. Bem's paper was widely understood as the provocation that made that demonstration urgent. Two years later Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken named the underlying mechanism the garden of forking paths: a researcher does not need to consciously fish for significance, because every dataset presents dozens of reasonable analytic choices, and a researcher who makes those choices after seeing the data walks one path through the garden while the p-value pretends she walked the only one. Nobody has to cheat. The multiplicity is invisible from inside.

Then came the replications. In twenty fifteen the Open Science Collaboration reported an attempt to replicate a hundred published findings from three leading psychology journals; about a third to a half replicated, depending on the criterion, and the effect sizes of those that did were about half the originals. John Ioannidis had published his argument that most published research findings are false a decade earlier, in two thousand five, with a model showing that in fields with small samples, small effects, flexible designs and strong prior beliefs, the majority of significant results would be false positives, and the two thousand tens turned his model into a series of headlines. Medicine had its own version of the funnel plot lesson from the same author in the same year. Ioannidis took forty-nine of the most cited clinical research papers of the previous fifteen years, the ones that had changed practice, and followed each claim forward to see what later, larger studies found. Around one in six of the claims had been flatly contradicted. A similar number had survived, but with an effect much smaller than the famous paper reported. Fewer than half had been replicated at roughly the original size. Those were not obscure studies from the tail of anyone's distribution. They were the dots that got shown to every clinician, and a third of them were in the wrong place. Parapsychology's most useful contribution to science was to hit that wall a few years before everyone else did, on a question where the answer was obvious enough that people looked at the method rather than the finding.

Two episodes ago this shelf spent an hour on the multipolar trap, and the machinery behind the crisis is one. A researcher who preregisters her analysis, reports her null results, and declines to run the seventh subgroup test publishes less than a colleague who does none of those things, and in a field that counts publications, she loses ground to him every year she keeps her standards. A journal that prints replications gives up pages that would have carried novel findings and citations, so for decades almost none did, which is why Wiseman's careful failure to replicate Bem was turned away by the journal that had printed Bem. Nobody in that system needed to be dishonest. Every actor was doing the locally correct thing, and the field as a whole drifted toward a literature that a determined reader could dismantle and a partisan could quote.
