The reforms that have made a difference since, registered reports, journals committed in advance to publish whatever the preregistered study finds, funders requiring data sharing, are all the same move that took the antibiotics off the farms: a change to what the competition rewards, imposed on every competitor at once, so that keeping your standards stops being a way to lose.

Chapter Eight: The Steelman, and the Case Against

Let me give the essays their strongest form before I test them. The claim is not that science does not work. It is that the standard statistical apparatus, a p-value below five percent, a significant meta-analysis, a positive replication or two, is necessary for a finding but nowhere near sufficient, and that a field which treats it as sufficient will fill its journals with results that a determined reader could dismantle and almost nobody ever does. The evidence for that claim is a natural control condition that returned positive, plus a mainstream literature in which allegiance effects rival treatment effects, plus a contested policy question on which two complete and contradictory evidence bases coexist. An admirer of the essays would sign off on that summary, and so would most methodologists writing today.

Now the objections, and they are real. The first concerns Alexander's own reading of the parapsychology literature, which is more selective than the essay's confident tone suggests. He treats Bem's meta-analysis as the field's best shot and dismantles it, but the field's actual flagship is the ganzfeld literature, sensory-deprivation telepathy experiments with a much longer history, and there the story is messier. A meta-analysis by Julie Milton and Wiseman in nineteen ninety-nine found no effect in the post-communiqué studies. A later one by Lance Storm and colleagues in twenty ten, with more studies and different inclusion rules, found one. The sceptics and believers have been arguing about which inclusion rules are correct ever since, in the pattern Alexander's own minimum wage essay describes, and he does not turn that essay's lens on his own choice of which parapsychology to examine. He picked the meta-analysis that happened to be easiest to take apart. The ganzfeld work is harder. Bem himself, with Honorton, had published a meta-analysis of the automated ganzfeld studies in the Psychological Bulletin in nineteen ninety-four, under the post-communiqué protocol the sceptics had helped design, reporting a hit rate well above chance, and Hyman's response, printed alongside it, conceded that the studies were well conducted while withholding belief in the conclusion. That is a more interesting object than Bem's solicited replications, because it is the field's best evidence produced under its critics' own rules, and the essay walks past it. A believer would say that is the man of one study, one level up.

The second objection is about the target. Alexander presents the control group result as an indictment of frequentist statistics, and then in the same essay shows that the Bayesians on both sides of the Bem dispute behaved just as badly: Bem multiplying a ten-to-the-twenty prior by his Bayes factor as if that settled anything, and his critic Erik-Jan Wagenmakers setting a prior so extreme that no conceivable data could move it. The problem was never the choice of statistical framework. It was that every framework takes the data as given, and the data were produced by a process, solicited studies, experimenter effects, undocumented flexibility, that no calculation performed afterwards can see. The essay knows this. Its title says the control group is out of control, not that the t-test is broken. But readers took the wrong lesson away in large numbers, and a decade of methodological reform has spent a great deal of energy on the statistics and rather less on the room in which Schlitz and Wiseman shook hands.

The third is an objection to the tone of the second essay, and it comes from within the same circle. If a smart reader cannot trust a study, a set of studies, a meta-analysis, a systematic review, an expert letter or an expert survey, and is told to distrust any source that promises to summarise the evidence, what is left is a counsel of despair dressed as sophistication. Alexander half-admits this, with a joke about radical scepticism sounding easier than doing the work. His positive advice is thin: lower your confidence on contested questions, and before accepting an overwhelming case, spend five minutes checking whether the other side has one. That is good advice. It is also advice that leaves the reader exactly where she started on the minimum wage, and on most things.

Chapter Nine: What a Trialist Owes

This show is written for someone who runs randomised trials, and these two essays describe the two temptations of that trade from the outside with unusual accuracy. The first temptation is to become the man of one study about your own study. A trial you ran is, to you, the most vivid piece of evidence on its question, because you know its every weakness and every strength and you watched the data arrive. It is also, to the literature, one dot on a funnel plot, and where it sits on that plot is not up to you. The discipline the first essay asks for is to write the paper so that the next reader can place the dot: state which version of the question was asked, in which population, at which dose, for which outcome, so that the study cannot be stripped of its scope and quoted as "Smith found the drug ineffective." Most of what looks like conflict between trials is two trials answering different questions, and the authors, not the readers, are the only people positioned to prevent that confusion, in the title if possible and in the abstract at the least.

The second temptation is the one the control group exposes, and it is harder, because nothing in the design protects against it. Preregistration closes the garden of forking paths for the primary analysis, and clinical trials now treat it as mandatory, which is a reform parapsychology adopted before psychology did, as Alexander notes with some embarrassment on his own field's behalf. But Schlitz and Wiseman preregistered, in effect, a single joint protocol, and the result still depended on who was in the room. In a trial where the intervention is delivered by people, a counselling programme, a feeding programme, a training, the people delivering it believe in it, and their belief travels through every interaction with the participant in ways a protocol cannot fix. The defence is not statistical. It is to build the trial so that the measurement is made by someone who does not know what the participant received and, where possible, does not much care, and to treat any outcome that requires the deliverer's own judgment as a different and weaker kind of evidence. Read a trial of a behavioural intervention in which the therapists rated the outcome, and you should hear Schlitz greeting her participants.

The programme where this bites hardest is the one this show's listener runs, a maternal mental health counselling programme across several districts of Sierra Leone, where lay counsellors deliver a talking therapy and record, on a phone form, how each session went. I have spent a good deal of time inside that programme's data, and the forms are where the two essays stop being theory. Those forms are the programme's nervous system, and they are also, every one of them, an outcome rated by the person who delivered the intervention and believes in it. A counsellor who has sat with a woman for six sessions and watched her improve is Schlitz in that room. She is not lying. She is a sincere experimenter reporting what she saw, and what she saw was shaped by what she hoped to see. So the programme's monitoring is built to carry a second channel that does not run through her: a follow-up call from someone who did not deliver the sessions, a symptom scale administered by a different person weeks later, an occasional recorded session reviewed by someone with no stake in that counsellor's numbers. None of that is a statistical fix. It is the Wiseman half of the joint experiment, built into routine, on the principle the essays argue for without quite stating: the only defence against an experimenter effect is a second experimenter.

Chapter Ten: The Dose

Put both essays through the dosage test and they come out well, with one warning. The diagnostic dose is a habit: when a colleague, a reviewer, a guideline or a grant application presents a study as settling something, ask to see the plot, or ask where on the plot this one sits, or ask what the control condition for this kind of claim would be and whether anyone has run it. That habit costs a few minutes and catches a great deal. The identity dose is the radical scepticism Alexander jokes about and half-endorses, the posture in which no evidence is ever good enough and every literature is a weapon, which happens to be the posture that a person who wants to keep believing something in the face of good evidence finds most convenient. The essays' own author reached a conclusion about Bem. He did the work, read the seven studies, and decided. The point of learning how evidence gets weaponised was never to stop being persuaded by it. It was to be persuaded by the shape of the whole and not by the dot someone handed you.

Chapter Eleven: The Plot You Have Not Seen

Somewhere in your working life there is a claim you repeat with confidence, a drug that works, a programme that fails, an intervention the guideline endorses, and you have never seen the plot. Not the study, the plot: every estimate on the question set against its precision, with the tails visible. This week, pick the claim you lean on hardest and go and look for it. If nobody has drawn it, that is information. If someone has and the scatter is wider than you assumed, you have just learned how much of your confidence was borrowed from whoever chose which dot to show you.

Next time, this shelf starts a new series with a reader rather than a writer: eight episodes built from the books Patrick Collison, the co-founder of Stripe, chose to publish under his own press, beginning with his own three pages, on projects that were finished fast, on questions nobody has answered, and on advice to his younger self, and with the question that connects them to everything this feed has covered so far: how do you get an adequate replacement rate in systems that have no natural way to die? Thanks for listening.

item.title: Scott Alexander, Considerations on Cost Disease: why a hospital bed, a classroom, and a subway tunnel cost ten times what they did, and nobody got the money
item.description: A 2017 essay's accounting of costs that multiplied while wages stood still, the eight suspects it interrogates and clears, the economists who answered it two years later with Baumol's old string quartet, and what the argument looks like from inside an academic medical centre that adds a safeguard every year and has never once removed one.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Fifteen-Hour Week

In June of nineteen thirty, with the Depression eight months old and getting worse, John Maynard Keynes gave a lecture in Madrid called "Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren." He told his audience to ignore the crash. The long trend, he said, was so obviously upward that anyone who could draw a straight line on a graph could see that a century out, their grandchildren would be somewhere between four and eight times richer than they were. And once people were that rich, Keynes reasoned, they would stop working so hard. He predicted a fifteen-hour week. The real problem of the twenty-first century, he thought, would be boredom: what to do with a life that no longer needed to be spent earning a living.

He got the arithmetic right. Output per person in the rich countries is now roughly four to five times what it was when he spoke. Almost nobody works fifteen hours a week. In the United States, a large and inconsistently measured fraction of households report living from one paycheck to the next, and the sectors that a middle-class family cannot avoid buying from, medicine, schooling, a house near a decent school, have grown expensive at a pace that eats most of the raise Keynes promised. Part of the gap between his prediction and the present is inequality: the gains went disproportionately to people who already had plenty. That part gets talked about constantly. Scott Alexander's essay of February two thousand seventeen is about the other part, the one that draws far less attention because nobody has a satisfying story for it. Even where wages did rise, the price of the things a person most needs rose faster, and the people providing those things did not get the money either.

Chapter Two: The Numbers That Started It

Alexander opens with a graph and works outward from it, and the graphs are the reason the essay travelled as far as it did. Spending per pupil in American public schools, adjusted for inflation, roughly two and a half times what it was in nineteen seventy. The national reading and mathematics test scores for seventeen-year-olds over the same period: flat. Not down, which would at least be a story, but flat, within a couple of points across four decades. College: around two thousand dollars a year in nineteen eighty, in today's money, and around twenty thousand now, a tenfold increase, while nobody serious claims a modern undergraduate learns ten times as much. Health care: about five times the nineteen seventy figure, and closer to eightfold since nineteen sixty. Alexander converts that into a unit a listener can feel. In nineteen sixty the average worker paid for a year of health insurance with about ten days of wages. That same worker's counterpart today pays for it with about sixty days, one sixth of everything they earn.

Then infrastructure, where the comparison stops being a matter of interpretation. The first New York subway opened around nineteen hundred at a cost that works out, in current dollars, to something like a hundred million per kilometre, a figure Alexander flags as rough. The Second Avenue line opening the year he wrote cost about two point two billion for the same distance. Paris, Berlin and Copenhagen were building subway at around two hundred and fifty million per kilometre, a tenth of New York's figure. Seoul was digging for forty million. Same tunnels, same trains, same century, a fifty-fold difference in the bill depending on which rich democracy happens to be holding the shovel.

Stay with the subway case, because it is the one where every explanation on offer can be tested against a control. Korean tunnellers are skilled workers in a rich economy, so Baumol's tide reaches Seoul as surely as it reaches Manhattan, and yet Seoul builds for a fiftieth of the price. The most careful attempt to explain the gap is the Transit Costs Project, a team at New York University led by the transit writer Alon Levy that spent several years comparing dozens of projects across countries and reported in twenty twenty-three. Their findings do not flatter any single camp. New York's stations were built two to three times larger than they needed to be, with full-length mezzanines nobody uses. The public agencies had hollowed out their own engineering staff and hired consultants to manage other consultants, at a premium and with nobody in-house able to tell when a bid was padded. Utilities and neighbouring agencies could each demand changes and delays without paying for them. Labour costs were higher, but not fifty times higher. Nothing in that list is a law of economics. All of it is the accumulated habit of institutions that stopped being able to say no, and I will come back to that pattern once the rest of the essay's suspects have been heard.

The essay's opening move, the one that turns a complaint into a puzzle, comes next. If medicine costs eight times more, somebody must be receiving that money. So Alexander goes looking for the recipient, and cannot find one. Teacher salaries, adjusted for inflation, are flat over the period, and have lost ground against other occupations. Professors' pay is up slightly per professor, while the average across all faculty has fallen because colleges have replaced tenured staff with adjuncts earning what a barista earns. Nurses went from about fifty-five thousand to about sixty-three thousand between nineteen eighty-eight and twenty thirteen, roughly the general wage trend, with the added detail that the share of nurses holding a degree doubled over the same stretch, so the profession was paying about the same for a more credentialed worker. Doctors: stable, with a growing fraction of that stable salary going to service medical school debt that has itself been multiplying. His summary, in his own words, is that health care and education costs "increase by ten times without a single cent of the gains going to teachers, doctors, or nurses." The money went somewhere. It did not go to the people doing the work.

Chapter Three: The Author's Own Kitchen Table

Last episode introduced the man properly: Scott Alexander, the pen name of Scott Siskind, a psychiatrist writing from the Bay Area, whose blog Slate Star Codex ran from twenty thirteen until he deleted it in twenty twenty and relaunched under his real name. What matters for this essay is a detail he adds himself. His father is a doctor. His mother is a teacher. He trained in medicine and practises it. The two sectors whose costs he is trying to explain are the two his family has spent its working life inside, and he reports what the essay's numbers cannot: that the people in those jobs are miserable, that his own medical school professors told him to his face they could not understand why anyone would still choose the profession, and that the rising price of the service arrived alongside a falling quality of working life for the people delivering it. That is the opposite of what you would expect if the extra money had bought either better care or happier carers. It bought neither. The essay is, underneath the graphs, a son trying to work out where his parents' raises went.

Chapter Four: The Orchestra

The one established theory of this problem is more than fifty years old and belongs to the economist William Baumol, who published it with William Bowen in nineteen sixty-six in a study of the performing arts and formalised it in a paper the year after. Baumol's example has been repeated so often it has become the theory's name in casual use: the string quartet. A Beethoven quartet written in the eighteen twenties needs four players and about forty minutes. It needed the same quartet and the same forty minutes in eighteen twenty-six, and no advance since has shaved a second off it. Two centuries of astonishing productivity growth in farming, manufacturing and transport have done nothing whatsoever for the productivity of playing chamber music. But the musicians live in the same economy as the factory workers. If wages in the productive sectors rise, and the orchestra does not raise its own wages to match, the would-be violinist becomes an engineer instead. So the orchestra has to pay more for the same forty minutes, year after year, without producing one extra minute of music. The price of the quartet rises relative to everything else. That relative rise is the "cost disease," and Baumol spent the rest of his career, up to a book of that title in twenty twelve, arguing that health care and education are the modern economy's string quartets: sectors where the product is a skilled person's time, and that hour cannot be made cheaper the way a car or a phone can.

Alexander knows the theory and states it fairly. Then he raises what seems like a fatal objection. Baumol's mechanism runs through wages. The orchestra has to pay musicians more. Health care and education should therefore be paying their workers more. They are not. Teachers, nurses and doctors have received, in real terms, roughly nothing. So, Alexander concludes, whatever is driving the increase, it cannot be Baumol, because Baumol's mechanism predicts a rise in the one quantity that stayed flat. Hold that objection in mind, because two years later it turned out to rest on a misreading, and the misreading is more instructive than the essay.

Chapter Five: Eight Suspects

With the standard theory set aside, Alexander does what a clinician does with a patient whose diagnosis will not come: he runs the differential. Eight candidate explanations, each tested against the numbers and most of them cleared.

Could the inflation adjustment simply be wrong, so that these things have not really become more expensive at all? He thinks not, because you can still buy the nineteen seventy version. Small religious and private schools educate children at a fraction of the public per-pupil cost, and a cash-only surgery centre in Oklahoma City posts prices a fraction of what a hospital bills for the same operation. The old price still exists. It has simply become impossible to buy at scale.

Run the Oklahoma case to its end and you can see what that price looks like when somebody insists on it. The Surgery Center of Oklahoma, run by an anaesthesiologist named Keith Smith, began posting all-inclusive prices on its website in two thousand nine: one number for a procedure, covering the surgeon, the anaesthetist and the facility, payable in advance, with no insurance billed. The numbers were routinely a fraction of what a hospital across town would bill an insurer for the same operation, sometimes a fifth. Self-paying patients started flying in from other states, and later from Canada. What the centre had removed was not surgical skill, which it pays for at market rates, and not safety, which its outcomes do not suggest it skimped on. It had removed the billing department, the negotiated discount off an inflated list price, the cross-subsidy, and most of the compliance apparatus that a hospital taking public insurance must carry. That is the essay's point in a single building: the nineteen seventy price is still achievable in twenty seventeen, and the gap between it and the hospital's price is made of things that are not medicine.

Is it a market failure, a case of buyers who cannot judge quality and so pay for prestige and amenities instead? Partly, he grants: colleges add climbing walls and speaker series that no student asked for and every student ends up paying for. But market failure predicts that government provision should be cheaper, or the private kind should, depending on your politics, and neither holds. For-profit hospitals are not cheaper than nonprofit ones. Private schools that charge public-school prices are rare. The public and private versions of the same service have inflated together, which is a strange result for any theory that blames one side of that line.

Is it regulation? This is the libertarian's answer, and Alexander gives it a hearing and finds it wanting on one test in particular. The United States went through two well-advertised deregulatory periods, under Reagan and then under the Gingrich Congress, and the cost curves of medicine and education do not bend at either one. Regulation almost certainly contributes, he says. It does not explain the shape.

Chapter Six: The Consult Nobody Ordered

The suspect Alexander knows from the inside is the fear of being sued, and here the essay stops quoting graphs and starts describing his own hospital. A man is admitted after a heart attack. During the admission someone records that he seems low in mood. From that moment a machine engages that no individual would design and no individual can stop. The patient gets a psychiatric consultation to assess for depression, whether or not anyone thinks he is depressed, because a patient who was noted to be sad and then, weeks later, harmed himself would generate a lawsuit whose central exhibit is that note with no consult attached. The consult generates its own documentation, its own follow-up, and its own bill. Everyone involved records the whole sequence as a well-justified clinical decision, because it is, in the sense that every step of it is defensible, and nowhere in the chart does the word "lawsuit" appear. Alexander's line about it is that people outside medicine have no idea how much of medicine is built on this principle. The surveys that ask doctors whether they practise defensively and report reassuring numbers are, in his experience, simply wrong, and every doctor he knows says so.

He then makes the distinction that travels furthest beyond the essay, and he makes it with a hip. Elderly people fall. An old man getting up in the night to use the bathroom is at some real risk of breaking a hip, and the old men Alexander knows accept that risk daily. They do not spend thousands fall-proofing the six metres from bed to toilet, or hire someone to watch them sleep. That is a revealed preference: at home, a person weighs the small chance of a fall against the cost and indignity of preventing it, and mostly chooses to live with the chance. A hospital cannot make that trade. A hospital where an elderly patient falls faces a lawsuit, an incident report, a reportable quality metric, and a story in the local paper. So the hospital puts rails on the bed, an alarm on the mattress that sounds if the patient tries to stand without permission, and a paid assistant whose job is to walk beside him to the bathroom. The individual's risk tolerance and the institution's risk tolerance are different numbers, and as more of life is delivered through institutions, the institution's number governs, whether or not any actual person's preferences have changed. The cost of care rises without anyone deciding that care should be safer. It rises because the entity paying for the safety is not the entity that would have chosen how much of it to buy.

The last two suspects get shorter shrift. Cross-subsidy is real: the uninsured patient's emergency admission is paid for by markups on the insured patient's bill, and the scholarship student's tuition is paid by the full-fare student's. Pensions and benefits might be absorbing money that salaries do not show, though he doubts they are growing fast enough to account for much. And then he stops, and writes the sentence the essay is remembered for. "What's happening? I don't know and I find it really scary."

Chapter Seven: Every Safeguard Has a Birthday

The listener this show is written for works in an academic medical centre, and Alexander's hip will be the least surprising thing in the essay to anyone who does. Widen it, because the mechanism he describes for one patient's bathroom trip runs at the scale of the whole building, and seeing it at that scale explains something his eight suspects could not quite reach: why the cost only ever moves in one direction.

Every safeguard in a hospital has a birthday. Somewhere in the institution's past there was an event, a fall, a wrong-site surgery, a missed lab result, a medication given to the wrong patient, and after that event a committee met, and the committee added a step. A second signature. A checklist. A mandatory screening question. A required consult. A new form in the record that cannot be closed until it is completed. Each step was added by reasonable people responding to a real harm, and each step, on its own, costs a few minutes of a skilled person's time per patient. Those minutes multiplied across every patient, every day, forever, are a salary. Multiply the steps across forty years of committees and you have a building full of salaries attached to no visible service, and a nurse who spends, by the better time-and-motion studies, more of her shift documenting care than delivering it.

Take the bed alarm from Alexander's own example and follow it further than he did. In twenty twelve a team led by Ronald Shorr published, in the Annals of Internal Medicine, a cluster-randomised trial across sixteen nursing units of a Tennessee hospital: units were assigned either to an intensive programme of bed-alarm use or to usual care, and the trial counted falls. The alarms went off, the staff responded, and patients on the alarm units fell at the same rate as patients on the units without them. The most widespread technological safeguard against the most litigated hospital harm was tested properly, once, and did nothing measurable. I do not know a hospital that removed its bed alarms in response. I am not sure I know one that could. The alarm's real function was never mainly to prevent the fall. It was to demonstrate, after the fall, that the institution had done what institutions do, and a safeguard that exists to be pointed at in a deposition is immune to evidence that it does not work.

Here is the part that turns a cost into a disease. Nobody can take a step away. The person who proposes removing the mandatory screening question is proposing to put their own name on the next bad outcome the question might have caught. Robert Jackall's managers, four episodes into this feed's run, protected themselves by making sure blame flowed away from them, and a hospital committee runs on the same hydraulics: adding a safeguard moves blame away from you, removing one moves it toward you, and a system in which every actor's incentive points the same direction moves that direction and no other. Dan Davies would recognise the shape too. The committee that added the step is not accountable for its cumulative cost, because the cumulative cost lands on the budget as a whole and on the patient's bill, both of which are accountability sinks in his sense, places where a consequence arrives with nobody's name on it. And the trap from last episode is here as well, at its most literal. A hospital that unilaterally strips its safeguards back to nineteen seventy levels would be cheaper, and would lose: in court, in the published safety ratings, in the newspaper the week its first preventable fall made the front page. Every hospital that keeps the safeguards keeps them partly because every other hospital does. That is a multipolar trap with malpractice law as the referee, and a ratchet is what a trap looks like when you graph it over time.

Chapter Eight: The Economists Answer

Alexander's essay was widely read, and in twenty nineteen two economists at George Mason University, Alex Tabarrok and Eric Helland, published a short book whose title comes from a New York gubernatorial candidate's slogan: "Why Are the Prices So Damn High?" It is, in large part, a reply to the essay, and its answer is that Alexander's fatal objection to Baumol was a misunderstanding of Baumol.

The string quartet, properly understood, was never about musicians getting raises. It is about the opportunity cost of skilled labour. What a hospital pays a nurse is set by what that nurse could earn doing something else, and what a school pays a teacher is set by what a graduate with those qualifications could earn elsewhere. As the productive sectors of the economy got richer, the alternative career available to the kind of person who becomes a nurse or a teacher got more lucrative, and the labour-intensive sectors had to keep pace with that alternative just to hold their staff. Whether teachers' pay rose relative to a factory worker's is the wrong comparison. The right comparison is between what the sector pays and what its workers could get across the street, and when Tabarrok and Helland run that comparison, the flat-wage objection dissolves. Their evidence for the mechanism is that it fits the shape of the data in ways the other suspects do not. The cost rises are consistent across every labour-intensive service, not just the regulated or litigated ones, which is what you would expect from a secular force and not from a policy. The fastest rises came in the nineteen sixties and seventies, when productivity growth in the rest of the economy was fastest, which is what Baumol predicts and what a regulation story cannot explain. And when they compare industries directly, the ones with the slowest productivity growth are the ones with the steepest price increases. They also test the administrator theory directly and find that administrative spending in colleges has held at about sixteen percent of the total since nineteen eighty, so bloat, whatever else it is, is not a growing share.

Alexander reviewed the book in June of twenty nineteen and did something writers rarely do in public: he conceded most of it. "I find their case pretty convincing," he wrote, and offered to share credit with anyone who could clear his remaining doubts. The doubts are a trialist's doubts, and they go like this. Real wages for factory workers have been close to flat for decades, so if the productive sector's wages are supposed to be dragging service wages upward, what exactly is doing the dragging? Teacher pay is up about six percent since nineteen seventy while spending per pupil has doubled, so even granting the opportunity-cost reading, the pay rise accounts for a small slice of the cost rise. And the one with the most bite: Baumol's disease, by its own logic, should not make anything less affordable. If the whole economy is getting richer and the quartet is merely getting expensive relative to cars, you can still buy the quartet. Yet a year of college took about five months of a median worker's wages in nineteen seventy-one and about fourteen months by twenty sixteen. Something made college harder to buy in absolute terms, and the string quartet does not do that.

Chapter Nine: The Other Camps

The Baumol reading did not win the field. Bryan Caplan, an economist at the same university as Tabarrok, replied the same day the review appeared with an argument about causation that a clinician should find familiar. Tabarrok and Helland had cleared regulation and government spending partly on the grounds that they had not changed much over the period. Caplan's point is that a constant can cause a change. A licensing rule that has been in place for fifty years still blocks the cheaper substitute that would otherwise have appeared in year thirty, the nurse practitioner doing what a physician does, the teacher without the master's degree, the immigrant worker not admitted. The rule did not have to tighten to raise the price. It only had to keep standing while the alternatives it forbids became more valuable. Caplan's own estimate was blunt: Baumol matters, but he doubted it "causes even half the price rise."

Caplan's point gets some support from a programme built on its inverse, the one this show keeps returning to. The maternal mental health counselling programme its listener runs across several districts of Sierra Leone delivers a talking therapy through lay counsellors, women from the communities they serve, trained for weeks rather than years, supervised in tiers by a small central team. The design is a deliberate answer to a Baumol problem: there are not enough psychiatrists or psychologists in the country to see even a fraction of the women who need help, and a skilled clinician's hour would cost more than the whole programme could bear. So the programme buys a cheaper hour and spends heavily on training and supervision to make that hour good enough. That is Caplan's blocked substitute, unblocked. It works, the trial evidence for this model of care is now substantial, and it is also the only reason the arithmetic closes. What it shows about the American version of the disease is that the substitute was always available. What stands between an American hospital and a cheaper skilled hour is not a shortage of people capable of it. It is the licence, the liability, and the committee, none of which Baumol put there.

The administrator camp has its own numbers and they are not small. Two Harvard physicians, Steffie Woolhandler and David Himmelstein, estimated in the New England Journal of Medicine in two thousand three that administration consumed about thirty-one percent of United States health spending, against about seventeen percent in Canada, and the gap has not narrowed since. That is a different quantity from Tabarrok and Helland's college figure, and it points at something the string quartet cannot see: the United States pays for a billing and insurance apparatus that a single-payer system does not need, and that apparatus employs people whose salaries appear nowhere in the "nurse, teacher, doctor" comparison the essay ran. When Alexander could not find who got the money, part of the answer was sitting in the claims-processing department.

So three things need separating, as they always do when a question has stayed open this long. What Alexander claims is that none of the standard explanations fits and the honest position is confusion. What the evidence, as it has developed since, supports is that Baumol accounts for a large share of the slope, plausibly the majority in education and a substantial minority in American medicine, and that the residual is real, is concentrated in the United States, and is made of administrative overhead, blocked substitutes, and institutional risk aversion of the kind his hip example describes. And what I conclude is that the essay was right to refuse the single-cause story and wrong about which cause to throw out first. Baumol is the tide. The ratchet is what has been built on the shore while the tide was coming in, and the ratchet, unlike the tide, is something a person could in principle do something about.

Chapter Ten: What the Money Would Have Bought

Alexander closes the section before his Keynes coda with an accounting I have not been able to shake since I first read it. If some government programme found a way to provide poor families with health insurance for a few hundred dollars a year, college for about a thousand, and housing at two-thirds of the current price, it would be, he says, the largest anti-poverty achievement in history. That programme already exists, in principle. It is called things costing what they cost a few decades ago. Every dollar of cost disease is a dollar that could have been the fifteen-hour week, or the raise Keynes promised, or a counsellor's salary in a programme that cannot afford one, and it has instead gone to the consult nobody ordered, the alarm on the mattress, and the person whose job is to code the claim for the alarm.

The dosage test this feed applies to every framework applies here with a twist, because this one is not cynical. The diagnostic use of cost disease is to ask, of any price you are asked to pay for a skilled person's time, how much of it is the tide and how much is the ratchet, since only one of those responds to effort. The poisonous use is the one Alexander's own "I don't know" was written to prevent: picking whichever suspect your politics prefers, administrators or regulators or lawyers or markets, and declaring the case closed. Every camp in this argument has a graph. Half of them are wrong about which graph matters, and what the essay leaves behind is the example of its author, who had every professional reason to blame the lawyers, declined to do it until the evidence arrived, and then changed his mind in public when it did.

Chapter Eleven: The Step With No Birthday Anyone Remembers

Somewhere in the institution you work in, there is a step that everyone performs and nobody can date. A form, a signature, a mandatory question, a required review. Find it this week, and ask two things of it: what event it was born from, and what it would cost you personally to propose removing it. If nobody can answer the first, and the answer to the second is "my name on the next bad outcome," you have found the ratchet in its native habitat, and with it the one kind of cost disease that Baumol's tide did not cause and cannot excuse.

Next time, this shelf finishes its run with the same writer on the subject closest to its listener's own work: a pair of essays from twenty fourteen, "Beware the Man of One Study" and "The Control Group Is Out of Control," about how a literature gets weaponised one paper at a time, and what it means for every other science that parapsychology, studying a phenomenon most of us are sure does not exist, produces significant results at about the rate everyone else does. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Scott Alexander, Meditations on Moloch: the coordination-failure engine that explains why nobody in a bad system is the villain
item.description: A 2014 essay's argument that arms races, races to the bottom, and rigged markets share one mechanism with no operator, tested against the antibiotics that took sixty years to get off American farms, and against the charge that the whole picture conveniently erases who profits from letting it run.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Farms That Couldn't Stop

In the early nineteen fifties, farmers feeding their livestock a low, constant dose of antibiotics discovered something nobody had gone looking for: the animals grew faster on less feed. Nobody could fully explain why. It didn't matter why. A farmer who fed his herd the drug got fatter animals to market sooner than a neighbor who didn't, and a market that pays by the pound doesn't ask a rancher to explain his biochemistry before it pays him. Within a decade the practice had spread across the American livestock industry. No single farmer had to think it was wise. A farmer who refused to do it was simply competing, at a real and measurable disadvantage, against every farmer who did.

By two thousand fourteen the United States Food and Drug Administration was reporting that livestock accounted for roughly eighty percent of all antibiotics sold in the country, some seventeen thousand tons a year, most of it going into healthy animals that had nothing wrong with them, purely to make them grow. Doctors and public health researchers had been warning since at least the nineteen seventies that dosing an entire national herd with low, constant antibiotic exposure was close to the best possible design for breeding resistant bacteria: a slow drip that kills the weak strains and hands the survivors, the ones already carrying resistance genes, the run of an empty field. The warning was not obscure. The British government's own advisory committee said as much in nineteen sixty-nine. And still the practice ran for another forty-eight years before a federal rule, Guidance for Industry number two thirteen, finally took the medically important drugs off the growth-promotion market on the first of January, twenty seventeen, and sales for that specific purpose fell, in a single year, from five point seven million kilograms to zero.

Ask why it took that long and the answer has nothing to do with any single person along the chain being careless or corrupt. A veterinarian who told a client to stop dosing his herd was giving him correct advice that would cost him money the day he took it, before any collective benefit to the human species could possibly reach him. A regulator who moved too fast risked a rule nobody in the industry would treat as anything but an attack on their livelihood, from ranchers who had done nothing differently from every rancher around them going back three generations. Everyone downstream was borrowing against a shared resource, the future usefulness of penicillin and its descendants, and no single farmer's restraint could have protected that resource on its own, since the bacteria on the next farm over don't respect a property line. This is the shape of problem Scott Alexander spent an essay in the summer of twenty fourteen trying to name properly, and the name he settled on was older than agriculture itself.

Chapter Two: The Vision on Nob Hill

On the night of October the seventeenth, nineteen fifty-four, a twenty-eight-year-old poet named Allen Ginsberg was in his girlfriend's apartment on San Francisco's Nob Hill, working through a peyote high, when he looked out the window and saw the Sir Francis Drake Hotel a few blocks away transform, in the fog, into a lit, skull-faced monster staring back at him. He rushed downstairs into a cafeteria and started writing. What came out of that night became the second section of "Howl," the poem that would make his name the following year and put his publisher on trial for obscenity the year after that. In it he gave the monster a name pulled from the Hebrew Bible: Moloch, the god to whom the ancient Canaanites were said to sacrifice their own children by fire, in exchange for victory in war or a good harvest. Ginsberg's Moloch became a stand-in for everything about mid-century American civilization he thought was devouring its young: the arms race, the asylum, the factory, the bank.

Scott Alexander's essay takes Ginsberg's monster and gives it a job description rather than a mood. "He is the god of child sacrifice," Alexander writes, and goes on to describe him as the furnace a person feeds their own children into for the promise of winning a war. Read the sentence as biography and it's a description of a bronze age cult. Read it as economics and it describes something considerably more contemporary: any system in which the actors competing inside it can improve their odds by discarding something they'd rather keep, and where any actor who declines to discard it simply loses the competition to one who will. Nobody worships this god on purpose. Everybody feeds him anyway, because the alternative to feeding him is losing, and losing is the one outcome the system actually punishes.

Chapter Three: The Man Who Already Owed You a Paragraph

The essay's author writes under the name Scott Alexander, itself a near-anagram of the blog he wrote it for, Slate Star Codex, and for most of the blog's life that pseudonym was doing real work: the man behind it, Scott Siskind, is a psychiatrist practicing in the San Francisco Bay Area, and he kept his clinical name off a blog that discussed, among a great many other things, drugs, sex, and his own patients' cases in generalized form. He started writing in twenty thirteen, built an audience in the low hundreds of thousands mostly through word of mouth among programmers, academics, and doctors, and became one of the few bloggers of his generation whose individual essays functioned as shared reference points the way a well-known book does, cited by strangers who had never read anything else he'd written. In June of two thousand twenty, told that a New York Times reporter intended to publish his legal name against his wishes, he deleted the entire blog rather than let the story land as anything but his own decision, then relaunched seven months later under his own name on a new platform, Astral Codex Ten, once the choice to be identified had become his rather than a newspaper's.

This show has actually already quoted him once, seventeen episodes ago, without properly introducing him: Scott Alexander wrote a widely read review of James Scott's "Seeing Like a State," and that review supplied one strand of the case against high modernism this feed built into its own account of that book. He earns a full episode now for the same reason a magazine profile eventually earns its subject a cover: enough of what he's written has kept turning up in enough other people's arguments, years after publication, that treating him only as a source for somebody else's case has started to undersell him.

Chapter Four: The Trap, Defined

Strip the essay's examples away and the underlying shape is almost insultingly simple. Take any competition that rewards one measurable outcome, whether it's speed to market, military strength, or a fatter cow. Somewhere inside that competition sits an opportunity to trade away some other value, one the competition doesn't measure or reward, for a better score on the value it does. The competitors who take that trade do better in the competition than the competitors who don't. So the ones who refuse the trade lose ground to the ones who take it, generation after generation or quarter after quarter, until refusing simply isn't a viable long-term strategy anymore. Alexander calls the resulting arrangement a multipolar trap, and the "multipolar" part matters: nobody is in charge of it. A monopolist who behaves badly can be regulated, boycotted, or replaced. This kind of arrangement has no single actor whose choice would fix it, because any one competitor who unilaterally stopped feeding it would simply be out-competed by everyone who kept feeding it, and the whole thing would carry on unchanged with one fewer name in it.

The economist Martin Shubik built a small laboratory version of the same mechanism in nineteen seventy-one that Alexander uses to show the logic at its most naked. Shubik's dollar auction auctions off an actual dollar bill, with an ordinary rule and one vicious addition: the highest bidder wins the dollar, but the second-highest bidder also has to pay their own losing bid and gets nothing for it. Bidding starts innocently, five cents, ten cents, each bidder trying to win a dollar for less than a dollar. Once the bids pass fifty cents, though, the second-place bidder is now facing a guaranteed loss either way, and the only question is how large: drop out and lose the fifty cents outright, or bid ninety-five cents and lose only a nickel if you win, or lose almost a dollar if you don't. Real auctions run this way have closed above twenty dollars for the same single dollar bill, both finalists trapped by a structure that makes escalation individually rational at every step even as it makes both parties worse off collectively across the whole climb. Nobody at the table is stupid or greedy in any unusual sense. Both are doing the locally correct thing, over and over, and the local correctness is exactly what drives the total outcome off a cliff.

Chapter Five: Two Traps Run to Their Ends

Move the same logic onto a fish farm and the abstraction gets a face. A fish farmer operating in a shared bay or river can, if he chooses, crowd his pens tighter than is healthy for the fish, dose the water with antibiotics to control the resulting disease, and let the runoff of waste and drug residue flow downstream into water everyone else's farm also draws from. He gets more fish per acre of water than a competitor who spaces his pens properly and skips the drugs. His downstream neighbors, meanwhile, absorb a fouled river they had no say in fouling, and if enough farmers upstream make the same individually profitable choice, the whole river eventually can't support healthy fish at any density, at which point everyone loses, including the farmer who moved first. He captured the early gain. The bill arrived later, addressed to everybody, including him.

The second case Alexander runs comes from closer to home for most of his American readers, and it borrows its name from the legal scholar Elizabeth Warren's research into family bankruptcy: the two-income trap. A single generation ago, in many American cities, one working parent's income was enough to buy a house in a school district good enough to educate the children reasonably well. Then some families started sending both parents into the workforce, and with two incomes bidding on the same finite stock of houses zoned into the same good school districts, prices in those districts rose to absorb the second income, the way any fixed supply absorbs new demand. A family with a single earner competing for the same house is now simply priced out of it, so the choice to send the second parent to work, made freely by one family after another for reasons that sound entirely sensible taken alone, has rewritten, one household at a time, the entry price for the whole competition. Every family that opts in gains, relative to families that don't, exactly nothing, because the good school district was never actually for sale at a fixed price. It was for sale at whatever price the collective decisions of every other family bidding on it happened to set that year, and every family that joins the bidding raises the price for the family behind it.

Chapter Six: The Trap That Ate a Way of Life

The largest-scale version Alexander offers goes back roughly ten thousand years, to the invention of agriculture, and it borrows an argument researchers including Jared Diamond have made from skeletal and demographic evidence: hunter-gatherer populations, by several measures anthropologists can actually check in the archaeological record, height, bone density, number of hours worked per week, appear to have been healthier and less overworked than the farming populations that eventually displaced them almost everywhere on earth. Agriculture did not spread because it made the individual farmer's life better than the forager's life it replaced. It spread because a fixed area of farmed land can feed, and eventually arm, many times more people than the same area could support under foraging, and a numerous, settled, organized population beats a smaller, healthier, more mobile one in the one contest that actually determines whose way of life survives to the next century: who has more people and more spears. Two populations in competition for the same territory don't get to vote on which lifestyle wins. The lifestyle that produces more competitors wins, whether or not it produces happier ones, and everyone alive today is descended from the side of that contest that chose the trap.

Run the same shape forward into the twentieth century and it explains an arms race without needing a single villain anywhere in the chain. Two nations that both suspect a nuclear weapon might be useful someday face a mirror version of the dollar auction: build the weapon and you're safer relative to a rival who doesn't, so long as you have it and they don't, but the instant they build one too, both nations are back to the relative safety they started with, now carrying the absolute cost and risk of a weapon that produces no lasting advantage for either side. Rational choices made in sequence by two governments that each want, above all else, not to be the side without the weapon, produce a world stocked with tens of thousands of warheads that nobody involved actually wanted to build for their own sake and that both sides would happily trade away in a verified, simultaneous disarmament neither side can fully trust the other to honor.

Chapter Seven: What Finally Stopped the Farms

Return to the antibiotics with the trap's full architecture in view and the sixty-three-year delay stops looking like negligence and starts looking like exactly what the model predicts. No farmer could unilaterally quit the practice without simply losing market share to farmers who kept using it, so restraint had to arrive from somewhere outside the competition itself, an actor not competing in the same race and therefore not punished by the same logic for imposing a cost that applied evenly to every competitor at once. A regulatory ban is, mechanically, a change to what each competitor stands to gain, made illegal for every player at the same moment, so that nobody loses relative position by giving up the winning move. The rule didn't ask any single rancher to be a better person than his neighbor. It removed the neighbor's advantage by removing everyone's access to it at once, the only kind of intervention a genuine multipolar trap actually responds to.

Be honest about how partial that fix has turned out to be. Growth-promotion sales did fall to nothing, but overall antibiotic sales for livestock in the United States have since drifted back upward in several of the years the Food and Drug Administration has reported since, now justified under the looser label of disease prevention rather than growth promotion, a reclassification that a skeptical reading would call the same trap finding a new door once the old one got locked. The mechanism that produced the original sixty-three-year delay hasn't been defeated. It's been out-maneuvered exactly once, on exactly one specific use of the drug, and the underlying incentive to find some other angle on the same competitive advantage is still sitting there, unregulated, waiting for the next door to be tried.

Chapter Eight: Elua, the God Still Standing

Everything so far describes what Moloch does. Alexander spends a shorter stretch of the essay on the question of what, if anything, stands against him, and reaches for a source considerably stranger than Ginsberg: the novelist Jacqueline Carey's Kushiel series, whose invented god Elua represents flowers, art, philosophy, and what Alexander's essay calls free love and all soft and fragile things. Set beside a god of child sacrifice, a god of flowers sounds close to a joke, and Alexander seems to know it, choosing the frailest possible image on purpose. Elua has no armies and enforces no rule of competition on anyone. He represents, in the essay's account, everything a person or a civilization values that a multipolar trap doesn't reward and will happily discard the instant discarding it improves the score: leisure, beauty, unhurried love, art made for no other reason than that someone wanted to make it. None of that wins a war, a market, or a dollar auction. All of it survives anyway, in the pockets and moments a trap hasn't yet colonized, and that survival is the only kind of victory this particular god has ever claimed.

This lands almost exactly where last episode left off. Max Weber, describing a disenchanted world in which the old religious authority that used to rank human values against each other has vacated the field, said the old gods climb back out of their graves and resume, in his words, their eternal struggle with one another, no longer wearing names or temples but no less real for that. Alexander's Moloch and Elua are two of those gods, stripped of temples exactly as Weber said they would be, fighting for the same unclaimed territory Weber's lecture described a century earlier from an entirely different angle: not disenchantment this time, but competition, and the question of which values survive contact with a system built to punish anyone who keeps them.

Chapter Nine: The Frames This Shelf Already Had

None of this mechanism is actually new to a listener who has stayed with this feed. Robert Jackall's corporate managers, four episodes into this show's whole run, protected themselves from blame by passing it downward and sideways rather than by doing better work, because a manager who accepted blame honestly lost standing relative to managers who didn't, and a manager who unilaterally stopped playing blame games in a building full of managers who hadn't simply got outmaneuvered by the ones who kept playing. That's a multipolar trap with careers as the currency. Charles Perrow's account of tightly coupled, interactively complex systems described a different mechanism entirely, accidents built into the physics and wiring of a plant rather than into anyone's incentives, but the England health service Bevan and Hood studied nine episodes ago ran on a trap of exactly Alexander's shape: a hospital manager who refused to game the eight-minute ambulance target watched his star rating fall behind managers who did game it, and the honest manager had no way to unilaterally opt out of a system that judged every trust by the same published number regardless of how any one trust chose to hit it.

Andy Grove's own career supplies the clearest case of an entire industry accepting Moloch's terms and calling it strategy. Grove ran Intel through the nineteen eighties memory chip business at the exact moment Japanese manufacturers, backed by cheaper capital and government support, started selling memory chips at prices no American firm could match and still turn a profit. Every year Intel stayed in that market to defend its position cost the company money it wasn't making back, and every year a competitor exited the race for good, ceding ground permanently to whoever stayed. Grove and his co-founder Gordon Moore eventually asked each other, in the story Grove tells in his own memoir, what a new management team walking in fresh would do with the company, and answered their own question by doing it themselves: they left the memory business entirely and bet everything on processors instead, the one move available to a company willing to stop competing in a race it recognized as a trap rather than a fight it could win by trying harder. Most competitors in most multipolar traps never get to make that choice, because exit only works if there's somewhere else to go. Intel had one. A fish farmer boxed into a single bay usually doesn't.

Chapter Ten: The God Is Losing Some Ground

The strongest reply to the essay doesn't come from an economist arguing the model is wrong. It comes from a writer well inside Alexander's own intellectual circle, Zvi Mowshowitz, who published a piece years later called "Moloch Hasn't Won" making a simple empirical observation: if multipolar traps really did grind every value that doesn't help you win down to nothing, human civilization would already look a great deal worse than it does. Art still gets made by people who will never recoup the hours they spent on it. Parents still take vacations instead of banking every spare hour toward the college fund arms race. Mowshowitz's explanation is that real-world competition is almost never as perfectly unforgiving as the dollar auction or the fish farm model assumes: most markets carry enough slack, friction, and outright irrationality that an actor can decline to feed Moloch and merely do somewhat worse, rather than get eliminated outright, and a great deal of what looks like a trap only tightens to a lethal degree once some additional social or signaling pressure gets layered on top of the ordinary competitive one.

This show has already met one of the clearest documented cases of a group escaping exactly this kind of trap on its own, without needing a Grove-style exit or an outside regulator. Elinor Ostrom spent decades cataloguing common-pool resources, alpine pastures in Switzerland, irrigation systems in Nepal, that should, by a naive multipolar-trap reading, have been strip-mined by whichever villager grazed the most sheep or drew the most water first. Most of them weren't, for centuries at a stretch, because the communities using them built local monitoring, graduated penalties, and locally accepted rules that made cheating cost something without needing a national regulator anywhere in sight. Ostrom's tribunals and Alexander's fish farm are the same trap described from opposite ends: one shows the mechanism grinding a shared resource down because nobody built an exit, the other shows a group that built one.

Chapter Eleven: The Toolbox

Alexander's own intellectual collaborator Eliezer Yudkowsky picked up the essay's argument three years later and tried to convert it from a diagnosis into something closer to an instruction manual, first in a book called "Inadequate Equilibria" and then in a companion pair of essays under the title "Moloch's Toolbox." Yudkowsky's contribution is a short list of the specific conditions that let a bad equilibrium survive contact with people who can plainly see it's bad: the people making a given decision are often not the people who bear its costs, so an executive who benefits personally from a corner-cutting choice has no built-in reason to weigh the cost to a customer who will never trace the harm back to him; the information needed to catch the corner-cutting is often available to nobody positioned to act on it, split between parties who each hold only half of what would be needed to prove the problem; and the whole arrangement is frequently propped up by the same coordination failure Shubik's auction demonstrates, where any single actor who tried to fix it alone would simply be replaced by an actor willing to keep exploiting it.

What naming these three conditions buys you is a way to sort what kind of fix might actually work. Misaligned incentives need a change to who pays for what. Scattered information needs a mechanism that lets the scattered pieces meet, an audit, a whistleblower channel, a second, independent measurement of the same thing the primary system reports. Pure coordination failure, where everyone privately agrees the current arrangement is bad and would happily switch to a better one if everyone else switched at the same moment, is the one kind a regulator, a treaty, or a widely trusted convener can sometimes dissolve overnight simply by giving every actor simultaneous permission to stop, the same mechanism behind the growth-promotion ban that finally got antibiotics off the farms that couldn't stop themselves.

Chapter Twelve: The Charge That the Villain Went Missing on Purpose

The hardest and most specific objection to the whole essay comes from a writer named Mike Travers, responding under a piece he called "Meditations on Meditations on Moloch," and his complaint isn't that the mechanism is wrong. It's that the mechanism, described the way Alexander describes it, conveniently erases every actor who benefits from a bad arrangement and has every reason to keep it running. Travers points out that treating a race to the bottom as a leaderless, agentless force of mathematics lets a factory owner who lobbies against a safety regulation, or a landlord who profits from an artificially tight housing market, disappear into the abstraction along with everyone else, when in fact some of the people inside these systems are not hapless competitors trapped by a structure beyond their control. They are the structure's active beneficiaries, spending real money and real political effort to keep the trap exactly as it is, because the trap that costs a fish farmer's downstream neighbors a clean river is also the trap that makes the fish farmer richer than his more careful neighbor, every single season the trap keeps running.

Travers's second charge goes after the essay's own literary borrowing. Ginsberg's Moloch section names "Moloch whose name is the Mind" as one of the demon's own faces, indicting rationality and calculation themselves as part of the sickness. Alexander inverts that specific line without acknowledging the inversion: his essay's whole proposed remedy is more and better rational calculation, a smarter, more coordinated application of the very faculty Ginsberg's poem blamed for the disaster in the first place. Whether that inversion is a flaw or simply an update depends on which decade's evidence you trust more, nineteen fifty-four's fear of the bomb the rational planners built, or twenty fourteen's fear of a coordination problem that better information and better institutions might actually be able to solve. Both writers were responding to the tools available to civilization in their own moment, and neither had the other's decades of additional data to work with.

Chapter Thirteen: The Gardener

Alexander's own proposed exit is the essay's most ambitious claim, and it should be stated plainly rather than softened. Every escape catalogued so far, Grove's exit into a new market, Ostrom's local monitoring, the federal ban on growth-promotion antibiotics, works only within a bounded competition that some larger actor can still stand outside of and regulate. Alexander's own worry is what happens once a trap operates at the scale of the entire global economy or the entire species, where no larger actor exists to stand outside it the way a national government stands outside a single industry. His answer, offered with more confidence than the argument up to that point has actually earned, is that a sufficiently capable and well-aligned artificial intelligence, acting as what he calls a gardener rather than a ruler, could occupy exactly that outside position for the whole of human civilization at once, coordinating away the traps that no merely human institution has the reach to dissolve.

That step is what it is: a speculative, unproven leap from a documented historical mechanism, real fish farms, real dollar auctions, real antibiotic sales figures, to a technology that in twenty fourteen existed nowhere outside a research paper and still, more than a decade later, has never been demonstrated to do anything resembling what the essay asks of it. The diagnosis rests on evidence a skeptic can check against actual farm data and actual auction results. The proposed cure rests on a hope about a technology whose safety and capability nobody, including its own most serious builders, currently knows how to guarantee. An essay this careful about grounding every other claim in a checkable case earns the benefit of the doubt on its diagnosis. Its prescription is a different kind of writing entirely, closer to a wager than a finding, and the two halves of the essay read as two different genres rather than one continuous argument.

Chapter Fourteen: The Ratchet Inside the Counselling Programme

A small, human-scale version of this same trap runs inside the maternal mental health counselling programme this show's listener runs at a distance, across several districts, staffed by lay counsellors supervised by supervisors who are in turn supervised by a small central team. The programme measures itself partly on enrollment, the count of women who start counselling in a given month, because enrollment is visible, comparable across districts, and easy to put on a dashboard. A supervisor whose district's enrollment count looks weak against every other district's, for reasons that might have nothing to do with the quality of care her counsellors are actually providing, feels the same pressure Alexander's fish farmer feels: push counsellors toward faster intake and lighter early sessions to keep the number competitive with the districts she's compared against, even where a slower, more careful intake would serve the individual woman better. She didn't invent that pressure, and she can't unilaterally opt out of it without her own numbers falling behind everyone else's, a multipolar trap running at the scale of one organization's internal dashboard rather than a market or a species. The exit, when it works at all, looks like Grove's paired indicators from three episodes back: measuring something enrollment can't fake, like counsellor-reported session quality or a woman's own follow-up report weeks later, so that gaming one number stops being free.

Chapter Fifteen: The Dose

Put Alexander's essay through the same dosage test this show applies to every cynical framework it takes seriously, and the results split cleanly along the same line that separated the essay's diagnosis from its prescription. Used diagnostically, on the antibiotics, the dollar auctions, the ambulance targets, the multipolar trap is one of the most useful single ideas this feed has covered, because it answers a question that blame alone never resolves: not who behaved badly, but what would have to change about the structure itself before behaving well stopped being a losing move. Used as an identity, treating every unfair outcome in your own life as Moloch's work and therefore nobody's fault and nothing anyone chose, the same framework becomes exactly what Travers warned against: a way of describing exploitation that happens to let the people extracting real, chosen advantage from it off the hook, because a trap with no operator is a trap nobody ever has to answer for. The honest reading holds both things at once. Some bad arrangements really do have no villain, only a structure that needs changing from outside. Others have a villain standing inside the structure, benefiting from it, and calling it Moloch instead of calling it by his name is its own kind of shortcut.

Chapter Sixteen: What You're Feeding

The question to hold onto is a specific one: name a competition you're currently inside, at work, in your field, in your household's own choices about money or schooling, where you already suspect the winning move costs something you'd rather keep, and ask honestly whether you could unilaterally stop making that move without simply losing ground to everyone still making it. If the answer is no, you've found a trap, not a personal failing, and the next question is who or what stands outside that competition with enough reach to change what it rewards, since that's the only kind of actor a multipolar trap has ever actually answered to.

Next time, this shelf stays with the same writer for a very different kind of essay: Scott Alexander's "Considerations on Cost Disease," an honest accounting of why healthcare, education, and construction now cost several times what they did in nineteen seventy for no improvement anyone can clearly point to, and a rare case of a writer this confident admitting, in print, that he doesn't actually know the answer. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Weber, Science as a Vocation: the lecture on the academic gamble, delivered by a man who hadn't held a normal teaching post in nineteen years
item.description: Max Weber's 1917 Munich lecture on the academic career as a lottery, the disenchantment science buys at the price of an old kind of death, and the many gods that keep fighting once no single authority is left to rank them, tested against Leo Strauss's charge that the whole argument collapses into relativism.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Man Who Hadn't Taught in Nineteen Years

On the seventh of November, nineteen seventeen, a room above a Munich bookshop filled with students who had come to hear a lecture with the deliberately dry title "Science as a Vocation." The shop belonged to a bookseller named Carl Georg Steinicke, and the lecture was the second in a planned series of four called "Intellectual Work as a Vocation," organized by a student group, the Bavarian Free Students' Union, under a young organizer named Immanuel Birnbaum. Germany was in the third year of a war it was losing. Some of the young men in that room had already served and would go back; others hadn't been called up yet and might still be. They had asked a well-known sociologist to tell them something true about the working life they were choosing, or might never get to choose, and the sociologist obliged, speaking without notes and without a single pause, for the better part of two hours, on a subject he understood from an unusually exposed angle.

Max Weber told them, more or less in these words, that an academic career is a mad hazard. He was not being provocative for effect. He meant it as a description, and the description carried a weight that came from somewhere specific: the man standing in front of that room in nineteen seventeen had not held a regular university teaching post since nineteen oh three. Fourteen years is a long time to have opinions about a job from outside it. By the time he stood up to deliver this particular verdict on the academic life, he had been out of the classroom for nearly two decades, and the reason he'd left tells you almost as much about the lecture's argument as the lecture itself does.

Chapter Two: What Kept Him Out

The break came in eighteen ninety-seven. Weber, then a professor at Heidelberg, had a violent quarrel with his father over the older man's treatment of his mother; the father stormed out, refusing ever to return, and died of a gastric hemorrhage a few weeks later without the two of them having reconciled. Within a year Weber was suffering from a collapse that his biographers describe in a consistent, grim vocabulary: insomnia, exhaustion, inner tension, anxiety that came in waves he couldn't predict or control. He tried repeatedly to resume teaching and repeatedly failed. The university eventually granted him leave without pay, and for roughly four years he was, by his own account and everyone else's, incapacitated. He came back to scholarly work around nineteen oh three, not as a teacher but as a writer and editor, co-editing a journal called the Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik and producing, over the following fourteen years, from outside any classroom, the essays that made his name: the Protestant ethic material, the studies of bureaucracy and authority this show has already borrowed vocabulary from more than once. All of it written by a man who had, for well over a decade, no institutional post that required him to stand in front of students and teach.

He tested the water again in the summer of nineteen eighteen, taking a one-semester position at the University of Vienna. The following year, nineteen nineteen, was crowded on both fronts at once. He accepted a full chair at Munich, the same one that had belonged to the economist Lujo Brentano, and became, at last, an ordinary working professor again, seventeen years after he'd stopped being one. In the very same months he was also doing the one thing his own lecture would soon tell every scholar in earshot never to do from behind a podium: he went into politics directly, in his own name, as a citizen rather than a teacher, sitting on the committee that drafted the Weimar constitution, arguing successfully for a directly elected, plebiscitary president and for the emergency powers eventually written into the constitution's Article Forty-Eight, a clause that would be used, a decade and a half later, for purposes Weber never lived to see. He served on the German delegation to the Versailles peace conference, opposing the treaty's terms, and ran, unsuccessfully, for a parliamentary seat on the German Democratic Party's ticket. None of that made him a demagogue in the sense his own Munich lecture had already condemned two years earlier, because none of it happened from a lectern with captive students in the seats; it happened in the ordinary, exposed, votable arena that lecture had insisted was the only legitimate place for that kind of argument. He taught three semesters. In June of nineteen twenty he came down with influenza that turned into pneumonia, part of the same pandemic wave that had already killed tens of millions of people across the world that year, and died in Munich at fifty-six. The lecture you're hearing about tonight sits almost exactly at the hinge of that story: delivered by a man out of the profession for nineteen years, describing a system he was about to rejoin for a year and a half before it, indirectly, buried him.

Chapter Three: The Machine You Have to Gamble Your Life On

Here is the system Weber described to that room, and the mechanics come before the argument they're in service of, because the mechanics are the argument's first piece of evidence. A young German scholar who wanted an academic career didn't apply for a job the way an American graduate student might. He wrote a second, harder dissertation, called a habilitation, and if a faculty accepted it, he earned something called the venia legendi, the right to lecture, but not a salary. He became a Privatdozent, unpaid, living off whatever fees the students who chose to attend his lectures happened to pay him directly, for years, sometimes many years, while he waited for a chair, an Ordinarius position, to open up somewhere and then competed for it against every other Privatdozent in the country doing the same thing.

Weber didn't pretend that competition sorted candidates by ability. Ability mattered, but so did what he called purely extraneous factors: a lecturer's speaking voice, his manner in front of a room, the size of the crowd he happened to draw, which was itself a poor proxy for scholarly quality since, as Weber put it, the number of students who show up is a statistically visible fact while the qualities of a scholar are not the kind of thing you can count.
