The regulatory failures at Fukushima, the ignored warnings about the size of tsunami the site's sea wall could withstand, the plant operator's history of falsified safety reports, were, he argued, failures his own theory was never built to explain. They were the same species of failure the Kemeny Commission had found at Three Mile Island: correctable, attributable, ordinary. What he added, past what the nineteen eighty-four book had argued, was a claim about ownership: nuclear safety is hardest to sustain, he wrote, where nuclear plants sit in private hands, because a private firm has both the incentive and, often, the political weight to resist the regulation that would cost it money, in a way that a state-run utility answering to a different set of pressures does not as reliably resist.

That is a theorist finding the edge of his own claim rather than stretching it to cover a new disaster, and it is worth as much attention as the original thesis. The book's afterword to its nineteen ninety-nine edition had already widened the frame once, past nuclear power to Bhopal, to Chernobyl, and to a computer problem, the Millennium bug, that Perrow treated as close to a pure specimen of his category: a trivial, uniform design choice, storing a year as two digits, buried inside millions of interdependent systems built by people who had never coordinated with each other, tightly enough coupled that no one could say in advance which failures would cascade and which would not. By the time he wrote The Next Catastrophe in two thousand seven, his policy recommendation had shifted from redesigning specific plants toward something plainer and harder to sell: reduce the concentration. Fewer people and fewer critical systems stacked in the same vulnerable place is a lever that works no matter whether the failure to come is a reactor, a hurricane, or an attack, and it does not require anyone to first agree on whether the next accident will be Perrow's kind or Hopkins's kind, because it helps against both.

Chapter Nine: A Programme with No Slack

I want to take the two dials off the reactor floor and put them somewhere I can use them, because a manager who runs anything distributed can ask the same two questions of her own design, not to find out whether she is running a nuclear plant, but to find the places where she has built in more tightness than the work required. Take a maternal mental-health counselling programme, run at a distance across several districts, lay counsellors reporting to supervisors reporting to a small central team through paper and digital forms: is there a step in that chain where a single missed form stalls a payment, or a supervision visit, or a client's continuation in care, with no substitute path and no time to catch the error before it becomes a consequence for someone who did nothing wrong? That is a tightly coupled step, however low-tech the paper. It does not need to interact with three other systems the way a reactor does to cause harm; it only needs no slack. The fix a programme manager has, that a reactor engineer usually does not, is that most of these steps were made tight by habit rather than physics, and can be loosened on purpose: a grace window before a missed form escalates, a second route to flag a client at risk that does not depend on the one supervisor who happens to be traveling that week. The dam cannot be told to relax. A workflow built by a small team almost always can be, and the question to ask of it is not whether anyone is careful enough, but whether the design has left anyone room to be.

That question is the same one Davies's accountability sink and Campbell's law, from earlier in this series, were circling from different directions. Davies's sink hides responsibility inside a process nobody can override; Campbell's law corrupts a number the moment someone's standing depends on it. Perrow's contribution is the third leg, and it is the least comforting of the three, because it does not require anyone's incentives to be wrong, and it needs no process hidden from view to work either. It asks only two properties of a system's physical or procedural shape, present at the same time, each one doing nothing more than it was designed to do.

This law gets the same two-sided hearing the measurement constellation got two episodes ago. Taken as identity rather than diagnosis, Perrow's law tells a manager that catastrophe is coming regardless of her care, which is a license to stop trying exactly where trying still helps: the carrier deck and the air traffic system are proof that vigilance, culture, and a deference to whoever is closest to the problem can hold off, for a very long time, an accident the matrix says should already have happened. Taken diagnostically, the same law answers a specific, narrow question better than anything else on the shelf: not "are we careful," but "where, in this design, has efficiency bought us coupling we didn't need, and what would it cost to buy some slack back." Read the Three Mile Island and marine chapters in full; they carry the book's evidence and its two most legible worked cases. Skip the chapters on space and genetic research unless you work in either field, where the classifications are thinner than the nuclear case and the book itself is more speculative. Read Sagan for the best version of the argument against fatalism, and read Hopkins if you want the strongest single challenge to the book's own flagship story, because a theory that cannot survive its best critics was never worth the trust the shelf has been putting in frameworks all season.

The question to carry into the week is a design question, in two parts. Find one process you run where a single missed step, caught late, cannot be undone before it costs someone something: the step with no substitute path and no grace period. Then ask what it would cost, in time or money or your own convenience, to buy that step a little slack, and whether you have ever weighed that cost against what the tightness is actually saving you, or only assumed the tightness was free.

Next time, the shelf goes to the disaster that keeps appearing at the edge of this one without ever quite belonging to it: Richard Feynman's own investigation of the Challenger disaster, his blunt appendix to the Rogers Commission report, set against Diane Vaughan's full account of the culture that made the O-ring's warning look like no reason to stop. Thanks for listening.

item.title: The measurement constellation 2 of 2: targets and terror, the spike at eight minutes, and how to keep a number honest
item.description: What happened when England ran its health service on targets with sanctions – Bevan and Hood's 2006 evidence: the ambulance response times that bunched just under eight minutes, the four-hour wait that fell from twenty-three percent to five, the nine hospitals that edited their waiting lists, the three kinds of gaming and the four kinds of people – then the design question the three papers never answered: how a programme that has to report numbers keeps them true, with paired indicators, random audit, denominators that count the people who never started, and a rule about what a number is allowed to cost the person who makes it.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Spike

Take a distribution. An English ambulance service in the early two thousands had a target: seventy-five percent of the most urgent calls, the ones classified as immediately life-threatening, were to be reached within eight minutes. The service's performance against the target was published, it fed into a star rating for the whole trust, and a trust that missed its targets could lose its chief executive. So imagine the histogram of response times, the count of calls reached in each minute from one to twenty. You would expect a hump somewhere around five to nine minutes, tailing away on either side, and in the services not managed hard against the target, that is what the data showed, a noisy decline. In several that had been, the researchers who looked found something else: a spike at eight minutes, and a hole at nine, the calls that had taken between eight and nine minutes having been recorded as taking less than eight. Nobody had made an ambulance faster. Someone, at some point in the chain between the stopwatch and the spreadsheet, had rounded, and the target had been met, and the number reported to the public meant something different from what the public thought it meant.

That is from a paper by Gwyn Bevan and Christopher Hood, published in Public Administration in two thousand and six, called What's Measured Is What Matters, and it is the evidence the last episode said the constellation lacked. Ridgway had an employment office and a Soviet plan; Campbell had a police department and a war. Bevan and Hood had a whole national health system that had, for five years, been run on the very principle the three papers warned against, with the data published, and they went through it. The question this episode asks is the one the three discoverers never got to. Once you know the law, and you still have to report numbers, what do you do?

Chapter Two: The Soviet Method

The system they studied had a name, given by the people who ran it, targets and terror, and Bevan and Hood take it seriously, because it names the mechanism. From two thousand and one the government in England published an annual star rating for every hospital and ambulance trust, from zero to three, computed from a set of targets: the share of emergency patients seen within four hours, the maximum wait for an operation, the ambulance response, and a dozen others. A trust with three stars was left alone and given money. A trust with zero stars was named, its board was exposed, and its chief executive was, in a phrase the government used without embarrassment, likely to be replaced. It was, the authors point out, the Soviet method, and they mean the comparison exactly as stated: a central plan with numerical targets for every unit, published league tables, and personal consequences for the manager who missed. The Soviet system ran for sixty years on that basis before it collapsed, and its sixty years produced the best-documented body of evidence about gaming that exists, and Bevan and Hood's move was to take the Soviet taxonomy and see whether the English health service had reproduced it.

It had. The Soviet literature described three kinds of gaming, and the English data showed all three. The first is the ratchet: if next year's target is set from this year's performance, a manager who expects to be in the job next year has a reason not to do too well now, and the Soviet saying, which the authors quote from a nineteen fifty-eight study, was that a wise director fulfils the plan a hundred and five percent but never a hundred and twenty-five. The second is the threshold: a target set at a fixed level, seventy-five percent within eight minutes, ninety percent within four hours, pulls all the effort to the patients just on the wrong side of the line and none to the ones far beyond it or safely inside it, so that performance crowds up against the target from below and a distribution that should be smooth acquires a cliff. The third is output distortion, the general name for meeting the number at the expense of the things the number does not count, and the cases live here.

For the four-hour emergency wait, the National Audit Office found five kinds of distortion. Patients were held in ambulances outside the door, since the clock started when they entered the department, so that on a bad afternoon the queue was in the car park and the ambulances that held it were not answering calls, which is one target being met by breaking another. Patients were moved, at three hours and fifty minutes, onto a trolley in a corridor that had been redesignated as an admissions area, so that they had left the emergency department in the data and not in fact; the inspection body recorded hospitals admitting patients to hallways. Staff were drafted in for the week the figures were sampled. Cases were reclassified. And the number went, on the official figures, from twenty-three percent of patients waiting over four hours in two thousand and two to five point three percent two springs later, which is a real change and not all of it gaming, and I will come back to that, because the honest reading of this paper is not that the targets did nothing.

For the waiting lists, the National Audit Office found in two thousand and one that nine trusts had inappropriately adjusted their lists, three of them for three years or more, affecting nearly six thousand patient records; five of the nine came to light only under outside pressure. The adjustments ranged from junior staff following an established procedure that happened to be wrong, which is Campbell's corrupted indicator without a corrupt person anywhere in it, to something more deliberate. And for the four-hour target there was a second channel of data, the patient survey, and Bevan and Hood put the two beside each other: in the year two thousand and two to three, on the official returns, a hundred and thirty-nine of a hundred and fifty-eight acute trusts had seen ninety percent of their emergency patients within four hours, and sixty-nine percent of the patients, asked directly, said that had been their experience. The gap between those two figures is not all gaming either; patients remember waits as longer than they were. But it is a second number, collected by a different route from people with no stake in the target, and the paired indicator, which Grove would recognise, is what made the gaming visible. Without the survey, the official figure would have stood.

Chapter Three: Four Kinds of People

The part of the paper I would give to any manager is the part that stops treating the people in the system as a single type. Bevan and Hood borrow a distinction from the economist Julian Le Grand, whose Hirschman-inflected work the shelf met in the Exit, Voice and Loyalty episode, between knights, who serve the public because they want to, and knaves, who serve themselves, and they stretch it into four.

There are saints, who share the goals of the centre so completely that they report their own failures unasked; the authors' example is a London hospital that, in two thousand, twice drew attention to bad results in its own transplant programme and suspended it. There are honest triers, who broadly want what the centre wants and do not game, but who will not volunteer what they are not asked. There are reactive gamers, who want it too, and will game the target when they have a reason and an opportunity, which under a regime of terror is often, and who are the majority in any large organisation. And there are rational maniacs, whose goals are not the centre's at all, and who will do whatever the target rewards, up to and including harm, if the system's checks are weak enough; the authors' example is Harold Shipman, the family doctor who murdered his patients for years while his practice statistics looked ordinary.

The reason the taxonomy matters is that a target regime is designed for a population of honest triers, and its consequences fall as though everyone were a maniac. The saints and the honest triers are punished by it, because they report the truth and the truth is worse than their neighbours' fictions, which is Campbell's Orlando Wilson, the honest chief whose crime rate rose. The reactive gamers are converted by it, since a system that punishes the truth teaches the truthful to stop, and the conversion is the real damage, because it is a change in the organisation's character rather than in its figures. And the maniacs are not caught by it, because the numbers are the last place a maniac shows. A regime that is severe on numbers and absent from the ward produces, over a few years, a workforce of gamers, a set of numbers that mean nothing, and a Shipman with a clean record, and it does this to people who began as knights.

Chapter Four: The Other Side of the Ledger

Now the honest complication, because the shelf's rule is that a two-sided fact is not flattened. England's waiting times fell. Between the year two thousand and three years later the proportion of patients waiting more than a year for an operation fell steeply in England and did not in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, which had the same health service and the same money and did not run the star ratings, and a series of later econometric studies by Carol Propper and colleagues, comparing England to the other nations of the United Kingdom over the decade, found that targets with sanctions reduced waiting times substantially and, as far as anyone could measure, without the collateral harm to unmeasured care that the gaming literature would predict. The four-hour figure fell from twenty-three to five, and the patient surveys, though they showed a gap, showed improvement too, and the National Audit Office found satisfaction had risen. Bevan and Hood say this plainly. Their argument is not that the targets failed. It is that the reported success was a synecdoche, a part standing for a whole, and that the regime had no way of knowing how large the part was, because it had been built on the assumption that measurement problems did not matter and that the people it measured would not respond to being measured, and both assumptions were false, and the second was false in the direction that the regime itself had caused.

So the finding is narrower and more useful than the law alone would suggest. Targets with consequences do change behaviour, and some of the change is the change you wanted. The problem is that the number cannot tell you which part, and the harder you lean on it the smaller the part you wanted becomes. That is a design problem, and design problems have designs.

Chapter Five: What They Recommended, and What Grove Would Add

Bevan and Hood end with remedies, and they are modest, which is a point in their favour, since the literature's grander remedies have mostly been tried. The first is randomness. If the units being measured do not know in advance which of their numbers will be checked, or when, or against what, then the reactive gamers have no target to game and the effort spreads back across the distribution. They compare it to the speed camera whose location is not announced: the deterrent is the uncertainty, and a system that publishes exactly what it will measure has published the instructions for gaming it. The second is audit, and specifically the audit hole. England in those years measured everything and verified almost nothing; the numbers went from the trust to the centre without anyone independent looking at how they were made, and the authors' proposal was face-to-face scrutiny with random visits, the inspector who turns up and walks the corridor that has been renamed. The third is a set of second channels: the patient survey beside the official return, the complaint data beside the satisfaction score, so that no number stands alone.

Put that beside Grove and the shelf's earlier material and a fuller design emerges, and I want to lay it out as a set of rules, because the listener who runs something will want to carry it. Every indicator has a partner that catches its gaming, chosen so that the two cannot be moved in the same direction by the same trick, which is Grove's rule and Bevan and Hood's second channel, and it is the first thing to do and most organisations never do it. Every indicator is reported as a distribution and not a threshold, since the threshold is what produces the spike at eight minutes, and a manager who sees the histogram sees the spike, and one who sees the percentage sees seventy-five. The sample that will be verified is chosen at random after the numbers are in, so that the people producing them cannot know which ones will be looked at. The verification is done by someone who walks the corridor, at a frequency the producers cannot predict, and it is done as often on the units with good numbers as on the ones with bad, since the good numbers are where the gaming lives. And the denominators are chosen with more care than the numerators, because the exception report, the patient excluded as unsuitable, the case reclassified as not applicable, is where the forty-nine-dollar larceny hides, and a number whose denominator is under the control of the person being measured is not a number.

There are two further rules that come from Campbell rather than from the English data, and they are the hard ones. The first is about stakes. Campbell's law is proportional to the consequence, and a manager who wants a true number has to decide what the number is for, learning or judgement, and cannot have both from the same figure. A figure used to find out how a programme is going can be honest if the people who produce it know that a bad result brings help rather than punishment; one used to rank and reward will drift, whatever the audit, because the audit catches the fraction it samples and the drift is in the whole. That means keeping the figures that judge people few and heavily verified, and the figures that tell you what is happening many and unpunished, and never letting the second kind slide into the first, which is what happens when a dashboard built for learning is shown to a funder. The second is about distance. The law is strongest where the number is made far from where it is read, by someone whose standing depends on it, in a process the reader cannot see. Every one of those three can be shortened: the reader can go to the place of making, the standing can be detached from it, the process can be made visible. Most managers shorten none of them and then complain about the numbers.

Chapter Six: A Programme on Forms

I want to run the design on a case, and the case I know is a programme delivered at a distance: a counselling programme run across a region from a small central team, in which frontline workers record each session on a form, supervisors record each supervision on another, and the centre sees a dashboard built from both. I will keep it general, since the shape is the shape of most community health programmes anywhere, and the numbers I use are illustrative and not drawn from any one of them.

Start with the indicator the centre watches most: sessions delivered. It is a single criterion in Ridgway's sense, and it has already done what such a criterion does. A form can be completed in a minute without a session having happened, and the dashboard cannot tell the difference, and a worker who is asked every month how many sessions she delivered has been told what the job is. The paired indicator is the first repair, and it has to be one the form cannot produce: the duration of the session where the device records it, a recording where the programme makes them, a client's own account gathered by a different route from a random handful of clients a month. Pick the partner so that a ticked form without a session fails it, and report the two together, sessions logged beside sessions confirmed, and watch the gap rather than the count. The gap is what matters, and a programme that reports only the count has published the instructions for gaming it.

Then the denominator. A programme of this kind has, typically, a large share of women who were enrolled and never started, and the temptation, exception reporting under a different name, is to compute completion among those who began. That number will look good and will mean nothing, because the population it describes is the population that did not fail, and the people who never started are the programme's largest finding. The rule is that every rate is computed on everyone enrolled, and the never-starters are reported as their own line, by site, beside it, so that the site with a fine completion rate and a large never-started column is visible as what it is.

Then the distribution. A supervisor asked whether each counsellor was supervised this month will say yes; asked for the date of each supervision she will produce dates, and the dates will cluster on the last two days of the month, which is Soviet storming on a form, and the clustering is the diagnostic. Report the histogram, not the percentage. A centre that sees the last-week spike has learned something the percentage would have hidden, and has learned it without accusing anyone.

Then randomness and the corridor. Each month a sample of forms is drawn after the month has closed, and someone, a supervisor from another district, a member of the central team on a visit, goes and asks the client whether the session happened and what was discussed. The sample is small and the fact of it is known and the selection is not, and the visits fall on the sites with the best numbers as often as the worst. The purpose is not to catch people. It is to make the number true by making it checkable, which changes what the reactive gamer does before anyone is caught.

And then the stakes, the rule the centre controls least and needs most. If a counsellor's continuation, or a supervisor's standing, or a district's funding, rides on the session count, then every rule above will be gamed in the end, because the audit samples a fraction and the incentive works on the whole. The centre has to decide which few numbers people are judged by, verify those heavily, and let the rest be what Campbell wanted them to be, indicators collected by people who know that a bad number brings a visit and a conversation rather than a consequence. The dashboard built for learning must not be shown to the funder as a scoreboard, or it will become one, and the moment it does the programme will have two sets of numbers, the ones it reports and the ones that are true, and will slowly lose the ability to tell them apart.

None of that is exotic. Every element of it is in a fifty-six paper, a seventy-five conference proceeding, a seventy-six occasional paper, and a two thousand and six article about English hospitals. The reason it is not done is the reason the three discoverers had to discover it separately: the people who build the dashboards do not read the people who studied what dashboards do.

Chapter Seven: The Objection, and a Verdict

The case against the constellation is that it proves too much. Stated at full strength, the law says that any number with a consequence drifts, and since every number a manager uses has a consequence, the law forbids management by numbers altogether, which nobody believes, and which the English waiting-time data contradict. The critics of the gaming literature, and there are some, argue that its examples are selected, that the spike at eight minutes is a small distortion in a large improvement, that the alternative to imperfect targets is not perfect judgement but no accountability at all, and that a regime under which an honest trier is occasionally punished still beats one under which nobody is ever asked. A tidy classification of the variants of Goodhart's law, by David Manheim and Scott Garrabrant in twenty eighteen, makes a related point from the other side: there are at least four different mechanisms behind the law, from the merely statistical, where the proxy and the goal were only ever correlated and optimising the proxy finds the part that was not, to the fully adversarial, where someone is deliberately breaking the link, and a remedy for one does nothing for the others. The random audit catches the adversary. It is no help against the surrogate endpoint that was never going to carry the outcome, and the cardiologists in the last episode were not gaming anything.

I accept most of that, and I think it changes the verdict from a warning to a prescription. The constellation is not an argument against measuring. It is an argument that a number is a made thing, made by a person, under conditions, and that the manager's job is to know the conditions before believing the number. Read Ridgway, all seven pages. Read Campbell's section on indicators and skip the rest unless evaluating programmes is your job, in which case read all of it, and then again. Read Bevan and Hood in full, because it is the one with the data, and read it with the histogram of your own reported numbers open beside it. Skip Goodhart's paper, which is about British monetary policy in nineteen seventy-four and is not the better for the law being in it, and read Strathern's sentence instead, knowing that it is hers.

The dose is the shelf's usual for a cynical frame, with one adjustment. Diagnostically, the law is a medicine, and a manager who applies it to every number she is given will be right more often than one who does not. Taken as identity, as the belief that all numbers lie and all reporters game, it is a poison, and a specific one, because it produces the manager who stops believing her honest triers, and Bevan and Hood's whole finding is that the honest triers are the ones a regime of suspicion converts.

The question to carry into the week is a design question, and it has three parts, and they are short. For the one number your work is most judged by, name its partner, the figure that would show if it were being gamed. Name the last time someone walked the corridor to see how it was made. And name what happens to the person who makes it if it comes in bad, because that, and not the number, is what the number is measuring.

Next time, the shelf leaves the measurement of organisations for the accidents they have: Charles Perrow's Normal Accidents, from nineteen eighty-four, on why some systems fail with nobody having erred, because they are built so that small failures find each other, and what Three Mile Island had in common with a ward. Thanks for listening.

item.title: The measurement constellation 1 of 2: Ridgway, Goodhart, Campbell, one law found three times
item.description: Three short papers staged as a rediscovery – Ridgway's 1956 catalogue of what a single number does to an employment office and a Soviet factory, Goodhart's 1975 aside about the money supply that collapsed the moment it was targeted, and Campbell's 1976 law from a president's war on crime, Chicago's honest police chief, and the body count – with the argument that the law is not about measurement at all but about the moment a number acquires a consequence for the person who reports it.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Employment Office

In the late nineteen forties a state employment agency in an American city had a problem that its managers thought they had solved. The interviewers who matched jobless applicants to employers' vacancies were being evaluated by a single figure, the number of interviews each conducted, and the figure had been chosen because it was the one thing the office could count without argument. The interviewers, being rational, conducted a great many interviews. They were short. Applicants were seen, noted, and sent away, and the count rose, and the number of people actually placed in jobs, which was the purpose of the office, did not. So the managers changed the measure. They began to evaluate interviewers on placements, and then on a set of eight figures, placements among them, and the sociologist Peter Blau, who was in the building watching, recorded what happened next. In one section the interviewers, now competing with each other for placements, began to hide the job openings that came across their desks, keeping the good vacancies in a drawer so that a colleague could not fill them first, and the section's placement rate fell. In another section, whose members had decided among themselves not to compete, the openings were shared and the placement rate held. The number had been improved. The office had been made worse. Blau published it in nineteen fifty-five in a book called The Dynamics of Bureaucracy, and the following year a researcher named V. F. Ridgway, whom almost nobody has heard of, read it and saw that it was an instance of something.

That is the first of three discoveries this episode is about, and I want to tell all three before saying what they discovered, because the interest of the constellation is not the law, which you will have heard stated in one form or another, but that it was found three times in three fields by three people who did not cite each other, and named after the last two. The shelf has been circling this mechanism since its first week. Davies's accountability sink, from episode two, was a process nobody could override; Grove's paired indicators, from three episodes ago, were a practitioner's defence against something he had seen in a fab and did not name. The thing they were both handling has a literature, and the literature is short, and this is it.

Chapter Two: Ridgway, Nineteen Fifty-Six

Ridgway's paper is seven pages long. It appeared in the second issue of a new journal, Administrative Science Quarterly, under the title Dysfunctional Consequences of Performance Measurements, and it is organised as a taxonomy of three ways to measure a person or a unit and what each one does. He begins by conceding, as everyone in this literature begins, that quantitative measures are useful and that the problem is not their existence but the confidence placed in them by people who have not looked at what they do.

The first way is the single criterion, and the employment office is his opening case. A single figure, he says, has the property of being the thing that is done: whatever the number counts, the organisation will produce, and whatever it does not count will be neglected, not from malice but because a person with one number to meet has been told, more clearly than any memo could tell them, what the job is. His second case for this is drawn from Joseph Berliner's interviews with Soviet managers who had left the country, published the same year, and from the general literature on the Soviet plan. A factory whose quota was set in tons produced heavy goods; set in units, it produced small ones; set by value, expensive ones, and in each case the quota was met and the economy was short of whatever the quota had not counted. The managers also, Berliner found, hoarded materials and labour against the next quota, rushed production into the last days of the plan period in what was called storming, and treated the customer as an irrelevance, since the customer was not the plan. The joke of the era, which Ridgway does not tell and which I include because it is the taxonomy in one image, was the cartoon of a nail factory whose plan was set in tonnage and which met it by producing one enormous nail.

Ridgway's second way is the multiple criterion, which is what the employment office turned to, and he argues that it does not solve the problem but moves it. A person given several numbers has to trade them off, and will do so according to which ones are noticed, which are easy, and which have consequences, and the trade-off is invisible to the people who set the criteria, since they see only the numbers and not the choices made between them. The Soviet manager with a dozen plan indices was not better controlled than the manager with one; he was a juggler, and he juggled for his own reasons.

The third way is the composite, in which several measures are weighted and summed into a single score, and Ridgway's objection to it is that the weights are a decision about what the organisation is for, made by whoever built the index, and that the people being scored will learn the weights and produce the score the same way they produced the single number, with the difference that now nobody can say what the score means. He ends without a remedy. His conclusion is that measurement changes what it measures, that this is a property of measurement and not a defect of the people measured, and that an organisation should know it before it builds its indicators, and the paper was read by almost nobody for thirty years.

Chapter Three: Goodhart, Nineteen Seventy-Five

The second discovery was made in a different country, in a different discipline, and in a footnote, more or less. Charles Goodhart was an economist at the Bank of England who was sent to a conference at the Reserve Bank of Australia in nineteen seventy-five to describe the British experience of trying to run monetary policy by targeting the money supply. The British had, from nineteen seventy-one, reformed their banking rules and begun to use the quantity of money in circulation as the thing they steered by, on the grounds that there was a stable, observable relationship between that quantity and the things they actually cared about, prices and output. The relationship had been real. It had been measured over years of data and it held. And then the Bank started using it, announcing targets for the money supply and acting to hit them, and it stopped holding, because the banks and their customers, who now knew what the Bank was watching, changed their behaviour to suit, and the quantity being measured no longer meant what it had meant when nobody was watching it.

Goodhart's paper stated the observation in a sentence that he has said he wrote half in jest and named after himself in the manner of Murphy's law: any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes. The paper is about monetary technicalities and the sentence is an aside in it. It was picked up by other economists, who found that the same thing happened to every monetary aggregate that any central bank adopted as a target, and the sentence acquired a name and a life. In nineteen ninety-seven an anthropologist, Marilyn Strathern, writing about the audit of British universities, rendered it in the form most people now know: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. That version is Strathern's, not Goodhart's, and it is broader than his, since he meant a statistical relationship and she meant any number at all.

I want to hold onto what is different about Goodhart's version, because the difference is the reason the constellation is worth three papers and not one. Ridgway's people were gaming. The interviewer who hid the vacancy knew what she was doing. Goodhart's banks were not, or not exactly. Nobody at a clearing bank sat down to break the Bank of England's model; they responded, each for their own reasons, to a policy that now made certain kinds of deposit cheaper or dearer, and the aggregate of their responses moved the number away from what it had meant. The regularity collapsed without anyone intending the collapse. This is the version of the law that applies when the people being measured are not employees at all, and it says that a number can stop meaning what it meant simply because it has been used, whether or not anyone is trying to fool you. An economist named Robert Lucas made a related argument the following year about why economic models fail when policy changes, and the two are usually mentioned together; Lucas's is a claim about models and Goodhart's about numbers, and Goodhart's is the one a manager needs.

Chapter Four: Campbell, Nineteen Seventy-Six

The third discovery is the one with the field cases, and the one that has been fought over most since, because its author was a psychologist working on how to evaluate government programmes, and the programmes he chose as examples were schools and police.

Donald Campbell was, by nineteen seventy-six, the most influential methodologist in American social science, the man who had taught a generation how to tell whether a reform had worked. In December of that year he gave a paper at Dartmouth, in an occasional-papers series that hardly anyone read, called Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change, and it was reprinted three years later in a journal called Evaluation and Program Planning, where it was read by everyone in that small field and by nobody outside it. Most of the paper is about how to evaluate programmes honestly. One section of it is about why the numbers a programme reports about itself cannot be trusted once the programme is judged by them, and that section contains the sentence now called Campbell's law: the more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures, and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor.

The cases are what make it stick. The first was the war on crime. Richard Nixon had taken office in nineteen sixty-nine promising to reduce crime and had made Washington, the one city the federal government policed directly, the demonstration. Two political scientists, David Seidman and Michael Couzens, went through the Washington figures afterwards and found how the reduction had been achieved: reported larcenies had been reclassified so that a theft worth fifty dollars, which counted as a serious crime under the federal definition, was recorded as forty-nine dollars, which did not, and the serious crime rate fell without any crime being prevented. Campbell's summary was that the main effect of a well-publicised, deliberate effort at social change had been the corruption of the indicator. His second case was the mirror of the first, and I think the more instructive. In nineteen sixty Chicago hired a reform police chief, Orlando Wilson, an honest man who insisted that crimes be recorded as reported rather than dropped, and the city's crime rate, on paper, rose sharply and stayed up, so that an improvement in policing appeared in the indicator as a crime wave. The number moved in the wrong direction because the reporting had got better, and the mayor who had hired the honest chief paid for it.

The third case was Vietnam. There the American command had begun by estimating enemy casualties and, when the estimates proved unbelievable, switched to counting bodies, on the reasoning that a body was a fact. The body count became the measure of a unit's success, and units produced bodies, and the bodies were counted more than once, and civilians were counted, and the figure that was meant to tell Washington whether the war was being won told it instead how badly the war wanted to be seen to be won. And the fourth case was the one that has since been quoted in every argument about schools: that an achievement test may be a good indicator of what a school teaches under conditions of ordinary teaching aimed at general competence, and that when the test score becomes the goal of teaching, it both stops indicating what it indicated and distorts the teaching, and Campbell was writing that fourteen years before anyone had heard of high-stakes testing and twenty-five before the law that made it national.

Campbell had a remedy, or the beginnings of one, and it is the place where his paper goes beyond the other two. He thought the corruption was a function of the stakes, and that the same indicator, collected by people who would not be judged by it, could be honest. He argued for multiple indicators, none of them decisive; for qualitative evaluation alongside the numbers; and, in an earlier paper on reforms as experiments, for a distinction between what he called the trapped administrator, who has staked his reputation on the programme's success and must therefore find it, and the experimental administrator, whose reputation rests on finding out whether the programme works and can afford the answer to be no. The whole difficulty, he said, was that the political system produced the first kind and needed the second.

Chapter Five: The Law in a White Coat

Before asking why the law had to be found three times, I want to show that medicine found it too, in its own material, and did not recognise it either, because the cases are the ones a clinician will carry longest.

The cleanest is a trial. Through the nineteen eighties cardiologists knew that patients who had survived a heart attack and who had frequent extra beats on their monitor, ventricular ectopics, died more often than those who did not. The extra beats were a good indicator; they had been measured for years and the association held. A new class of drugs suppressed them very effectively, and on the strength of that surrogate the drugs were being prescribed to hundreds of thousands of people. In nineteen eighty-seven the National Institutes of Health began a randomised trial, the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial, to confirm what everyone assumed, and two years later the monitoring board stopped it early, because the patients on the drugs, whose ectopics had been beautifully suppressed, were dying at more than twice the rate of the patients on placebo. The indicator had been a good indicator of risk under conditions in which nobody was acting on it. The moment a drug was chosen for its effect on the indicator, the indicator stopped meaning what it had meant, and the estimates of what the drugs had cost before the trial run into the tens of thousands of lives. That is Goodhart's version, the one with no gaming in it: no patient and no cardiologist cheated, and the regularity collapsed anyway, because the pressure applied for control purposes had been applied to the wrong point in the causal chain. The shelf said, two episodes ago, that Grove's biomarker proposal needed the paired-indicator rule applied to itself. This is what happens when it is not.

The second case is Campbell's version, in an English general practice. From two thousand and four the National Health Service paid family doctors a substantial share of their income according to a list of clinical indicators, the proportion of their diabetic patients with blood sugar below a threshold, of their hypertensives with pressure controlled, and so on, and the list was long and the money was real. Performance on the indicators rose fast, faster than the underlying care could plausibly have improved, and part of the reason was a provision called exception reporting, which allowed a practice to exclude from the denominator any patient it judged unsuitable for the target, and which some practices used, on the audits that followed, considerably more than others. The measured population got healthier partly because the hard patients had left it. It was a forty-nine-dollar larceny, done with a tick box, by people who mostly believed they were making a clinical judgement, and the honest practices, the Orlando Wilsons, who excluded nobody, scored worse.

The third case is closer to home for a researcher than either, and it is the one the field has been slowest to admit. A scientist's standing is judged, in most institutions, by numbers that were once indicators and are now targets: the count of papers, the citation count, the impact factor of the journals. Each of those was a reasonable proxy for a body of work under conditions in which nobody was managed by it. Each is now produced. One paper becomes three; the citation goes to a friend, or to oneself, rather than to the best source; the journal that once published what came in now manages what it publishes to protect a ratio, and there are journals whose impact factor has been withdrawn by the people who compute it for citing themselves too enthusiastically. None of this requires a villain. It requires a number with a consequence, a person who produces the number, and a distance between that person and whoever reads it, which is Campbell's law exactly, applied to the people who are supposed to know about Campbell's law. The taxonomy of research metrics gaming is now its own literature, and I think a listener can predict its findings from Ridgway's seven pages without reading a word of it.

Chapter Six: Why Three Times

So: an organisational sociologist in fifty-six, a central banker in seventy-five, an evaluation methodologist in seventy-six, each finding that a number used to judge people stops describing what it described, each in his own vocabulary, none citing the others. There was a fourth, in fact, in the year between the second and third: Steven Kerr, a management scholar, published a paper in nineteen seventy-five called On the Folly of Rewarding A While Hoping for B, the same law seen from the reward side, and which the management literature adopted as its own without noticing that the sociologists had been there twenty years earlier. And there was an ancestor, Robert Merton, whose nineteen forty essay on bureaucratic personality described the clerk who comes to treat the rule as the goal, and whom the shelf has in its queue.

The rediscovery is not an accident and it is not stupidity, and the reason is the one the shelf keeps finding. Each of these men was inside a field that did not read the others. Ridgway's paper is in a management journal, Goodhart's is in a central-bank proceedings volume, Campbell's is in an occasional-paper series on programme evaluation, and the citation networks of those three literatures did not touch. Each discovery got the name of the discoverer who was loudest in the field that later needed it: the economists needed a law when the monetary targets collapsed, so it is Goodhart's; the educators needed one when the tests took over the schools, so it is Campbell's; nobody needed one in nineteen fifty-six, so Ridgway has seven pages and a footnote in the literature review. It is a small, exact instance of a thing the shelf has been describing since Whyte: knowledge that exists in an organisation and cannot travel, because the channels run between people who already agree.

Chapter Seven: What Was Discovered

Now the law itself, and I want to argue that the common statement of it, the Strathern version, is not quite what any of the three found, and that the difference matters for what you do about it.

The common version is about measurement. It says that when you measure something and act on the measurement, the measurement goes bad. Stated that way it is a counsel of despair, and a manager who believes it has two options, to stop measuring or to measure and shrug. But look again at the three cases. The employment interviewer did not respond to being measured. Blau's office had counted interviews for years. She responded when the count became the thing she was judged by. The Bank of England's money supply had been measured, published, and modelled for a decade before it collapsed; it collapsed when the Bank started to act on it, and the banks knew it would. Washington's police had always recorded the value of stolen goods. The forty-nine-dollar larceny appeared when the crime rate acquired a president. In every case the number was fine until it acquired a consequence for the person who produced it, and the consequence, not the measurement, is the mechanism.

That reframing has three implications, and they are the reason the constellation is worth a listener's hour. The first is that the law is not about numbers. It applies with the same force to a qualitative judgement, an inspection, a supervisor's rating, the moment any of those carries a consequence for the person rated; it is easier to see in numbers because numbers make the drift visible. The second is that the corruption is proportional to the stakes and to the distance. Campbell's honest police chief could report a crime wave because he did not need the crime rate to fall; the interviewers in Blau's cooperative section could share vacancies because they had agreed not to be ranked by them. Where the number is collected far from where it is used, by people whose pay or standing depends on it, and where the people using it cannot see the process that made it, the drift is at its maximum, and the description I have just given is the description of every reporting chain in every distributed organisation on earth, including the ones that report on health.

The third implication is the delayed one, and it is where the constellation joins the rest of the shelf. Davies's accountability sink was a process that produced an outcome nobody was responsible for. Campbell's law describes the same object from the reporting side: a number that everyone in the chain has an interest in and nobody in the chain is accountable for the truth of, because the person who could check it is the person it is meant to inform. Jackall's managers, from episode one, kept every number vague for exactly this reason. And the connection to Grove is the useful one: his paired indicator is a Ridgway remedy, a second number chosen so that the two cannot be gamed in the same direction, and it works exactly as far as the pairing holds and no further, which is why the last episode found him, in his own Parkinson's, distrusting any score that the scorer could move by wanting to.

What none of the three papers says, and what the next episode has to, is what to do. Ridgway had no remedy. Goodhart's remedy, in monetary policy, was to stop targeting aggregates, which is not available to a programme that has to report something. Campbell's remedy was a change in the stakes, and the stakes are usually not the programme's to change. The shelf has, in the twenty years since these papers were rediscovered, a body of evidence about what happens when a health system is run on targets with consequences, and a smaller body about what has been tried against the drift, and the second half of the constellation is about that.

The question to carry into the week is Blau's, from the drawer. Somewhere in the work you run there is a number that people are judged by, and somewhere near it there is a vacancy in a drawer, a thing someone is doing to the number that you would not see from where you sit. Name the number. Then ask who produces it, what happens to them if it is bad, and whether you have ever once looked at how it is made rather than at what it says.

Next time, the second half of the constellation: what the English health service found when it ran hospitals on targets with terror attached, the spike at eight minutes in the ambulance data, the three kinds of gaming and the four kinds of people who do it, and what a programme that has to report numbers can do so that its numbers stay true. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Grove on medicine: the patient with a spreadsheet, the JAMA essay, and the physicians who wrote back
item.description: Andy Grove's third appearance on the shelf, as patient, funder and critic – the 1996 Fortune cover on his prostate cancer, worked out from published outcome tables with a spreadsheet; the 2005 JAMA essay on why medicine's knowledge turns are so slow; the Parkinson's years, the Society for Neuroscience speech and the e-trial proposal; and the case against, from Derek Lowe's 'Andy Grove fallacy' to the confounding his own cancer analysis walked into, with a verdict on which of his complaints medicine has answered and which it has not.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: A Number of Five

In the autumn of nineteen ninety-four, a few weeks before the Pentium became a story, Andy Grove had a routine blood test that came back with a prostate-specific antigen of five, against a normal range that stopped at four. He did what most fifty-eight-year-old men do with a number like that, which is nothing, for a while. Then, on a sabbatical the following spring, he had it measured again at two laboratories and got six point zero and six point one, and the arithmetic of a rising number did what the first number had not. A biopsy found cancer. The urologist recommended surgery, which is what urologists recommend, and Grove, who had spent thirty years running an organisation on the principle that a decision belongs to the person closest to the data, went to find the data.

He wrote up what he found in Fortune in May nineteen ninety-six, on the cover, under the title Taking on Prostate Cancer, and the article is the document I want to start from, because it shows the method of the two management books applied to a body, and because the method's strengths and its blind spot are both visible in it. He downloaded papers from a CompuServe forum. He read Thomas Stamey's work from Stanford on what PSA levels meant. He found the tables from Johns Hopkins that related what a surgeon found at operation to what happened afterwards, and he worked out that for a man with his PSA and his tumour grade the recurrence rate after surgery was about fifteen percent if the cancer was confined to the gland and about sixty percent if it had escaped it. He then did something that, he says, no one he consulted had done, which was to take the published outcome series for surgery, for external radiation, and for radioactive seeds, and cross-plot them against the patients' starting PSA, so that he was comparing treatments in men who started in the same place rather than in the mixed populations each specialty happened to treat. On that comparison the radiation results looked as good as surgery's, with fewer of the complications the surgeons' papers understated and the patients he interviewed did not. He consulted over fifteen physicians. The three eminent surgeons among them were, in his word, ferociously opposed to radiation. The radiation oncologist who offered the newest method, a high-dose-rate implant through sixteen needles combined with external beam, was asked what he would do himself and said he would probably have surgery. Grove went to Seattle and had the implant and twenty-eight mornings of external radiation, missed three days of work, and lived another twenty years, and died of something else.

A clinician hearing that story hears two things at once, and the shelf should hold both. The first is that a patient with a spreadsheet had found something the specialties had not, which is that nobody was comparing across them on matched patients, and that every specialist's recommendation was a recommendation for the thing that specialist did. Grove's line for that, which he says with no malice, is that urologists are surgeons and surgery is what they know. The second thing, which Grove half-saw and did not fully weigh, is that the cross-plot he built could not tell him what he needed to know, because the men who had been sent to radiation in those years were different from the men sent to surgery in ways that a starting PSA did not capture, and a treatment that looks as good in a sicker population may be better or may be worse. Epidemiologists call that confounding by indication, and it has ended careers. He noticed the selection problem, wrote a sentence about it, and went on to the balance sheet, which was drawn up, characteristically, on a bicycle trip. A Fortune reporter fact-checking the piece found an arithmetic error in the chart he had proudly built himself, which he acknowledged, and which I mention because it is the kind of detail Grove would have wanted kept.

The question this episode asks is what happens when the best-documented manager of his generation, having run his method on his own cancer and found it worked well enough, turns it on medicine as a whole. He did that three times over the following fifteen years, as an essayist, as a funder, and as a critic from the platform, and the field wrote back each time. The argument between them is, I think, the most useful thing Grove left for anyone in medical research, and it is more useful than either side would admit, because both were right about different layers of the same building.

Chapter Two: Knowledge Turns

In July two thousand and five the Journal of the American Medical Association published a three-page essay by Grove called Efficiency in the Health Care Industries: A View From the Outside. It is a curious document to find in that journal, and the journal knew it; the piece was invited, and it has the tone of a guest who has been asked to be frank and has decided to take the invitation literally.

The argument is built on a comparison and a number. In the forty years since he had joined Fairchild, the number of transistors that could be put on a chip had doubled every year or two, the pattern that his colleague Gordon Moore had named. In the same forty years, the war on cancer, declared by Nixon in nineteen seventy-one, had produced what Grove, looking at the mortality curves, called slow progress. He did not think the people were the difference. He said in so many words that both industries were populated by dedicated and well-trained people working from science. He thought the difference was the rate at which each industry turned knowledge over, and he gave the rate a name, knowledge turns, by analogy with inventory turns in a warehouse: the time it takes for an experiment to produce a result that generates the next experiment. In the semiconductor business a knowledge turn was measured in weeks, because you could build the thing, test it, and build the next one. In medicine, he argued, it was measured in years, because the test was a clinical trial, and the trial took years, and the result, when it came, was often a single number that told you the drug had not worked without telling you why.

From that he drew three recommendations, and they were specific, which is why the essay is still cited. The first was biomarkers: he wanted the National Institutes of Health to put something like a tenth of its budget, which he computed at two point eight billion dollars, into finding measurable signals that would tell a trial in months what it now learned in years from survival. The second was translational institutions: hospitals built for the purpose of moving discoveries into practice, on the model of the development fabs that Intel ran alongside its research, where a process was proven at scale before it went to production. The third was operational, and it was the one that made him angriest. He had found that no more than fifteen to twenty percent of American medical institutions used any kind of electronic record, in a year when the rest of the economy transacted hundreds of billions of dollars online. He wanted Medicare to require a common data standard as a condition of payment, and he called it a Rosetta stone, so that a patient's information could move between institutions the way a purchase order moved between companies.

Read that essay as a manager's document and the structure is familiar from the two books. There is a limiting step, the knowledge turn, and everything is arranged around shortening it. There is a leverage argument, that a measurement which shortens every subsequent trial is worth more than any single trial it could have funded. There is a paired indicator, though he does not call it that: he wanted the survival curve, the outcome, paired with a biomarker, the process signal that tells you early whether the outcome is likely to move. And there is the operational floor beneath the science, the records, which he treated as the equivalent of a fab that did not know its own yield. The essay is High Output Management with the breakfast factory replaced by an oncology ward.

What it does not have is any theory of why medicine's knowledge turns are slow, beyond the assumption that they are slow for the same reason a badly run factory's are, and that is where the physicians came in.

Chapter Three: The Funder

Grove's second engagement with medicine was not as a writer. In two thousand, two years after he stepped down as chief executive, he noticed a tremor in his right index finger, and the diagnosis was Parkinson's disease. He kept it private for some years, treated it the way he treated most things, with a programme, doubling his coffee, ninety minutes of exercise a day, delaying medication to preserve its effect for later, and then, when it became public, did what a person of his means and temperament would do, which was to fund the research and then to manage it.

The numbers, reported by Forbes in January two thousand and eight, were twenty-two million dollars committed to Parkinson's research over the decade and a forty million dollar bequest to the Michael J. Fox Foundation, where he served as an adviser. The programme was characteristic. Five million went to stem cell work at the University of California in San Francisco early in the decade, when almost nobody was funding it, with a joint grant alongside the Fox foundation to eight more laboratories; by two thousand and four the attempt to turn embryonic cells into dopamine neurons had failed, the cells reverting or forming tumours, and Grove noted the failure and moved the money. Two million went to something he called the At Home Box, an Intel-built device that measured a patient's speech and movement objectively, because the standard rating scale for the disease, the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale, was a clinician's subjective score and Grove regarded a subjective score as no measurement at all. He funded a neurosurgeon, Krystof Bankiewicz, who was working on delivering a growth factor, GDNF, directly into the brain, and Bankiewicz said afterwards that the funding had moved his work forward by years. And when the drug company Amgen abandoned its own GDNF trial, Grove tried, in late two thousand and seven, to license the programme and restart it, because one patient in the abandoned trial had improved by eighty percent and, as far as Grove could discover, nobody had gone back to find out why.

That last detail is the one I would keep, because there Grove's experience and the field's practice were furthest apart. In a fab, a failed lot is the most valuable thing that happens all week: the failure is analysed until it is understood, because the understanding is what stops it happening again, and a fab that threw away its failed lots without analysis would not survive a quarter. A trial that fails is closed. The drug is shelved, the data are archived, the one patient who responded is a footnote, and the field moves on, partly because the incentives run that way and partly because a single responder in a failed trial is, statistically, more likely to be noise than signal, which is a real reason and not one Grove had much patience for. The Forbes profile quotes him telling a room of researchers that if they could not get a drug to the target repeatedly and reproducibly they had wasted a career, and it quotes the blood-brain barrier as the thing he could not believe so little work went into. He was, in that room, the Cassandra of his own second book, the outsider who sees the ten-X problem the insiders have learned to live around. He was also a man who had not run a trial and did not know what one costs.

Chapter Four: The Speech, and the Reply

The third engagement was from a platform. In November two thousand and seven Grove gave a talk at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience in San Diego, to several hundred people, and around the same time gave an interview to Newsweek, and between them he said what he had been building up to for a decade. He criticised the National Institutes of Health for how it allocated money. He criticised researchers for not sharing data. He criticised the pharmaceutical industry for a culture that valued caution over what he called time to money, and for discarding failed drugs instead of mining the trials for what they could teach. He called, in a phrase that the reports all picked up, for a cultural revolution that valued curiosity, follow-through, and a problem-solving orientation, and that put all the data being generated in full view, where anyone could scrutinise it. And he made the comparison that had been implicit in the JAMA essay explicit: his industry had delivered Moore's law, and medicine, with comparable money and comparable people, had delivered levodopa, a forty-year-old symptomatic drug, and not much else for his disease.

The reply came within days, and the person who wrote it has to be named, because his phrase for the argument has outlived Grove's. Derek Lowe is a medicinal chemist who had spent his career in drug discovery and who wrote, and still writes, a widely read blog about it called In the Pipeline. His post was titled Andy Grove: Rich, Famous, Smart and Wrong, and the premise it attacked he named the Andy Grove fallacy, and the name stuck. Lowe's argument was that Grove had walked into a field where the equivalent of Moore's law is linear and was wondering where the curve had gone. Semiconductors were built on a century of solid-state physics that was, by the time Intel existed, essentially complete: the engineers knew how every component worked because they had designed every component. Biology was not designed by anyone, had a few billion years' head start, and was still yielding new components, and new interactions between old ones, every week. A chip that failed could be redesigned and retested in a month; a molecule that failed in a person could not be modified without risking a toxicity nobody could predict. And the two industries' failures were not the same kind of thing. David Hamilton, writing in VentureBeat the same week, made the point with a name: a failed chip cost Intel money, and a failed drug was Vioxx. The FDA existed because the failures were bodies, and the caution Grove was calling a cultural defect was, in part, the memory of the bodies.

Grove did not retreat. Four years later, in September twenty eleven, he wrote an editorial for Science called Rethinking Clinical Trials, and it was the knowledge-turns argument taken to its conclusion. Once a drug had passed its early safety testing, he proposed, patients who wanted it should be able to take it, with their physicians entering what happened into a shared database, so that the evidence would accumulate from use rather than from a trial, and be analysed by what he called, borrowing from the encyclopaedia, a Wikipedia-like process. He was proposing to replace the randomised trial with an observational registry and to let the crowd do the statistics. Lowe wrote back again, in a post he called A Note to Andy Grove, and this time the objection was one that any reader of this shelf could have supplied, because it is the objection to Grove's own cancer analysis: patients who choose a drug differ from patients who do not, and a database of the chosen tells you what happened to the people who chose, and nothing about the drug. The randomised trial exists because the alternative had been tried for two centuries and had produced bloodletting.

Lowe and Hamilton were, I think, right, and the shelf's own instruments say why. Grove's whole method depends on a fast, cheap, informative test, the thing that makes a knowledge turn short. The breakfast factory works because you can taste the egg. Everything in the two books, the paired indicator, the experiment, the debate, assumes that the world will answer a question in a reasonable time if you ask it clearly. Biology often will not, and the reason is not culture but the object. Grove had run into what the Seeing Like a State episodes called the limits of legibility from the other direction: not a state that could only see what it had simplified, but an engineer who assumed the object was as legible as the one he had spent his life with.

And yet. Hamilton, in the same piece that refuted him, said what Grove could usefully do instead, and it was the thing Grove was already doing: fund the unglamorous translational work between an academic finding and a company's willingness to spend on it, the validation nobody's incentives cover. And Lowe's fallacy, correctly stated, is about the science layer. It has no bearing on the records, or on whether specialists compare outcomes across modalities, or on whether the one patient who improved by eighty percent gets a phone call. Grove's critics won on knowledge turns and did not contest the floor beneath them, and the floor was where most of his complaints lived.

Chapter Five: What He Was Right About

I want to score the essay, since it is twenty-one years old and most of its claims can now be checked, and to do it honestly, which means separating the layers his critics ran together.

On records he was right, and the field agreed with him within four years. The American stimulus law of two thousand and nine put something over twenty-five billion dollars into paying hospitals and practices to adopt electronic records, with penalties for those that did not, and the adoption rate went from Grove's fifteen to twenty percent to something over ninety percent of hospitals in a decade. Whether it produced what he wanted is another matter, since the systems that were built do not talk to each other much better than the paper did, and the Rosetta stone he asked for, a common standard enforced by the payer, is still being argued about in twenty twenty-six. But the diagnosis was correct and the remedy he named was the remedy that was used, and a manager who is right about the mechanism and early about the timing has done what a manager can.

On biomarkers he was half right, and the half matters. A measurable signal that predicts the outcome months before the outcome arrives is exactly what the field has spent the last two decades building, in oncology above all, and the fraction of trials that use one to decide whether to continue is far higher than it was. But the essay's assumption was that the biomarker would shorten the knowledge turn without changing what was learned, and the field's experience has been that a biomarker can be moved without moving the patient, that a tumour can shrink on the scan while the person dies on schedule, and the last twenty years of drug regulation are, in part, a record of the surrogate endpoints that were trusted and should not have been. Grove's paired-indicator rule from the first book would have told him this. The biomarker is the process signal; survival is the outcome; and an organisation that rewards the first will get the first. He knew that about factories. He did not apply it to the thing he was recommending.

On translational institutions he was right about the gap and wrong about the model. The gap between a finding and a treatment is real, careers and molecules die in it, and the field has built things with the word translational in their name ever since. But the fab he was modelling them on works because the process being scaled is understood and the yield can be measured next week; the equivalent in medicine is a trial, and a trial is not a scale-up but an experiment whose answer is not known, and that is why it is being run. He was proposing to shorten the time between hypothesis and test. The time is mostly in the test, and the test's length is set by the disease.

And on the culture, on data sharing and failure analysis and the patient who improved and was never called, I think he was right and the field has been slow to say so. The data-sharing argument he made in two thousand and seven is the argument that produced trial registration mandates, results-reporting requirements, and the current pressure toward sharing participant-level data, none of which were the norm when he spoke. The failure-analysis argument has been made since by people inside the field, and the practice of going back into a negative trial to ask who responded and why is now done under a respectable name, though not often enough, and not usually with the urgency of a fab that has lost a lot. Grove did not cause any of that. He was one loud voice among many, and a rich one, which helped and also made him easy to dismiss. But the direction he pointed in is the direction the field went, and the fallacy Lowe named, which was real, was a fallacy about the part of the building Grove cared least about.

There is a fourth thing, and it is smaller and I think it is the one to carry. In his own cancer, and again with the Parkinson's rating scale, Grove's instinct was to distrust a measurement that depended on who was doing the measuring, and to build one that did not. The At Home Box was a two-million-dollar argument that a clinician's score on a scale is not a measurement, and the field's move since toward wearable sensors and objective motor assessment in that disease is the argument being accepted. That instinct, that an indicator which the person being measured or the person measuring can move by wishing it moved is not yet an indicator, is the one that connects this episode to the next, and it is the instinct a person running any programme on reported data should hold onto hardest. The shelf will spend two episodes on what happens when it is ignored.

Chapter Six: Swimming Across

A word on the memoir, because it explains the temperament, and because it is the best of his books as writing. Swimming Across, from two thousand and one, covers the twenty years before the Andy Grove that Intel knew existed. András Gróf, born in Budapest in September nineteen thirty-six, nearly killed by scarlet fever at four and left partly deaf; the German occupation of forty-four, hidden with his mother under a borrowed Christian name while his father was in a forced labour battalion on the eastern front; the siege; the Soviet liberation and the things the liberators did; the Communist years, in which the family's small dairy business was taken and a boy who wanted to be a journalist learned that the newspaper printed what it was told; the uprising of fifty-six, and, at twenty, the walk across a marsh to the Austrian border with nothing, and a ship to New York. Kirkus called the book tight, simply told, and extremely intimate, with what it called a sardonic but unmistakable faith in the American dream, and that is fair. The title is a teacher's remark that life is a lake to be swum across, and the book is not about Intel and never mentions it.

The connection to this episode is that a person who has lived through three changes of regime before the age of twenty, each of which arrived without warning and punished the people who had adapted to the previous one, is going to run a company on the assumption that the rules can change at any moment, and is going to treat a medical establishment that has not changed its rules in forty years as something between a puzzle and an affront. The paranoia of the second book and the impatience of the JAMA essay are the same trait, and Swimming Across is where the trait was formed. It does not make him right. It explains why he could not leave it alone.

Chapter Seven: The Case Against, Stated Hard

The objections to Grove's medical writing were made by people who knew the field, and I have given the best of them. Let me put them together as a case, because the shelf's rule is that the case against is stated at full strength before the verdict.

He extrapolated from a designed system to an evolved one and did not see the difference until it was pointed out, and, on the record, did not accept it afterwards. The knowledge-turns argument is not a management insight applied to medicine; it is a category error, and a manager of Grove's quality should have caught it, because the first question his own method asks is what the limiting step is, and in a trial that step is the disease. His cancer analysis, which he offered as the model of what a patient can do, walked into confounding by indication and came out with the answer he preferred, and it is possible to admire the effort and to say that a patient with a spreadsheet can be as wrong as a surgeon with a bias. His Parkinson's funding, on the Forbes numbers, produced a failed stem cell programme, a measurement device that was ahead of its time and did not change practice, and an accelerated growth-factor line that has still not produced a treatment; what it produced was pressure, and pressure is not a result.
