What Scott describes is what it is like on the ground, and he leans on the anthropologist James Holston, who lived there and wrote The Modernist City. The plan had abolished the street. There were no corners, because the superblocks were set in open space; no doorsteps, because the buildings stood on pillars; no crowds, because the sectors had sorted the crowd's reasons for existing into separate districts miles apart; no small shops beneath the apartments, because commerce had its own sector. The residents developed a word, brasilite, Brasília-itis, for the condition of living there, and Holston's informants described it as the absence of the small pleasures of city life, the crowd, the chance meeting, the sense that a place was being used. People who could afford to left for the satellite towns that grew up, unplanned and illegible, around the plan's edge, which is where most of the capital's population has lived ever since. The planned city was built, exactly as drawn. The city that people wanted to live in built itself, next to it, the way the underbrush comes back in the plantation.

And here is the observation that makes Brasília the book's hinge rather than one more example. The plan did not fail because it was badly executed. It was executed superbly, on time, by gifted people, and the failure is the execution. Every previous book on this shelf has found competence leaking out of an organization somewhere between intention and result: Parkinson's paperwork, Peter's final placements, the sinks that absorb what nobody wanted to know. Scott's cases invert that. Brasília is what happens when nothing leaks, when a plan meets an authority strong enough to carry it out without friction and a population unable to resist. The competence was all there. It was pointed at a picture of a city rather than at a city, and no amount of competence corrects that, because the correction would have had to come from the ground, and the ground was the thing the picture could not see.

Chapter Eight: What the Shelf Now Has, and What It Still Needs

Set this half of the book beside the last two episodes and a shape appears that neither Graeber nor Orwell had on their own. Orwell caught Burnham predicting a continuation of whatever was happening, and diagnosed the lean: a mind enchanted by power reads the present as the future. Scott's high modernist has a lean of the same family running the other way. He does not read the present as the future; he reads the plan as the present, and everything in the present that fails to match the plan as noise. Burnham's error was to trust the map of the winners. The planner's error is to trust a map he drew himself, which is a harder error to catch, because the map is very good, and because the person best placed to catch it, the villager or the resident or the forester's labourer, has been defined in advance as the person whose knowledge does not count.

And Graeber's structural stupidity, which two episodes ago looked like a moral failing of the powerful, now looks like something closer to a design constraint. A state cannot govern what it cannot read, and the tangle cannot be read without being simplified, and the simplification will always leave out the things that are hardest to write down, which are, as a rule, the things that keep the place alive. That is not a claim about bad people. It is about what a large organization is, and it lands, for this series, as a limit on every antidote the shelf has yet to consider. Whatever repair the later books propose, rotation, rival power, formal addresses for complaints, the repair will be administered by an institution that sees like a state, and its first act will be to make the problem legible enough to repair, which is where the trouble began.

The question part one leaves on the table is the one the four conditions pose, and it is a question about people rather than trees or streets. Brasília cost money and comfort; nobody starved in a superblock. What happens when the same aesthetic, backed by the same authority, facing the same prostrate society, is applied not to where people live but to how they eat, to the fields and herds that feed a country, by planners who have never farmed and are certain that farming is a science? Scott has two answers, one Soviet and one Tanzanian, and they are the darkest material this shelf has handled. He also has a word for what the planners destroyed, and a chapter arguing that the word names the kind of knowledge a society can least afford to lose. And then the critics arrive, some of whom think Scott has written the book he denied writing, and one of whom, an economist, suggests that the book's real hero is a man Scott never mentions, Friedrich Hayek. That is part two.

Next time, Seeing Like a State, part two: collectivisation, villagisation, mētis, and the case against. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Bullshit Jobs (Graeber): five types, and the two surveys that disagree
item.description: David Graeber's 2018 book on paid work that even the worker cannot justify – the five types, managerial feudalism, the polls that launched it, and the two surveys that later disagreed about whether any of it is real.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Computer That Moved Four Hundred Kilometres

One of the testimonies in the book comes from a man who worked for a subcontractor to the German military, and I want to tell it at its own pace because the whole argument is folded inside it. A soldier in a barracks wants to move a computer from one office to the office next door, a distance of about five metres. He cannot simply carry it. The army has outsourced its logistics to a private firm; that firm has passed the IT portion to a second one, and the second has handed the actual moving of equipment to a third. So the soldier fills in a form. The form goes to the first firm, which forwards it to the second, which forwards it to the third, and the third dispatches the man telling the story, who drives several hundred kilometres to the barracks, signs a document, unplugs the computer, carries it into the next room, plugs it in, signs another document, and drives home. The book's narrator does not need to add a moral; the day's mileage is the moral. Somewhere in that chain a number of people were paid, a contract was honoured, a compliance requirement was met, and a computer travelled five metres by way of a motorway.

Now ask the clinician's question about that story, the question this episode is going to keep asking: what is the denominator? The moving of the computer is a case. How many cases like it are there, out of how many working days in the German economy, and is the man telling it typical of anything or is he a memorable outlier who wrote to an anthropologist because anthropologists were asking? The book you are about to hear described is built almost entirely out of stories like this one, hundreds of them, collected from people who volunteered them. It is the most read book this shelf has covered and the least measured, and the interesting part is that the measuring was done afterwards, twice, by people who disagreed with each other about what it showed.

The question the book is about predates it by a long way, and this series has been circling it since the Parkinson episode. An organization is supposed to be a machine for turning effort into some output somebody wants. Parkinson found the effort multiplying regardless of the output; Peter found it settling into positions where it could no longer produce; the Davies episodes found the output nobody wanted being produced with enormous care because a process demanded it. What none of those books asked, because their authors were all looking at a single institution at a time, is the aggregate version. Add it all up across a whole economy, every Colonial Office clerk and every final-placement supervisor and every duplicate reporting line, and how much of the paid work in a rich country is, on the honest account of the person doing it, for nothing? Graeber's answer is a number, and the number is the problem.

Chapter Two: An Essay, a Poll, and a Book

David Graeber was introduced two episodes ago, and the biography that matters here is the same: London School of Economics, Debt: The First Five Thousand Years, the planning meetings of Occupy Wall Street, and a mother's paperwork. What comes between The Utopia of Rules and this book is an essay, and the essay's reception is half the story.

In the summer of two thousand and thirteen a small radical magazine called Strike! asked Graeber for something provocative and he gave them three thousand words titled On the Phenomenon of Bullshit Jobs. The premise was a question he attributed to Keynes: in nineteen thirty, Keynes had predicted that by the end of the century technology would have advanced enough that countries like Britain or the United States would be working a fifteen-hour week. The technology arrived. The short week did not. Graeber's essay proposed that the missing hours had not been absorbed by more production of things people want, but by the invention of work, whole categories of employment that exist without producing anything, and that the people inside those categories know it. His phrase for the damage was that it is a scar across our collective soul. The essay's most quoted move was a thought experiment: imagine a class of workers vanishing overnight and ask whether anyone would miss them. Nurses, refuse collectors, mechanics, teachers, dock workers gone, and the world is in trouble within days. Private equity executives, lobbyists, public relations researchers, actuaries, telemarketers, bailiffs, legal consultants gone, and it is not obvious how anyone would suffer. From which he drew a general rule, that the more obviously a job benefits other people, the less it tends to pay.

The essay went around the world. The magazine's website fell over under the traffic; the piece was translated into more than a dozen languages within weeks. And then the poll. In two thousand and fifteen the polling firm YouGov asked British workers whether their job made a meaningful contribution to the world. Thirty-seven percent said no, and a further thirteen percent were not sure. A Dutch survey around the same time produced a figure near forty percent. Graeber had written a provocation with a made-up range in it, somewhere between twenty and fifty percent of all jobs, and now a real poll had landed inside the range, and the provocation had become a finding, or something that could be presented as one. He asked people who felt they had bullshit jobs to write to him, several hundred did, and the book that came out in two thousand and eighteen, Bullshit Jobs: A Theory, is built on those testimonies, the poll, and a theory of why a market economy would produce this at all.

The definition, in the book, is tighter than the essay's and it needs to be got exactly right because most of the later argument depends on what it includes. A bullshit job is paid employment so pointless, unnecessary, or pernicious that even the person doing it cannot justify its existence, though the terms of employment oblige them to pretend otherwise. Two clauses carry it. The first is even the employee: this is not an outsider's judgement that your job is worthless, it is your own. The second is the obligation to pretend, which is what distinguishes a bullshit job from a merely bad one. A bad job, in Graeber's vocabulary, is one that is useful and awful: cleaning, care work, the kind of thing that would be missed within a day and is paid as though it would not. A bullshit job is one that is comfortable and hollow, and the hollowness has to be concealed, from the boss, from the family, sometimes from the worker's own account of the week.

Chapter Three: Five Ways to Be Paid for Nothing

The book's taxonomy is the part people remember, and it earns the memory, because each of the five types names a mechanism rather than a job title. Graeber is careful about that: no occupation is bullshit as such; the types describe what a role is for within an organization, whatever it is called on the door.

Flunkies exist to make somebody else feel or look important. The receptionist in an office that gets three calls a day is not there for the calls. She is there because a firm of that kind has a receptionist, and a partner who walks past an empty desk in the morning is a partner at a lesser firm. Graeber's own examples run from doormen to the assistants of assistants, and the mechanism is feudal in a way he will make explicit later: retainers whose function is the standing of the person they are attached to.

Goons exist because the other side has goons. Lobbyists, corporate lawyers, telemarketers, the publicist whose job is to counter a competitor's publicist. Graeber's test is that the role only makes sense in an adversarial frame: if every firm's lobbyists vanished at once, no firm would be worse off relative to any other, which means the aggregate contribution of the category is zero by construction. Note that the goon's job is often not pointless from the employer's point of view, which is why this type sits awkwardly in a definition built on the worker's own judgement; a good deal of the book's later trouble with critics lives in this category.

Duct tapers exist to fix a problem that should not exist. The programmer who spends his life patching code that was written badly because the firm would not pay for it to be written well; the airline employee whose entire role is calming passengers whose luggage the airline has lost, when the money spent calming them would have paid for not losing the luggage. This one connects straight back to Davies, three episodes and a companion piece into the series: the duct taper is an accountability sink with a salary, a person whose presence lets an organization keep a fault permanent by making its consequences absorbable.

Box tickers exist so that an organization can claim to be doing something it is not doing. The officer whose reports on a hospital's patient-consultation process are produced, filed, and never read, so that the hospital can say consultation occurs. The whole audit society Davies described is staffed by box tickers, and the sharp thing in Graeber's account is the worker's experience of it: box tickers frequently know the box is the product, and their job is to keep producing it convincingly.

And taskmasters exist to assign work to people who would work without being told to, or, in the second and more corrosive variant, to invent work for others, the manager who generates the checklists and the forms and the strategic-alignment exercises that the box tickers below then tick. Taskmasters of the second kind are the ones who produce bullshit jobs downstream, and Graeber's diagram of an organization in this condition is one where taskmasters at the top manufacture tasks, box tickers in the middle complete them, and duct tapers at the bottom absorb the damage, with flunkies attached to everyone senior and goons on the perimeter.

Read that structure against the shelf and it maps onto the last five books with almost no adjustment. Parkinson's officials who make work for each other are taskmasters and box tickers in a closed loop. Peter's final-placement supervisor, the person promoted one rung past competence, is very often a taskmaster of the first kind, supervising people who need no supervision because that is the only supervision he is now capable of. And Whyte's organization man, the well-adjusted middle who identified with the firm, is what a box ticker looks like before he has admitted to himself what the box is. Graeber's contribution is not that he found these people. Everyone on this shelf found them. His contribution is the claim that they are now a large fraction of the workforce, and that the fraction is not a side effect of bureaucracy but the product of a specific economic arrangement, which he names.

Chapter Four: Managerial Feudalism

Here is the puzzle the theory has to solve, and Graeber states it fairly. Under the textbook account of a market economy, bullshit jobs should not exist. A firm that pays people to do nothing is a firm with higher costs than a competitor that does not, and competition should eliminate it. That is the argument every economist made against the essay within a week of its publication, and it is a good argument. Governments might pad payrolls for political reasons, the objection goes, but private firms cannot afford to, so if the phenomenon is real it must be a public-sector phenomenon, which would be an old and unsurprising finding.

Graeber's answer is that the textbook is describing an economy we no longer have. What we have, he argues, is managerial feudalism: a system in which a growing share of the economy's surplus is captured not by producing things but by controlling flows of money, rent, and administrative position, and in which the people who capture it distribute a portion of it downward in the form of retainers, because in a system of that kind having retainers is how standing is displayed and maintained. A feudal lord does not employ a hall full of attendants because they are productive. He employs them because a lord with a small retinue is a small lord. Graeber's claim is that the managerial class in finance, in the professional services that orbit finance, in the administrative layers of universities and hospitals, has recreated exactly that logic, and that the growth of the administrative layer in every large organization since the nineteen seventies is what feudal retinues look like when they are wearing lanyards.

The mechanism has three parts, and each connects to something the shelf has already documented. The first is the one Graeber shares with the flying-cars essay two episodes ago: the redirection of the economy's investment from making things toward administering, monitoring, and financialising the things that already exist. If the profitable activity is control rather than production, then the labour that control requires, compliance, reporting, reconciliation, the manufacturing and completion of forms, grows regardless of whether anything is being made. The second part is political, and it is where Graeber is most a moralist: a population kept busy is a population that does not have the time to ask what the arrangement is for, and he suggests, without quite claiming it as a design, that the ruling class of any period has understood that a leisured, unemployed, healthy population is a danger. The third part is cultural, and it is the one his critics find hardest to dismiss. Work has become, in the rich countries, the primary source of moral standing, so that a person who does not work is a person without a claim on the respect of others, regardless of what the work produces. The result is that everybody, including the worker in a bullshit job, has a stake in the job continuing, because the alternative is not leisure but disgrace.

That third part is Whyte's Social Ethic, seventy years on and stripped of its optimism. Whyte's organization man believed that belonging to the group was a moral good in itself. Graeber's box ticker believes, or has been made to believe, the same thing about having a job, and the two beliefs are one belief with the group replaced by the payroll. What Whyte saw as the birth of a new ethic Graeber sees at the end of its life, when the belief has outlived the conditions that made it plausible, the productive firm with a real product and a real career inside it, and continues to run on its own momentum. The organization man at least had an organization. The bullshit worker has a badge that opens a door to a desk at which nothing happens.

And I would push the shelf's own frame one step further than Graeber does, because the series has an instrument he lacked. He explains why an economy would pay for hollow work. He does not quite explain why nobody inside the organization stops it, given that many of them know. The Davies series answered that: nobody in a position to stop it is running the organization. Command left the owners and did not arrive at the managers; it dissolved into the procedures between them. A taskmaster who realised tomorrow that his department produced nothing could not abolish it, because the department is now an input to three other departments' reports, and a report that arrives without its input is a compliance failure with a name attached. Bullshit jobs persist for the same reason the sinks persist: the machine that would have to catch them is the machine they are part of.

Chapter Five: The Book at Its Strongest

Before the numbers, the steelman, because the book's best chapter is not the theory. It is the chapter on what the condition does to the people in it, and here the testimonies stop being anecdotes and start being clinical material.

Graeber's expectation, and the reader's, is that a job where nothing is required of you would be experienced as a kind of freedom. Eight paid hours, no output, an internet connection. The testimonies say otherwise, consistently and in detail. The people writing to him describe anxiety, depression, a corrosion of self-respect that they cannot explain to friends who work real jobs and cannot mention to the employer who has, after all, done nothing wrong. Several describe the specific torment of having to look busy, of maintaining a performance of work for a manager who may or may not know it is a performance. One of the book's most-quoted contributors, a man whose entire job was to be present in case a rarely used system failed, describes the experience as being paid to be a piece of furniture. Graeber reaches for a concept from developmental psychology to explain the damage: the pleasure of being the cause, the infant's discovery that its actions produce effects in the world, which he argues is the root of the human sense of self. A job in which nothing you do produces any effect is not rest. It is a slow attack on the faculty that makes you a person.

That is a real observation, and it is the part of the book that the later surveys confirmed without controversy. Whatever the prevalence of the condition, the people who report it are measurably worse off. I will come back to how much worse. But the steelman is that Graeber identified a form of harm that the discipline of work had not been looking for, because its instruments measured hours, pay, safety, and satisfaction, and this harm survives all four being fine. You can be well paid, safe, working reasonable hours, reporting satisfaction on the annual survey because the survey does not have a box for this, and still be coming apart in a way that only the plain question, would anyone miss your job if it vanished, can reach. The book made that question askable. That is not nothing, and it may be most of what the book will be remembered for.

Chapter Six: The Two Surveys

Now the measuring, which is where this shelf's home lens is needed, and the finding is that the answer depends entirely on which question was asked.

The first serious test came from a Cambridge and Birmingham group, Magdalena Soffia, Alex Wood and Brendan Burchell, published in Work, Employment and Society in twenty twenty-two under the title Alienation Is Not Bullshit. They went to the European Working Conditions Survey, which asks a very large sample of workers across the European Union, every five years, a battery of questions about their jobs, one of which is how often they have the feeling of doing useful work. Take the people who answer rarely or never as the bullshit-job population and the numbers come out like this. In two thousand and five, seven point eight percent. In twenty ten, five point five. In twenty fifteen, four point eight. Not twenty to fifty percent; under five, and falling. The regional pattern was the reverse of Graeber's expectation too: the Nordic countries lowest at three percent, the British Isles and the Mediterranean highest at about five and a half. And the occupations at the top of the uselessness table were not the lobbyists and the compliance officers. They were labourers in mining, construction and transport, at fifteen percent; refuse workers, near ten; cleaners, at eight. The refuse collectors, the very people Graeber's thought experiment held up as the workers society could not do without, were among the most likely to say their own work was useless. Teachers, doctors and lawyers were at the bottom, around one percent. Graduates reported the condition at half the rate of non-graduates. The group's conclusion was that Graeber's account could not be sustained: the perception of useless work was real and was strongly associated with poor wellbeing, but it tracked bad management, lack of autonomy and disrespect rather than occupation, so that what it tracked was what Marx called alienation, a much older idea, and one that does not require a theory of managerial feudalism to explain.

The second test came a year later from Simon Walo at Zurich, in the same journal, and it reached the opposite headline. Walo used the American Working Conditions Survey from twenty fifteen, about eighteen hundred workers, and a different question: whether the respondent's job was, in their own view, socially useless, or gave them the feeling of making a positive impact on their community and society. Nineteen percent said their job was useless. And when he sorted by occupation, Graeber's categories showed up. Sales workers were two and a half times as likely as everyone else to consider their jobs useless; business and finance roughly twice; managers nearly twice; office and administrative support about one and three-quarter times. Legal work leaned the same way but did not reach significance. Those ratios survived adjustment for the very factors Soffia's group had said explained everything, the routine content of the work, the autonomy, the quality of management. Walo's verdict was that Graeber's theory had robust support, at least in what he called the heavily financialised Anglo-Saxon economies, while also finding that the alienation variables mattered too, so that useless work was multifactorial rather than any one thing.

So one study says five percent and falling and the wrong occupations, and the other says nineteen percent and the right ones. Both are competent. Both are in the same journal. How does a listener decide?

This is the moment the shelf's own instruments earn their keep, because the disagreement is not really about bullshit jobs. It is about a question this series has met twice already in other clothes: the rate you get depends on what you count, and the same statistic differs when the frame differs. Look at the two questions. The European survey asks how often you feel you are doing useful work. That is a question about the experience of the working day; a refuse collector on a bad crew under a contemptuous supervisor, doing objectively vital work, can answer never, and he is not wrong about his week. The American survey asks whether the job is socially useless or makes a positive impact on society. That is a question about the job's standing in the world, and a sales executive who is well managed and autonomous can answer useless, and he is not wrong about the job. Graeber's definition was the second kind of question: the worker's judgement of the job's contribution, not the worker's feeling of usefulness on a Tuesday. Soffia's group measured alienation and found alienation. Walo measured the thing Graeber described and found something like it, at a rate about half of the YouGov figure that started the whole affair, and concentrated where the book said it would be.

Which means the honest reading is narrower than either headline. The book's number, twenty to fifty percent, does not survive. Its map, that the condition concentrates in finance, sales, administration and management rather than in the useful-and-awful jobs, does survive, at least in the United States, at around one worker in five, and about one in nine in the occupations the book did not accuse. And the mechanism that best explains the remainder of the variation is not feudalism but the old and boring one, the quality of the relationship between a worker and the people above him. Graeber is right about where the hollow jobs are and wrong about how many there are, and the thing he most wanted to be right about, that the hollowness is a structural product of financialised capitalism rather than of bad bosses, is the part the evidence splits on, with the better-designed test of his own definition leaning his way.

Chapter Seven: The Case Against

The critics had assembled before either survey and their counts should be heard at full strength, because the strongest of them are about the book's method rather than its number.

Michael Robbins, reviewing it for The Nation, put the central objection in one sentence: the book's reliance on workers' subjective impressions of whether their work has value is its major weakness. A testimony is a self-selected story told to a sympathetic collector. The several hundred people who wrote to Graeber were people who had read an essay about bullshit jobs, recognised themselves in it, and wanted to be in the book. No one who read the essay and thought, that is not me, wrote in to say so. The book's evidence base is a case series with no controls. A series like that can establish that a condition exists and describe what it looks like, which Graeber did well, but it cannot say how common the condition is, and the book's central claim is about prevalence. Robbins also caught a factual problem the Bureau of Labor Statistics could have fixed for free: the fastest-growing job categories in the United States are not information and administrative work but care work and food service, useful-and-awful jobs, the opposite of what the theory predicts is expanding.

The second count is the feudalism. Robbins again, and he is not alone: an economy in which surplus is extracted from the labour of others by the owners of capital is a capitalist economy, whatever its retinues look like, and calling it feudal does not make the profit motive disappear from the firms that employ flunkies. The word does rhetorical work; it does not do analytical work. The taskmaster who hires a retinue is still, on the shelf's account, a component of a machine optimising for something, and the interesting question, which the book never quite reaches, is what that something is. Davies's answer, that the machine is optimising for the survival of its own procedures, explains the retinue without needing the lord.

The third count is about the taxonomy, and Andrew Anthony in The Observer made it briskly: the five types are arbitrary distinctions dressed as discoveries. A goon's job is not bullshit to the firm that pays for it; a duct taper is doing real work on a real problem; a flunky in a service economy is delivering a service, standing, that the customer demonstrably wants. The categories name the worker's discomfort and then treat the discomfort as evidence of pointlessness, when several of them describe work that is pointed, just not at anything the worker respects. Nathan Heller, in The New Yorker, added the gentlest and most damaging version: some of these jobs are apprenticeships, training that looks like nothing because it is being done by someone not yet able to do the real thing, and some are a form of workfare the society has decided it prefers to unemployment, and that is a policy, not a scandal.

And Emma Duncan, in The Times, supplied the number Graeber's Keynes framing needed and did not have. The British working week fell from about fifty-six hours in nineteen hundred to about thirty-one in twenty eighteen. Keynes's fifteen did not arrive, but half of the distance to it did, and a theory that opens by asking where the promised leisure went has to account for the leisure that actually came. She called the book enjoyably overstated, and the adverb is doing a lot of the reviewing.

I want to add a count of my own, the one the shelf's history of Graeber makes visible. Two episodes ago The Utopia of Rules argued that bureaucracy persists because it does not have to earn your understanding; it only needs the standing to make you do the interpretive labour. That was a structural claim about power, and it did not depend on anyone's feelings. Bullshit Jobs is the same author making a claim that depends entirely on feelings, the worker's own verdict, and then treating the verdict as a measurement of the economy. The earlier book's method was better. The later book's subject was more popular. It is not a coincidence that the popular one is the one with the number in it.

Chapter Eight: The Verdict and the Dose

The verdict is that this is a good essay that became a famous book, and that the famous book contains one durable finding and one number that should never be quoted. The finding is the harm: paid work that the worker cannot justify produces a specific and measurable injury, invisible to every conventional measure of job quality, and both later surveys, whatever else they disagreed about, confirmed that the people who report it are substantially worse off. The number is the prevalence. Twenty to fifty percent was a provocation that a poll happened to land inside, and the two proper tests since put the figure at under five percent by one definition and around nineteen by the other, with the higher figure the better match to what Graeber actually meant. If you must carry a single figure, carry Walo's: about one in five American workers, concentrated in sales, finance, administration and management, and the rate in those occupations roughly double the rate elsewhere.

The dose is diagnostic, and the book is better taken in a specific order. Read the two thousand and thirteen essay first, in twenty minutes; it contains the whole idea and none of the padding. Then read the book's chapter on the psychological effects, the part the testimonies were made for. Skip the feudalism until you have read Davies, because Davies explains the same persistence without the costume. And read Soffia's paper and Walo's paper together, in that order, as an exercise in the pattern this series keeps finding: the same phenomenon, two competent groups, two questions, two answers, and the difference lives in the wording of a single survey item.

What this leaves you asking is Graeber's own, and it survives every objection to his book because it was never a claim. Take your own job, and the three jobs nearest to it in the building, and ask of each one, not whether it is hard, not whether it is paid, not whether it is respected, but whether anything would happen if it stopped. Be specific about the anything. A report that would not be filed is not a consequence unless somebody would act differently for lack of it; a meeting that would not occur is not a loss unless a decision would go unmade. If you can name the consequence, you have a job, whatever the survey says. If the only consequence you can find is that someone would remark on the absence of the activity, and nothing downstream of the activity would change, then you have found one of Graeber's, and the useful part of his book is the reminder that the person in it already knows, and has been told, by everyone including himself, not to say so.

Next time, the shelf leaves the cynical core and begins its systems turn with a book about what happens when the people at the top of a state can see everything except what matters: James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State, part one, on forests, surnames, and the city built from the air. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Orwell, Second Thoughts on Burnham: how to tell a forecaster from a fan
item.description: Orwell's 1946 essay read as a method for telling a forecaster from a fan, with the twist that Orwell's own prediction at the end of it took forty-five years to come in.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Ledger

Suppose a colleague has been confidently wrong about the same thing four times in a row, and each time the wrong answer pointed in the same direction. You would not, at that point, be very interested in his fifth answer. You would be interested in the direction. Misses that scatter are bad luck or a hard problem; misses that all lean the same way are a finding about the person doing the forecasting, and the polite thing, the clinical thing, is to stop arguing with the forecasts and start looking for the lean.

That is the method in the essay this episode is about, and most of us never apply it, least of all to ourselves. This shelf has now met James Burnham three times. Episode seven found his managerial revolution, the claim that command was migrating from owners to administrators, and set it against Whyte. Episodes ten and eleven read The Machiavellians, the best of his books, and caught its school taking fascist professorships. Both times George Orwell's nineteen forty-six essay in Polemic, Second Thoughts on James Burnham, was cited the way you cite a verdict, in a subordinate clause. It has earned a reading of its own, and the verdict is the least interesting thing in it. What Orwell built is an instrument, and the instrument has a use far past Burnham.

Orwell, for the two people listening who need the biography: the Eton scholarship boy who went to Burma as an imperial policeman and came back sick of it, who washed dishes in Paris and went down the mines in Wigan and took a fascist bullet through the throat in Spain, and who by nineteen forty-six was thin, tubercular, widowed, and writing at a rate that suggests he knew how long he had. He had four years left. In them he produced most of the essays people still read and the novel that everybody reads, and the essay on Burnham sits at the hinge between the two, because it is where he worked out, in public, the psychology he then installed in Nineteen Eighty-Four. He had reviewed The Managerial Revolution in nineteen forty-four and taken its thesis seriously, doubts and all. The word in the title is second thoughts. He had changed his mind, and the essay is the record of why.

Here is the ledger he lays out, presented as flatly as he presents it. In nineteen forty, writing The Managerial Revolution, Burnham treated German victory as effectively settled and described the coming world on that basis. In the supplementary note of nineteen forty-two he wrote as if the Soviet Union were already beaten. By the winter of forty-four, in articles and the book that followed The Machiavellians, the Red Army was moving fast through eastern Europe, and Burnham's prophecy switched: now the future was Russian conquest of the whole of Eurasia. Orwell simply puts the dates next to the forecasts and lets them sit there. Every forecast was written at the high-water mark of the power it predicted, and every one mistook the mark for the tide.

So the lean is established before the theory is touched. That is the first thing to take from the essay: Orwell audits the track record before he argues the model. Most critics do it the other way around, and so, in my experience, do most journal clubs.

Chapter Two: The Diagnosis

What does a run of same-direction misses tell you about the forecaster? Orwell's answer comes in one sentence that this shelf has already quoted, about Burnham predicting a continuation of whatever is currently happening, and then in a second, cruder one that I think is the better instrument: whoever is winning at the moment will always seem to be invincible. He gives the examples with a straight face. If the Japanese have taken south Asia, they will hold it for ever. If the Germans have taken Tobruk, they will take Cairo. Then he names the mechanism, and the name has aged well: power worship. It blurs political judgement, he says, because it leads almost unavoidably to the belief that present trends will continue.

Now, a modern reader will hear that and reach for the vocabulary of the cognitive-bias literature, recency, extrapolation, the hot hand, and the reach is fair as far as it goes. But Orwell's claim is narrower and nastier than a bias. A bias is a lean everyone has. He is saying Burnham's lean has a direction, that it does not just extend trends but extends them on behalf of the strong, and that this tells you something about what Burnham wanted. The evidence he uses is not the forecasts at all. It is the prose. And the passage he chooses is the one I would have chosen, which is a little alarming.

In nineteen forty-five Burnham published an essay called Lenin's Heir, in which the man who had for years described Stalin as a jumped-up bureaucrat, the gray clerk who had betrayed the revolution, suddenly rediscovered him as a colossal figure, and Orwell quotes the paragraph where the rediscovery happens. It is a description of a Kremlin banquet. Burnham lingers on the toasts, the vast table, the silent secret police standing behind each guest, and, as the backdrop to all of it, the starving multitudes of the winter outside. Burnham presents this as analysis, a sober register of the scale of the thing. Orwell reads it as what it is: prose that has fallen in love. He calls the tone a sort of fascinated admiration. The starving multitudes are there for contrast, the way a painter puts shadow behind a face, and the face is Stalin's.

Then Orwell does the move that turns a review into an essay. He asks why Burnham needs the shadow at all, and answers that the cruelty is not incidental to the admiration but its source. Burnham finds Stalin admirable, in this passage, in proportion to the scale of the brutality, because to a mind of a certain kind, naked force looks like the realest thing there is. Everything softer, law, custom, the possibility that people might refuse, registers as sentiment, and sentiment is what a realist is proud of having outgrown. So the realist's forecasts lean toward the whip, not because he has weighed the evidence and the whip won, but because the whip is the only evidence his instrument is built to detect. Orwell's phrase for the whole condition, applied to the intellectual class and not only to Burnham, is that it is a major mental disease with roots partly in cowardice and partly in the worship of power, which, he adds, is not fully separable from cowardice.

That last clause is where the essay stops being about one American. Put it against the shelf. Jackall's managers in Moral Mazes had a rule, look up and look around, and the looking was worship of a very small local power; Whyte's organization man surrendered his interior to the group because the group was, locally, what was winning. The disease Orwell names at the scale of world history is the ordinary condition of the middle of any hierarchy, and his diagnosis is the one this series has kept reprinting in the form of a dosage warning. Diagnostic doses of the cynical frameworks are medicine. Identity doses are poison. Orwell caught the overdose in a distinguished patient, and what the banquet passage shows is what the overdose looks like on the page: the analyst's sentences start to glow when the subject is cruel.

Chapter Three: The Steelman, Which Orwell Supplies Himself

Is the diagnosis fair? The test of a critic is what he concedes, and Orwell concedes a great deal, more than the essay's reputation suggests. He grants that Burnham has probably been right about the present and the immediate past, that for fifty years the general drift has been toward oligarchy, toward the concentration of economic and political power in fewer hands and the decline of the representative institutions that were supposed to check it. He grants the managerial class is real. He grants, and this is the concession that matters, that the world Burnham describes, three great super-states, each too large to be conquered, each run by a self-selected elite, is a plausible destination for the drift if nothing interrupts it. He simply refuses to grant that nothing will interrupt it.

That is a lot to give away. A lesser critic would have used the four bad forecasts to throw out the structure. Orwell keeps the structure, discards the forecast, and treats the forecast's failure as information about the forecaster rather than about the world. That is the separation this shelf has tried to keep in its own hands, between what the author claims, what the evidence supports, and what the reader concludes, and Orwell keeps it under pressure, about a man whose politics he found repellent. His Burnham is not a fool. His Burnham is a mind of real gifts running a good structural model through a bad instrument.

And the essay contains one more concession that is really an accusation against the rest of us. Orwell notes, almost in passing, that Burnham never stops to ask why people want power. He treats power hunger as a natural instinct that needs no more explanation than hunger for food. Orwell thinks it is a pathology, historically conditioned, no more natural than the want of a title, and that a theory which cannot see that will always mistake the current shape of the disease for the permanent shape of the species. The shelf has a running version of this objection. Episode eleven's case against The Machiavellians was that the iron law of oligarchy is iron only if you stop counting, that organizations have held oligarchy at bay for generations by engineering rival power inside their walls. Orwell got there first, in nineteen forty-six, in one sentence: the realist has assumed the constant he most needed to test.

Chapter Four: The Prediction at the End

Here the essay rounds on its author, and it is the part nobody quotes. Having demonstrated that a forecaster's lean can be read off his forecasts, Orwell ends by making a forecast of his own. Burnham's managerial society, he argues, is an unstable form, because slavery is no longer a stable basis for human society, and so the Russian regime will either democratize itself, or it will perish. He does not put a date on it. He suggests, in a hedge that is easy to miss, that it could take some time.

Now score it, the way he scored Burnham. In nineteen forty-six the sentence was wishful. Ten years later, after Hungary, it was wrong. In nineteen sixty-eight, after Prague, it was still wrong, and Burnham's three-bloc world was, at that point, the better description of the map. The prediction came in, in a form Orwell did not specify, in nineteen ninety-one, forty-five years after he made it, which is a longer horizon than any of the four Burnham forecasts he had lined up for execution. If you had audited Orwell in nineteen seventy, by his own method, you would have had a forecaster whose one big call had been open and losing for a quarter century, and whose lean was plain: he predicted the fall of the thing he hated.

I raise this not to even the score but because it is the actual lesson, and the essay's admirers, who tend to read it as Orwell winning, mostly miss it. The track-record audit is a real instrument. It found Burnham's lean, and Burnham's lean was real, and his later career confirmed it: the harder line always, the Cold War as a fight already decided, the medal from Reagan. But the instrument cannot, by itself, distinguish a lean from a long-horizon call. Both look identical for as long as the horizon stays open. The only thing that separated them, in the end, was that one of the forecasters had a mechanism and the other had a mood. Orwell's prediction had a reason attached: a state that runs on terror cannot get the effort out of its people that one running on some measure of consent can, and the gap will compound. Burnham's predictions had no mechanism except momentum. That is what the same-direction misses were detecting. Not that he was wrong, but that he had no way of ever being told he was.

Which changes what the audit is for. It grades nobody. It finds the forecasters who cannot lose, and those are the only ones you should never trust.

Chapter Five: The Case Against, and the Revival

The essay faces two counts, and the second is livelier now than it has been since nineteen forty-six.

Count one is about method, and it is the objection Orwell's own instrument invites. Reading a man's motive off his prose is a diagnosis, not a demonstration. The banquet passage is presented as a tell, and it is a tell, but a critic who reads tells has to accept that he is doing psychology on a text, that the text cannot answer back, and that the same reading applied to Orwell would find, in the lovingly detailed tortures of the Ministry of Love, a fascination he would not have enjoyed having named. Orwell's biographer Michael Shelden calls the essay a brilliant criticism of the whole concept of power worship, and he is right, but a demolition of a concept is not a fair trial of a man, and the essay knows it and does not care. Orwell chose that risk with his eyes open, and you should read him knowing he chose it.

Count two is that the world has spent the last decade deciding Burnham was right after all, and the deciding has come from a direction Orwell would have recognized. The managerial revolution has had a revival on the American right. Samuel Francis, whose posthumous Leviathan and Its Enemies is essentially Burnham applied to the postwar United States, made the managerial elite the villain of a whole political tendency, and the tendency now has its own writers. N. S. Lyons, in a long twenty twenty-three essay called The China Convergence, argues that the American and Chinese systems are converging on the same form, a hegemonic, self-reinforcing system of overlapping managerial elite interests, hard in Beijing, soft in Washington, and builds the argument from The Managerial Revolution outward. Read a certain way, this is Burnham vindicated: the structure Orwell conceded was true has become the thing everyone can see, and the forecast Orwell refused has come in under another name.

I do not think it holds, and the best reason it does not comes from the left, from Branko Milanovic, who marked the book's eightieth anniversary by re-reading it as an economist. Milanovic gives Burnham full credit for the structural move, grounding both capitalist and managerial society in who actually controls production, and then points out that on every predictive claim the book is simply wrong: capitalism did not collapse into managerialism, it won, globally, in nineteen eighty-nine; the three-bloc world never arrived; and even China, the managerial regime's supposed proof case, gets most of its value and employment from a private sector that the state constrains but did not build. His verdict on the American revival is blunt: the dominant class here still owns its property, defends it, and controls the government, which is what a capitalist class does, whatever its employees' job titles. The managers Burnham saw rising are, in Milanovic's reading, exactly where episode seven of this shelf left them: better paid than the workers, more comfortable, and not in command.

And the revival has Burnham's lean. It finds the managerial regime everywhere, describes it as total, treats its consolidation as the thing that is happening and therefore the thing that will continue. Lyons opens with an Orwell epigraph, the one about the constant struggle to see what is in front of one's nose, from the essay on language. He does not engage the Orwell essay about himself. It would have been the harder reading.

Chapter Six: The Verdict and the Dose

What is Second Thoughts on James Burnham, then, and how much of it should you take? It is the best short instrument I know for reading a forecaster, and it is short: an hour's reading, free, in print everywhere. Read it whole, once, and then go back over the closing pages with a pencil, because that is where the author turns the instrument on himself without saying so, and where this episode found its conclusion. Do not read it as the man who was right about Burnham. He caught Burnham's lean and stayed wrong about Burnham's world for forty-five years, and the reason his wrong answer eventually came good is the reason the essay is worth your hour.

The dose is diagnostic and it is portable. This week, find one forecast you are living by, a projection in a grant, a trajectory a consultant showed the board, a colleague's confident read of where the department is going, and run the ledger on it. Not the argument, the ledger. When were the last three times this source called a direction, and which way did the misses lean? If they scatter, you have an ordinary forecaster working a hard problem, and you can argue the model. If they lean, stop arguing the model, because you have found something the model cannot tell you: what its author wants, or, more often, what he is afraid of. And then the harder half, which the essay demonstrates rather than states. Ask what mechanism the forecast has. A forecast with a mechanism can be wrong for a long time and still be a forecast. A forecast with only momentum is not a prediction at all; it is a description of the present with a date stamped on it, and the person offering it has arranged to never be told he was wrong.

The question to hold onto is the one Orwell did not quite ask, because he was too busy being right. Where, in your own work, are you predicting a continuation of the thing that is happening, and which power, exactly, does the continuation flatter? The ledger works on the person keeping it. That is the part of the instrument he left out of the instructions.

Next time, the shelf returns to Graeber, and the jobs bureaucracy actually generates, in Bullshit Jobs. Thanks for listening.

item.title: The Utopia of Rules (Graeber): why deregulation makes more paperwork
item.description: David Graeber's 2015 essay collection on bureaucracy, structural violence, and the death of the future – why deregulation always produces more paperwork, why rules feel like a relief to the people who don't have to interpret anyone, and what a Batman movie has to do with any of it.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: A Form for Every Signature

An anthropologist's mother had a stroke. What followed was not the medical crisis but the paperwork that trailed it: a power of attorney that needed signing while she could still sign it, a bank that wanted one notarized form, a nursing home that wanted a different one, a second bank employee who contradicted the first, days lost to phone trees and waiting rooms and photocopies of photocopies, none of it moving the actual crisis forward by an inch. His mother died a few weeks later, the paperwork still not fully resolved. Afterward he found himself asking his friends a plain question, the kind that sounds naive until you realize nobody has a good answer to it: is this ordinary life, for most people, most of the time? Running around feeling like an idiot all day?

The anthropologist was David Graeber, and the book that grew out of that question, published in 2015, is called The Utopia of Rules: On Technology, Stupidity, and the Secret Joys of Bureaucracy. He taught at the London School of Economics, had already written a sprawling anthropological history called Debt: The First 5,000 Years, and by the time this book came out he was better known to the public for something that happened outside a university altogether: in the late summer of 2011 he sat in on the planning meetings that became Occupy Wall Street, and is often credited, though he insisted the credit belonged to a chain of people editing each other's phrases, with the line "we are the 99 percent." That biography matters here for a specific reason. Every book this season has come from someone who watched an organization from a chair inside it: Jackall interviewing managers, Whyte inside a corporation, Freeman inside a movement she helped build. Graeber's vantage is different. He is watching bureaucracy from the position of someone who spent a fall discovering that even grief has a required form, and who then spent a summer helping several thousand strangers build a plaza-sized structure with no chain of command at all. He has seen both ends of the same question this season keeps circling: what a rule is actually for, and who it is actually protecting.

Chapter Two: The Iron Law

Here is the puzzle Graeber opens the book with, and it needs stating before any of his answers, because both the political left and the political right think they already know the answer and they think it's the opposite answer. The story the right tells is that markets are lean and bureaucracies are bloated, so every deregulation, every privatization, every push to "run government like a business" should shrink the paperwork. The story the left tells, less often out loud, assumes something similar in reverse: that the state is where the forms live, and market actors are comparatively free of them. Graeber spent the book's introduction pointing out that neither story survives contact with an actual filing cabinet. He watched, across four decades of American and European policy, market reform after market reform promise to cut red tape, and watched the total volume of regulation, paperwork, and administrative staff rise anyway, almost every time, on both sides of every reform. He named it, half as a joke and half as a serious sociological claim, the iron law of liberalism: an attempt to reduce bureaucracy through market mechanisms will reliably produce more bureaucracy, not less, because someone still has to write the contracts, audit the compliance, credential the providers, and enforce the boundary between the newly private thing and everything it used to be answerable to.

The season has already met this law without a name for it. Davies's audit society, three episodes and a companion piece into this run, was built entirely from sinks that private markets generate to absorb their own liability, each one a new office nobody voted for. Whyte's Organization Man worked inside a corporation that had, by the 1950s, already grown its own internal civil service, complete with personality tests and a training pipeline, decades before anyone called that neoliberal. What Graeber adds is the claim that this was never an accident or a failure of implementation, the thing free-market advocates always say about the last round of deregulation before proposing another one. It is what happens, structurally, every time, because the boundary between "market" and "bureaucracy" was never where either side of the argument thought it was. Total bureaucratization, his name for where four decades of that iron law lands an economy, does not describe a state that grew too big. It describes a species of institution, public or private, that keeps generating the same kind of form-filling, box-checking, credential-checking activity regardless of which sign is on the building, because that activity is doing something for somebody, and the something is not efficiency.

Chapter Three: Interpretive Labor

What, then, is the form-filling actually doing. Graeber's answer runs through the book's first long essay, "Dead Zones of the Imagination," and it starts from an observation blunt enough to sound almost too simple: rules only work, in the end, because somebody can call the police. Not every form, not every day, not for most people who fill them out. But the whole apparatus, the notarized signature, the bank's insistence on its own version of the paperwork over the nursing home's version, rests on a chain that terminates, if you refuse for long enough, in someone with a badge and the legal standing to make you comply. Graeber calls this structural violence, and he is careful about the word: not that a teller might hit you, but that a system built on the threat of force does not need to make the threat explicit to organize behavior around it. It only needs everyone to understand, correctly, where the chain ends.

What structural violence buys the person at the top of that chain is the thing Graeber calls, running against the discipline's grain, structural stupidity. Rules are what you fall back on when you can no longer be bothered to actually understand the person standing in front of you, and you can only get away with not bothering when you hold enough power over them that their understanding you, not yours of them, is what the situation requires. Picture the bank employee and the anthropologist's dying mother again: the employee did not need to grasp why the family's situation didn't fit the form, because the family, not the bank, was the one who would pay for the mismatch. Graeber's term for that asymmetry is interpretive labor, and Graeber traces it furthest through a feminist literature on who does the emotional work of understanding whom in an unequal relationship: the employee who has to read the boss's moods, not the reverse; the customer who has to translate her own crisis into the bank's categories, not the reverse. He calls the abridgment of that work, when someone with power simply declines to do any interpreting at all, a kind of institutionalized laziness, and the phrase is exact rather than cute. The powerless end up doing most of the actual labor a bureaucracy generates and also most of the mental labor of understanding it, and the two kinds of labor are the same asymmetry wearing different clothes.

This recasts something the last episode left as an individual's problem. Peter and Hull's escape hatch, creative incompetence, works because the mechanism it exploits is a promotion committee's own selection error, a mistake a single badly parked car can correct. Graeber's structural stupidity is not a selection error. Nobody is misjudging anybody. The bank employee reads the form correctly and processes it correctly; the family is simply the party required to do the two-way work of interpretation for both of them, because the family is the party with less power in the room. There is no badly parked car for that. It is not a bug in how bureaucracy selects people. It is the thing bureaucracy is for.

Chapter Four: Where the Flying Cars Went

Graeber's second essay asks a stranger question, and it takes a moment to see why it belongs in the same book: whatever happened to the future. Children's magazines from the middle of the last century promised flying cars, moon colonies, robots doing the dishes, and by any straight-line extrapolation from the Apollo program's engineering pace, quite a lot of that should have arrived. It did not, and Graeber's explanation is not that the science failed. It is that somewhere around the 1970s, capital stopped funding what he calls poetic technologies, engineering projects aimed at making an impossible fantasy real, in favor of what he calls bureaucratic technologies, projects for organizing, monitoring, and disciplining the people who already exist. A moon landing is a poetic technology: absurd, expensive, aimed at nothing except the fantasy itself, requiring an administrative apparatus in service of the fantasy rather than the other way around. A logistics platform that tracks a delivery driver's every bathroom break is a bureaucratic technology, aimed entirely inward, and it is where the money actually went.

The essay's title calls this the declining rate of profit, a wink at the Marxist debate it is picking a fight with, and Graeber's specific claim is that the shift was not a natural maturing of capitalism but a political choice, made by people who had watched what engineering ambition on the Apollo program's scale had also produced along the way: organized, well-paid, self-confident technical labor, the very workforce a nervous owning class spent the 1970s and 1980s learning to fear. Here the season's earlier reading of managerial capture pays off in a way this book did not plan for but earns anyway. Burnham argued that ownership was migrating out of the hands of individual capitalists into the hands of the people who actually ran the machinery, and predicted that this migration itself would be the future of power. Graeber's essay describes what the managers who inherited that migration actually did with it once they arrived: not build the future Burnham's managers were supposed to command, but redirect the whole apparatus toward administering the present more tightly. The managerial revolution won. It simply chose spreadsheets over spaceships.

Chapter Five: The Fear of Play

The book's title essay asks the question its title promises, and answers it by way of a distinction that sounds almost too playful for the argument it is carrying: the difference between a game and play. A game, in the narrow technical sense Graeber uses, is bounded by fixed rules that hold constant no matter what happens inside them; chess does not stop being chess because one player is having a bad day. Play, in his sense, is what a small child does with a stick that is a sword and then a horse and then a telephone inside the same five minutes, improvisation with no fixed rule at all, meaning generated fresh in the moment rather than checked against a rulebook written in advance. Bureaucracy, Graeber argues, is what a society builds when it has decided that play, in that sense, is dangerous, and would rather have Calvinball's opposite: an environment where the rules are fixed, known in advance, and do not require you to read anybody's intentions to know what happens next.

The essay's real claim lands here, and it is a strange one to hear from a professed anarchist: bureaucracy is not merely tolerated, it is loved, because it offers a version of fairness that asks nothing of you except correct paperwork. A rule-bound system cannot be charmed, cannot play favorites in the room, cannot require you to correctly read a stranger's mood the way an informal, personality-driven system can. Max Weber called this the iron cage and meant it mostly as an indictment; Graeber's addition is that the cage is also, for the person locking themselves inside it, a relief, because the alternative to the cage is not freedom, it is exposure, and exposure is what the interpretive labor of chapter three describes from the other side. Total bureaucratization does not spread because everyone hates it. It spreads because everyone with less power than the person across the counter has already learned what it costs to be judged by someone's unstructured, personal, unaccountable read of them, and a form, however maddening, cannot look at you funny.

Chapter Six: What the Cape Cannot Imagine

The book's strangest chapter is not really a chapter, it is an appendix, built out of a piece Graeber published in October 2012 under the title "Super Position," about, of all things, Christopher Nolan's Batman film The Dark Knight Rises. Read the appendix as a punchline and it is a bad joke; read it as the place the whole book has been walking toward and it is the delayed thesis this season keeps training you to expect. Graeber's move is to separate two things every modern state pretends are the same thing: constituted power, the rules already on the books, backed by the badge at the end of the chain from chapter three, and constituent power, the capacity to make new rules from nothing, the thing that had to happen, by definition illegally, before any constitution existed for anyone to follow. Every government's legitimacy runs back to an act its own laws would now call a crime. Most political imagination since has worked hard to keep that fact out of view.

Superhero films, Graeber argues, are where American culture keeps its residual memory that constituent power exists at all, and they can only imagine it wearing one costume: solitary, violent, and enormously wealthy, a billionaire in armor deciding unilaterally what the city needs, because that is the only version of world-remaking power the genre's imagination has been trained to hold. What broke The Dark Knight Rises for Graeber was not a plot hole. It was that the film was written and largely shot before Occupy happened, and Occupy was, for a few months, actual constituent power showing up in public, nonviolent, leaderless, without a cape or a wristband anywhere in sight, the kind of thing the film's entire moral universe had no shelf for. Once it appeared, Graeber wrote, the fictional universe built to make Batman's methods look inevitable "shriveled into incoherence," a fourteen-word verdict from a man who had spent the same season taking minutes in the actual meetings where several thousand strangers built something Nolan's script had insisted only a billionaire in a cave could build.

Set this beside chapter three and the shape of the whole book snaps into focus at once. Structural violence is constituted power working exactly as designed: the badge at the end of the chain, asking nothing of you but your paperwork. Structural stupidity is what it feels like to live inside that chain without the standing to rewrite it. And the imagination that could rewrite it, Graeber's real subject in every essay in this book, has been starved on both ends: bureaucracy trains you not to need it day to day, and popular culture trains you to believe, when you do reach for it, that only an armored billionaire is allowed to hold it.

Chapter Seven: The Verdict and the Dose

The book's own reception gave it the fight its scope invites. Bart Zantvoort, reviewing it for the Marx and Philosophy Review of Books, credited Graeber with fascinating material and a real synthesis of violence, technological stagnation, and bureaucratic psychology into one argument, then pushed back hard on the evidence underneath it: claims about rising paperwork and lengthening working hours arrive, across long stretches of the book, without the data to back them, and the third essay in particular tries to do too much at once, reaching for theories of value and the state without landing any of them cleanly. He worried, in terms sharp enough to quote fairly, that the book sometimes blurs the line between social theory and political pamphleteering. NPR's Tomas Hachard, reviewing it the same spring, liked where the arguments eventually arrived but called the route "serpentine," and singled out the flying cars essay as the place he stopped being sure Graeber was being entirely serious, a book blaming the absence of anti-gravity shoes on bureaucracy being, on its face, a strange thing to ask a reader to take at face value.

Both objections are fair, and neither one touches the claim the book rests on, which this season is now in a good position to test against everything that came before it. Every prior book asked where an organization's competence or power went: into paperwork that multiplied on its own arithmetic, into an apparatus that outlived the cause it was built to serve, into an elite too informal to be named, into a rung a good employee could climb past without ever being wrong about anything. Graeber asks a different, prior question: why does any of that machinery hold together at all, session after session, decade after decade, without anyone at the bottom of it organizing to take it apart. His answer is that it holds together because it does not have to earn your understanding. It only has to have, somewhere down the chain, the standing to make you supply the understanding yourself, and a culture that has agreed the only people allowed to remake the rules from scratch are wearing a cape or a title deed.

The dose here is not despair, whatever the case against total bureaucratization might suggest. It is diagnostic, and cheap to administer: find, this week, one moment where you did the interpretive labor in a relationship with unequal power, translating yourself into somebody else's form rather than the reverse, and separately one where a rule stood in for a decision because the alternative would have required someone to actually look at you. Those two moments, named out loud, are most of Graeber's argument compressed into an afternoon. The bigger question, the one to leave with, is the one the Batman appendix leaves sitting in the room: when was the last time you saw an ordinary group of people build a working rule from nothing, in public, without asking anyone's permission first, and what would it take to see it as the same kind of event this book insists it is, rather than filing it, as bureaucracies are so very good at teaching you to do, under something too disorganized to matter.

Next time, the shelf turns from bureaucracy's rules to the jobs bureaucracy actually generates, in Graeber's Bullshit Jobs. Thanks for listening.

item.title: The Peter Principle: promotion to incompetence, and the data that proved it
item.description: Laurence Peter and Raymond Hull's 1969 satire on the last promotion everyone eventually gets – hierarchiology's mock science, the sales-floor data that later proved the joke true, and the one individual-level antidote the book actually offers.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Nurse Who Ran the Ward

Think of the best nurse you have ever watched work a ward. Fast without being rushed, the kind of competence that reads as calm because nothing is ever a crisis by the time she reaches it. Eighteen months later she is the nursing supervisor, and the ward is worse. Not because she stopped caring, and not because anyone lied about her file. The schedule she builds does not survive contact with a bad flu week. The staff meetings run long and settle nothing. She is doing, with total sincerity and her full former competence, a job that does not reward the thing she was competent at. Swap the ward for a sales floor, a classroom, a fire hall, an engineering team, and the story does not change shape. The best individual performer becomes the department's weakest manager, on schedule, almost every time, and everyone who has worked inside an organization for more than a few years has watched it happen at least once without being able to say exactly why. This series has spent thirteen episodes asking where the competence of an organization actually goes – Parkinson found it drowned under paperwork that multiplied by its own arithmetic regardless of the work available; Michels found it converted into apparatus, the party's radicalism migrating into a formula recited at congresses while the practice protected the treasury; last episode found it denied an address altogether, dissolved into a friendship network that could not even be named by the people it governed. Those were all organizational stories – something happening to the institution as a whole. Tonight's book asks the same question one level down, about a single career, and answers it with a mechanism so mechanical that once you have heard it you cannot stop finding it. It was published as a joke. It has since been run through a hiring dataset and a physics simulation, and the joke came back confirmed.

Chapter Two: A Schoolteacher's Fieldwork

The man who noticed this first was not a management consultant. Laurence Peter started teaching in Vancouver in nineteen forty-one and spent the next two decades inside one of the most legible hierarchies available for the purpose, a public school system, watching the specific way it broke its best people. A gifted classroom teacher gets promoted to vice-principal, a job made of budgets, discipline hearings, and parent complaints, none of which the gift had anything to do with; a natural administrator is made district superintendent, where the job is politics, a different animal again. Peter earned a doctorate at Washington State in nineteen sixty-three and three years later moved to the University of Southern California, where he ran a centre for what the job title called prescriptive teaching and coordinated programs for children the system had already found difficult to place, which meant his working life was now two systems deep in the same observation: competence at one rung predicts almost nothing about the rung above it, and the promotion happens anyway, because promotion is how a hierarchy says thank you, and a hierarchy has no other language for gratitude. He needed a co-writer, and he found one in a theatre lobby. Raymond Hull, a Vancouver playwright, was complaining to Peter during an intermission about a bad play that had somehow made it to the stage, and Peter explained the mechanism to him on the spot, the same one he had been watching for twenty years: every employee tends to rise to his level of incompetence. It is the kind of sentence a playwright recognizes as a good line before he recognizes it as a theory, and Hull did both, and the two of them spent the rest of the decade trying to sell it. Fourteen publishers said no over roughly two years. The idea that finally worked was to stop asking whether the book was serious. Hull wrote almost the entire manuscript, in the voice of a mock scholar founding a new discipline he calls hierarchiology, complete with a case-study apparatus, a glossary, and footnotes citing evidence the reader is clearly not meant to check – a deadpan academic costume worn over a rigorous piece of observation, the arrangement that got it past fourteen editors who could not tell whether they were buying a joke or a diagnosis. William Morrow published it in nineteen sixty-nine. It was an immediate bestseller, and both men had, without quite planning to, built the costume as a delivery mechanism, because a diagnosis this uncomfortable goes down easier wearing a lab coat that is visibly a prop.

Chapter Three: The Mechanism, Run to Its End

Strip the costume off and the argument is small enough to fit in one sentence, which is why it survived the joke: in a hierarchy, every member tends to rise to the level at which they are no longer competent, and there they remain, because there is no longer anything at that level to see and reward. Follow the logic all the way through, because the ending is the part people usually skip. Selection for promotion runs entirely on performance in the current job – it has to, since performance in a job nobody has done yet cannot be observed – so a person keeps climbing exactly as long as they keep being good at whatever they are currently doing. Sooner or later the climb reaches a job whose demands are different enough from the last one that the very skill that earned the promotion stops applying: the best technician need not have the temperament to manage technicians; the best manager may lack the political stomach to manage managers. At that rung, performance drops, and the mechanism that has been pulling this person upward for years simply has nothing left to grab. No further promotion follows an incompetent performance – organizations promote strength, not weakness – and demotion is rare enough in most institutions to round to never, because admitting the promotion was a mistake costs the person who made it more than leaving the mistake in place costs everyone else. The climb does not overshoot and correct. It overshoots by exactly one level and stops there, permanently, and Peter and Hull gave that terminal rung a name with the flat precision of an engineering term: final placement. Run this rule across every member of an organization for long enough and Peter's Corollary follows without needing a single new assumption – every post, eventually, tends to be filled by someone who has reached that state with respect to that post. That is no claim that most people are incompetent at their jobs on day one.
